t: Overflow a stack buffer and redirect execution to win() (ret2win)
desc: On a non-PIE 64-bit lab binary with a gets()/read() into a fixed buffer, overflow the saved return address so control jumps to a win()/print_flag() function. Watch 16-byte stack alignment.
check: Running your exploit makes the program print the flag via win()
You can state the exact byte offset from buffer start to the saved return address
Your payload includes a ret padding gadget when needed to fix movaps stack alignment

t: Find the exact saved-RIP offset with a cyclic De Bruijn pattern
desc: Feed a pwntools cyclic() pattern into a crashing binary, read the faulting address in GDB/core, and use cyclic_find() to compute the precise overflow offset to the return address.
check: You derive the offset to saved RIP in a single crash, not by brute force
cyclic_find on the leaked value matches the offset you then use successfully
Your notes explain why a 4-byte pattern slice maps to a unique position

t: Master the x86-64 System V integer calling convention
desc: Learn how the first six integer/pointer arguments and the return value are passed in registers, and why this matters for building ROP calls to functions like system().
check: Which registers hold the first six integer arguments, in order?
Where is a function's integer return value placed, and who cleans the stack?
Why does a ret2libc call to system("/bin/sh") need a pop rdi; ret gadget?
a: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9; further args go on the stack right-to-left.
In rax. Under SysV the caller cleans up stack-passed args (callee-cleanup is not used).
Because the "/bin/sh" pointer must be in rdi before the call, so you load rdi via the gadget.

t: Leak libc with puts(GOT), then ret2libc to spawn a shell
desc: On a dynamically linked NX binary, build a ROP chain that calls puts on puts@GOT to leak its runtime address, returns to main, computes libc base, then calls system("/bin/sh").
check: Your exploit prints a shell even though libc is ASLR-randomized
The leaked puts address minus the known libc offset gives a page-aligned base
You explain why returning to main (or _start) lets you send a second-stage payload

t: Build a ROP chain to call execve("/bin/sh",0,0) in a static binary
desc: With no libc import to abuse, use a gadget finder (ROPgadget/ropper) on a statically linked binary to set rax=59, rdi->"/bin/sh", rsi=rdx=0, then syscall.
check: Your chain runs execve and drops to a shell with NX enabled
You locate or write the "/bin/sh" string into writable memory and point rdi at it
You can name every register the execve syscall reads and the syscall number

t: Understand stack canaries and the ways they are bypassed
desc: Learn how the compiler places and checks a stack canary, where the value comes from, and the main strategies attackers use to defeat it.
check: Where is the canary stored relative to local buffers and the saved return address, and when is it checked?
Why does the canary's least-significant byte conventionally being 0x00 both help and hinder attackers?
Name two ways to exploit a vulnerable function without ever corrupting the canary.
a: Between the local buffers and saved RBP/RIP; it is validated just before ret, calling __stack_chk_fail on mismatch.
The null byte stops string functions from leaking it, but also terminates attacker strings/leaks at that byte.
Leak the canary first then include it in the payload; or overwrite non-return targets (GOT, func pointers) without passing the canary.

t: Leak a stack canary with a format string, then overflow to win()
desc: Use a printf format-string bug to leak the canary off the stack with a positional %p, then in a second input overflow the buffer, replace the canary with the leaked value, and overwrite RIP with win().
check: The binary reaches win() without triggering __stack_chk_fail
The value you leak ends in a null byte, confirming it is the canary
You identify the correct %N$p index that lands on the canary slot

t: Use a format-string bug to leak stack values and find your input offset
desc: Send a controlled printf format like AAAA.%p.%p.%p... (or %N$p) to a vulnerable program and determine which positional argument index corresponds to your own input on the stack.
check: You print 0x41414141 (or 0x4141414141414141) proving you found your input's index
You can read an arbitrary stack slot with a single %N$p
You note the difference in argument consumption between 32-bit and 64-bit here

t: Overwrite a GOT entry with a format-string %n write
desc: On a Partial-RELRO binary, use %n/%hn with width specifiers to write the address of win() (or system) over a GOT entry such as printf/exit, so the next call redirects.
check: Calling the hijacked function transfers control to your target
You split the write into two %hn halves to avoid printing billions of bytes
You confirm Full RELRO would have blocked this and explain why

t: Understand GOT/PLT lazy binding and why GOT overwrites work
desc: Learn how calls to shared-library functions route through the PLT and GOT, how the dynamic linker resolves them on first use, and what RELRO changes.
check: Walk through what happens the first time a program calls puts@plt versus later calls.
Why does overwriting a GOT entry hijack control flow on the next call?
How do Partial RELRO and Full RELRO each change the exploitability of the GOT?
a: First call goes PLT -> GOT -> dynamic resolver, which writes the real address into the GOT; later calls jump straight to it via the GOT.
Because the PLT reads the target from the GOT each call, so a forged GOT entry sends the call to attacker-chosen code.
Partial RELRO leaves the GOT writable (overwrite works); Full RELRO resolves at load and makes the GOT read-only, blocking it.

t: Use ret2csu to control rdx when gadgets are scarce
desc: Leverage the __libc_csu_init universal gadgets to populate rdx/rsi/rdi and call a function through a pointer, enabling calls that need a third argument in a gadget-poor binary.
check: Your chain sets rdx to a chosen value and makes a controlled call
You correctly account for the pop rbx/rbp/r12-r15 sequence and the loop's add rbx,1 compare
You explain why ret2csu is useful when no clean pop rdx; ret gadget exists

t: Defeat PIE with a partial return-address overwrite
desc: On a PIE binary where you can overwrite only the low bytes of the saved return address, redirect execution to a nearby function/gadget within the same page without knowing the full base.
check: You redirect control by rewriting only 1-2 low bytes of saved RIP
Your target lies within the bytes that are not randomized by page alignment
You explain why the lowest 12 bits (3 hex nibbles) are fixed under 4KB-page ASLR

t: Understand what ASLR randomizes and how one leak defeats it
desc: Learn which memory regions ASLR randomizes, what it leaves fixed, and why leaking a single pointer into a module collapses the whole randomization for that module.
check: Which regions does ASLR randomize, and what stays at a fixed address in a non-PIE binary?
If you leak one libc function's runtime address, how do you compute the base of libc?
Why does page alignment mean the low 12 bits of an address are not secret?
a: Stack, heap, mmap/shared libraries, and the PIE base; a non-PIE executable's own image stays at its fixed link address.
Subtract that function's known file offset within libc from the leaked address to get the page-aligned base.
mmap/segment bases are page-aligned (4KB), so the bottom 12 bits come from the fixed in-file offset, not randomization.

t: Poison a tcache fd pointer to get an arbitrary malloc chunk
desc: On a glibc ~2.31 heap challenge with a use-after-free or overflow, corrupt a freed tcache chunk's fd pointer so a subsequent malloc returns an attacker-chosen address (e.g. over a function pointer or __free_hook).
check: A later malloc returns a pointer to your target address
You account for the tcache count field so the allocator hands back your chunk
You explain how this differs on glibc 2.32+ due to safe-linking pointer mangling

t: Understand the glibc tcache: binning, reuse, and double-free checks
desc: Learn how per-thread tcache bins store freed chunks, how allocation reuses them, and what double-free protection was added across glibc versions.
check: How are freed chunks organized in the tcache and in what order are they handed back?
What is the default maximum number of chunks per tcache bin, and what selects a bin?
What check did glibc 2.29 add against tcache double-free, and how does safe-linking (2.32) differ?
a: In per-thread singly linked LIFO bins keyed by request size; malloc pops the most recently freed chunk first.
Seven chunks per bin by default (tcache_count), with one bin per small size class.
2.29 added a per-chunk key field checked on free to catch double-frees; 2.32 added safe-linking, XOR-mangling fd pointers with the chunk's address.

t: Understand NX/DEP and why return-oriented programming exists
desc: Learn how the no-execute bit stops classic shellcode injection and why reusing existing executable code (ROP) is the standard response, contrasted with ret2shellcode.
check: What does the NX bit enforce on the stack and heap, and what attack does it stop?
Why can a ROP chain still run arbitrary logic despite W^X?
In what situation is ret2shellcode viable instead of ROP?
a: It marks data pages (stack/heap) non-executable, so injected shellcode on them faults instead of running.
ROP chains short existing instruction sequences ending in ret, performing computation using only already-executable code.
When a region is both writable and executable (NX disabled or an RWX mapping), you can jump to injected shellcode directly.

t: Inject and run shellcode on a stack with NX disabled
desc: Compile a lab binary with an executable stack (or use one provided), generate shellcode with pwntools shellcraft, place it in the buffer, and overwrite RIP to jump to it.
check: The program executes your shellcode and gives a shell
You jump to the correct in-memory address of your shellcode (leak or jmp rsp style)
You confirm the stack is executable (checksec / readelf GNU_STACK)

t: Pop a shell with a one_gadget given a libc leak
desc: Run the one_gadget tool against the target libc, pick a magic gadget, satisfy its register/stack constraints, and jump to libc_base + gadget offset to exec /bin/sh in a single hop.
check: Jumping to your chosen one_gadget yields a shell
You verified the gadget's constraints (e.g. rsi/rdx NULL) actually hold at jump time
You can explain why one_gadget is shorter than a full system("/bin/sh") chain

t: Understand integer bugs that turn into buffer overflows
desc: Learn how signed/unsigned confusion and integer truncation/overflow let a length check pass while a copy writes far more than the buffer holds.
check: How can a negative signed length defeat a bounds check and still cause a huge memcpy?
What happens when a 16-bit length counter wraps while the real data is larger?
Why is comparing a signed length against a buffer size with < dangerous?
a: A negative int passes an "if (len < size)" check but is reinterpreted as a huge size_t by memcpy, copying far too much.
The counter wraps to a small value so the check passes, yet the loop/copy still processes the full oversized input.
An attacker-controlled negative value is < size as signed but becomes enormous once widened to unsigned for the copy.

t: Pivot the stack with leave;ret to run a longer ROP chain
desc: When the overflow only gives you a few bytes past RIP, use a leave;ret or pop rsp gadget to move rsp into a buffer you fully control (e.g. a bss/read area) and continue a larger chain there.
check: Execution continues into your relocated chain and reaches the final goal
rsp lands exactly at the start of your staged chain after the pivot
You explain how leave (mov rsp,rbp; pop rbp) enables the pivot when you control saved RBP

t: Read an x86-64 function prologue and epilogue in disassembly
desc: Learn to recognize how a compiled function sets up and tears down its stack frame so you can find function boundaries and locals in raw disassembly.
check: What do push rbp; mov rbp, rsp; sub rsp, N accomplish at a function's start?
What does the leave instruction do, and how does it relate to the prologue?
Given mov rbp,rsp then an access to [rbp-0x8], where does that local live relative to the frame?
a: They save the caller's frame pointer, set rbp to the new frame base, and reserve N bytes for locals.
leave does mov rsp, rbp; pop rbp, undoing the prologue's frame setup just before ret.
In the current frame's local area, 8 bytes below the saved frame-pointer base (inside the sub rsp region).

t: Triage an unknown binary with file, strings, nm, and checksec
desc: Run file, strings (ASCII and -el for wide), nm/readelf -s, and checksec on a mystery binary to classify it, spot interesting strings/symbols, and note protections before deep analysis.
check: You report architecture, linkage (static/dynamic), and whether symbols are stripped
You surface at least one interesting string or symbol relevant to the challenge
You list the active mitigations (NX, PIE, RELRO, canary) from checksec

t: Decompile a crackme's password check in Ghidra and recover the input
desc: Load a simple crackme into Ghidra, find the comparison in the decompiled password routine, and determine the exact string/number that makes it accept.
check: You enter a value the binary accepts as correct
You can point to the decompiled line that performs the accept/reject decision
You renamed the key function and variable to document your understanding

t: Break a license check by reading strcmp arguments in GDB
desc: Set a breakpoint on strcmp (or the relevant compare) in a lab binary, run it, and inspect the two arguments to read the expected secret directly at runtime.
check: You read the expected value from a register/memory at the breakpoint and use it to pass
You can explain which register held the pointer to the expected string (SysV)
You note at least one case where this fails (e.g. value computed, not compared literally)

t: Recognize a compiled C switch statement and its jump table
desc: Learn how compilers lower a dense switch into a jump table plus bounds check, and how to identify that pattern in disassembly versus a chain of comparisons.
check: What asm pattern signals a jump-table-based switch rather than if/else chains?
Why does the compiler emit a bounds check (ja/above) before the indirect jump?
When will a compiler prefer a comparison chain or a hash over a jump table?
a: A bounds compare then an indirect jump through a table, like jmp [table + index*8], with the table in .rodata.
To ensure out-of-range switch values fall to the default case instead of indexing past the table.
When case values are sparse or few, a comparison chain (or binary search) is smaller/faster than a huge table.

t: Reverse an input-transform crackme and write a Python keygen
desc: Analyze a crackme that transforms the input (e.g. XOR with a constant then add, compared to a stored buffer), invert the transform, and script a generator that outputs a valid key.
check: Your keygen produces a key the binary accepts, for the target constant
You can describe the forward transform and show your inverse is correct
The keygen works for the embedded target without brute forcing each byte

t: Detect a UPX-packed binary and unpack it
desc: Use entropy/section clues (UPX0/UPX1 sections, high entropy) to identify a packed sample, then restore the original with upx -d before analysis.
check: You confirm it is UPX-packed from section names or a tool report
upx -d yields a working, analyzable binary with readable strings/imports
You explain why packed binaries show high entropy and few readable strings

t: Tell static from dynamic linking and spot library calls in asm
desc: Learn how statically and dynamically linked binaries differ in size, imports, and call patterns, and how to recognize an external library call in disassembly.
check: How does a dynamically linked binary call a libc function at the asm level?
What differences in file size, imports, and the PLT distinguish static from dynamic linking?
Why can a stripped static binary be harder to reverse than a dynamic one?
a: Via a PLT stub, e.g. call puts@plt, which routes through the GOT to the resolved libc address.
Static binaries are larger, have no (or minimal) dynamic imports and no libc PLT; dynamic ones list shared libs and use PLT/GOT.
Its libc code is inlined and unlabeled, so you cannot rely on named imports to identify standard functions.

t: Trace a flag check with ltrace and strace
desc: Run a lab binary under ltrace and strace to watch library/syscall activity, locating where it reads input, compares, or opens the flag, to shortcut static analysis.
check: You identify the call where the comparison/decision happens from the trace
You can distinguish a libc-call observation (ltrace) from a syscall one (strace)
You note when tracing is defeated (static binary hides ltrace, anti-debug blocks it)

t: Rename functions in Ghidra to recover a stripped binary's logic
desc: Work a stripped binary in Ghidra: follow calls from main, rename functions/locals/structs as you deduce their roles, and reconstruct the algorithm until you can describe end-to-end behavior.
check: You produce a clear written description of what the program computes
At least the main logic functions and key variables are meaningfully renamed
You can trace the data path from input to the win/lose decision

t: Understand what 'stripped' means and how function boundaries are recovered
desc: Learn what information stripping removes from an ELF and how disassemblers rebuild function boundaries without a symbol table.
check: What does stripping remove, and what stays that still lets the program run?
How do tools infer function starts without symbols?
Why can .eh_frame / unwind tables help recover function boundaries?
a: It removes the symbol table and debug info (names); the dynamic symbols needed for linking and all code/relocations remain.
By prologue signatures, call/jump targets, and control-flow analysis to guess where functions begin and end.
Unwind/exception tables list per-function address ranges for stack unwinding, which doubles as a map of function extents.

t: Patch a conditional jump to bypass a check
desc: Locate the branch that decides accept/reject in a lab binary and patch it (e.g. jz to jnz, or je to an unconditional jmp/nops) so the program takes the success path regardless of input.
check: The patched binary always reports success / reveals the flag path
You flip the correct branch and the file still runs (no misaligned bytes)
You can explain the opcode change you made and why it inverts the condition

t: Understand position-independent code and RIP-relative addressing
desc: Learn why PIE/PIC code must address data relative to the instruction pointer and how that appears in disassembly, which is key when the load base is randomized.
check: Why can't PIE code hardcode absolute addresses for its own data?
What disassembly pattern loads the address of a global in PIC x86-64?
How does RIP-relative addressing interact with ASLR of the module base?
a: Because its load base is chosen at runtime, so absolute addresses would be wrong; it uses offsets from the current location instead.
lea reg, [rip + disp], which computes a global's address relative to the next instruction.
The whole module (code+data) shifts together, so RIP+offset stays valid at any randomized base.

t: Solve a crackme's input constraints with angr symbolic execution
desc: Model a crackme in angr: set the success address as the target, mark input as symbolic, run explore(find=...,avoid=...), and extract the satisfying input from the solver.
check: angr returns a concrete input that the real binary accepts
You chose sensible find/avoid addresses and symbolic input length
You can explain why path explosion or unconstrained data might make angr stall here

t: Reverse a small bytecode-VM crackme: find the dispatch loop and handlers
desc: Analyze an obfuscated crackme built as a custom VM: identify the fetch-decode-dispatch loop, map opcodes to handler routines, and reconstruct the program it interprets to recover the key.
check: You document the opcode-to-handler table and the VM's register/stack model
You can hand-trace the bytecode that validates the key
You recover an input the binary accepts based on your VM reconstruction

t: Understand common anti-debugging tricks and how they show up
desc: Learn how programs detect debuggers (ptrace self-attach, /proc checks, timing) so you can recognize and plan around them during analysis.
check: How does a single PTRACE_TRACEME call let a process detect an attached debugger?
How can rdtsc timing reveal that code is being single-stepped?
What does reading TracerPid in /proc/self/status tell a program?
a: A process can be traced by only one tracer; if it TRACEME's itself, a later debugger attach fails, signaling a debugger.
Single-stepping adds large time gaps, so a big delta between two rdtsc reads implies a debugger is stepping the code.
A non-zero TracerPid means some process is currently tracing it, i.e. a debugger is attached.

t: Defeat a ptrace anti-debug check by patching or LD_PRELOAD
desc: On a lab binary that calls ptrace(PTRACE_TRACEME) to block debugging, neutralize it by patching the call out or LD_PRELOAD-ing a stub ptrace that returns 0, then debug normally.
check: You can attach/step the binary in GDB without it bailing out
Your bypass (patch or preload) leaves program logic otherwise intact
You explain why an LD_PRELOAD ptrace stub intercepts the real libc call

t: Extract and decompile a PyInstaller-packed Python binary
desc: Use pyinstxtractor to unpack a PyInstaller executable, recover the main .pyc, fix its header if needed, and decompile with a tool like decompyle3/uncompyle6 to read the source logic.
check: You recover readable Python source for the main module
You correctly reattach the pyc magic/header so decompilation succeeds
You identify the flag-check logic in the recovered source

t: Understand endianness and two's complement in hex dumps
desc: Learn how multi-byte integers are stored little-endian on x86 and how signed values use two's complement, so you can read raw bytes correctly.
check: In a little-endian dump, how is the 32-bit value 0x12345678 laid out in memory bytes?
What signed decimal value does the byte 0xFF represent as an 8-bit two's-complement integer?
How do you negate a two's-complement integer by hand?
a: As 78 56 34 12 (least-significant byte first).
Invert all bits then add one (and the sign bit indicates negativity).

t: Reverse a custom checksum and forge an input that passes it
desc: Analyze a binary that validates input against a homemade checksum/hash loop, re-implement the algorithm, and craft an input (or collision) that satisfies the expected value.
check: Your forged input passes the binary's validation
Your standalone re-implementation reproduces the binary's checksum on test data
You can explain why the custom function is not collision-resistant

t: Understand XOR properties and why one-time-pad key reuse is fatal
desc: Learn the algebraic properties of XOR and why reusing a keystream/pad across two messages destroys secrecy.
check: What are the identity and self-inverse properties of XOR that make it usable as a cipher?
If two messages are XORed with the same keystream, what does c1 XOR c2 equal and why is that dangerous?
What three conditions make a one-time pad information-theoretically secure?
a: a XOR 0 = a, a XOR a = 0, and it is its own inverse, so p XOR k XOR k = p.
c1 XOR c2 = p1 XOR p2, cancelling the key and leaking the XOR of the two plaintexts (crib-draggable).
The key must be truly random, as long as the message, and never reused.

t: Break single-byte XOR with frequency scoring
desc: Given a hex string XORed against one unknown byte, try all 256 keys, score each candidate plaintext by English letter frequency, and pick the best to recover the message (cryptopals Set 1).
check: Your script outputs the correct plaintext and the single key byte
Your scoring function reliably ranks English text above garbage
You can explain why only 256 keys need to be tried

t: Break repeating-key XOR via keysize detection and column transposition
desc: Recover a Vigenere-style repeating-key XOR ciphertext: estimate key length using normalized Hamming distance, transpose into per-key-byte columns, then single-byte-break each column.
check: You recover the full key and plaintext
Your Hamming-distance keysize estimate matches the true key length
You explain why transposing lets you reduce the problem to single-byte XOR

t: Understand AES-ECB vs CBC and why ECB leaks structure
desc: Learn how ECB and CBC modes differ, and why ECB reveals plaintext patterns while CBC chains blocks.
check: Why do identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks under ECB?
How does CBC chain blocks, and what role does the IV play?
What visual/structural leak lets you detect ECB from ciphertext alone?
a: ECB encrypts each block independently with the same key, so equal input blocks map to equal output blocks.
Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption; the IV seeds the first block.
Repeated 16-byte ciphertext blocks appear wherever plaintext repeats (the ECB-penguin effect).

t: Decrypt an AES-ECB byte-at-a-time oracle
desc: Against an oracle that encrypts your_input || secret under ECB with a fixed key, recover the secret one byte at a time by aligning blocks and matching against a dictionary of guesses.
check: You recover the full hidden suffix from the oracle
You first confirm the mode is ECB and determine the block size from output length jumps
You explain why controlling input length isolates one unknown byte per query

t: Forge admin access with a CBC bit-flipping attack
desc: Against a token encrypted in CBC where you control part of a block, flip bytes in the preceding ciphertext block to change a chosen plaintext byte (e.g. set admin=true) in the next block.
check: The decrypted/parsed token grants admin or your target value
You correctly compute which ciphertext byte to XOR and by what delta
You explain why the block you modified becomes garbage and why that is acceptable here

t: Decrypt CBC ciphertext with a padding-oracle attack
desc: Use a server that only reveals whether PKCS#7 padding is valid to recover plaintext without the key, byte by byte, by manipulating the previous ciphertext block to force valid-padding states.
check: You recover the full plaintext using only the padding valid/invalid signal
You correctly derive the intermediate (D(C)) bytes and XOR to get plaintext
You explain why forcing padding 0x01, then 0x02 0x02, etc. reveals each byte

t: Understand PKCS#7 padding and how a padding oracle leaks plaintext
desc: Learn how PKCS#7 pads messages to the block size and why an oracle that distinguishes valid from invalid padding is enough to decrypt CBC.
check: How does PKCS#7 pad a message that is 3 bytes short of a block boundary?
In CBC, how does changing the previous ciphertext block affect the current decrypted plaintext?
Why does learning that padding is valid reveal one byte of the intermediate state?
a: It appends three bytes each equal to 0x03; a full extra block of 0x10 bytes is added if already aligned.
Plaintext = D(C_i) XOR C_{i-1}, so flipping a byte of C_{i-1} flips the same plaintext byte deterministically.
Valid 0x01 padding means D(C)[last] XOR your_byte = 0x01, so D(C)[last] = your_byte XOR 0x01.

t: Understand modular exponentiation and the discrete log problem
desc: Learn why g^x mod p is easy to compute but hard to invert, and how that asymmetry underpins Diffie-Hellman key exchange.
check: Why is computing g^x mod p fast even for huge x?
What exactly is the discrete logarithm problem that makes DH secure?
How do two parties derive the same shared secret in classic DH?
a: Square-and-multiply does it in O(log x) modular multiplications rather than x multiplications.
Given g, p, and g^x mod p, recovering x is believed computationally infeasible for well-chosen large p.
Alice sends g^a, Bob sends g^b; each raises the other's value to their own secret, both getting g^{ab} mod p.

t: Recover RSA plaintext with small e via cube root (no padding)
desc: Given textbook RSA with e=3 and a message so small that m^3 < n, recover m by taking the exact integer cube root of the ciphertext, since no modular reduction occurred.
check: You recover the plaintext by integer root extraction, not factoring n
You verify m^3 equals c exactly (no reduction wrapped around)
You explain what padding (OAEP) would have prevented this

t: Exploit RSA common-modulus with two coprime exponents
desc: Given two ciphertexts of the same message under the same modulus n but different public exponents e1,e2 with gcd=1, use the extended Euclidean algorithm to recover the plaintext.
check: You recover m from c1,c2 without factoring n
You find integers a,b with a*e1 + b*e2 = 1 and apply them correctly (handling negative exponents via inverses)
You explain why gcd(e1,e2)=1 is required

t: Factor a weak RSA modulus with Fermat's method (close primes)
desc: When p and q are close together, factor n by searching for a such that a^2 - n is a perfect square (n = a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b)), recovering p and q and then the private key.
check: You factor n into p and q for a close-prime modulus
Your search starts at ceil(sqrt(n)) and finds b quickly because the primes are near
You explain why Fermat's method fails when p and q are far apart

t: Understand why textbook RSA is malleable and how OAEP fixes it
desc: Learn how deterministic, unpadded RSA's homomorphic property enables attacks and why randomized padding like OAEP is required in practice.
check: What does multiplying two RSA ciphertexts do to the underlying plaintexts?
Why does deterministic encryption of small/known message spaces leak information?
What two things does OAEP add that break these attacks?
a: (m1^e)(m2^e) mod n = (m1*m2)^e mod n, so ciphertexts multiply to the product's ciphertext (malleable).
An attacker can just encrypt candidate messages and compare, since the same plaintext always gives the same ciphertext.
Randomness (so encryption is non-deterministic) and structured padding that makes malformed/forged ciphertexts decode to garbage and be rejected.

t: Compute an RSA private key from p, q, and e
desc: Given primes p and q and public exponent e, compute phi = (p-1)(q-1), the private exponent d = e^{-1} mod phi, and decrypt a sample ciphertext to confirm.
check: You compute d and successfully decrypt the provided ciphertext
You obtain d via modular inverse (extended Euclid), not trial division
You can state why gcd(e, phi) must be 1 for d to exist

t: Understand hash length-extension and why H(secret||msg) MACs are forgeable
desc: Learn why Merkle-Damgard hashes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) let an attacker extend a hashed message without the secret, breaking naive MAC constructions.
check: What property of Merkle-Damgard construction makes length extension possible?
Given H(secret||msg) and len(secret), what can an attacker forge without knowing the secret?
Why is HMAC not vulnerable to this attack?
a: The hash output is the full internal state, so an attacker can resume hashing from it as a new starting state.
A valid H(secret||msg||padding||attacker_data), i.e. a MAC for an extended message, by continuing from the known digest.
HMAC nests two keyed hashes (H(k2 || H(k1 || m))), so the output is not a usable intermediate state to extend.

t: Forge a MAC with a hash length-extension attack
desc: Given a token of the form MAC = H(secret || message) with known message and secret length, use a tool like hlextend/hashpump to append data and produce a valid MAC for the extended message.
check: Your forged (message', MAC') pair validates against the server
You correctly include the original glue padding before your appended data
You brute-force or are given the secret length and confirm it matters

t: Peel layered encodings (base64, hex, base32, rot13)
desc: Given a blob wrapped in several encoding layers, identify each layer by its alphabet/structure and decode iteratively until you reach the plaintext flag.
check: You recover the final plaintext flag
You correctly identify each layer (e.g. base64 padding =, hex 0-9a-f, base32 A-Z2-7)
You can explain why encoding is not encryption

t: Recover two plaintexts from AES-CTR keystream (nonce) reuse
desc: Given two ciphertexts encrypted under AES-CTR with the same key and nonce, XOR them to get p1 XOR p2 and use crib-dragging/known structure to separate the two plaintexts.
check: You recover meaningful plaintext from both messages
You use c1 XOR c2 = p1 XOR p2 and a crib to peel bytes
You explain why reusing a CTR nonce reduces it to a two-time pad

t: Distinguish a hash, a MAC, and a digital signature
desc: Learn which security properties (integrity, authenticity, non-repudiation) each primitive provides and when to use which.
check: Which of integrity and authenticity does a plain hash provide, and which does it not?
What does a MAC add over a hash, and what key model does it use?
What does a digital signature provide that a MAC cannot, and why?
a: A plain hash gives integrity against accidental change but no authenticity, since anyone can recompute it.
A MAC adds authenticity using a shared secret key, so only key holders can produce or verify it.
Non-repudiation: a signature uses a private key only the signer holds, so anyone can verify origin; a MAC's shared key means either party could have made it.

t: Recover an ECDSA private key from two signatures reusing a nonce
desc: Given two ECDSA signatures over different messages that share the same nonce k (same r value), solve for k, then recover the long-term private key d.
check: You compute the private key d and verify it reproduces both signatures
You recover k = (z1 - z2) * (s1 - s2)^{-1} mod n, then d = (s1*k - z1) * r^{-1} mod n
You explain why an identical r across two signatures proves nonce reuse

t: Understand file magic bytes and how 'file' identifies types
desc: Learn how file formats are identified by leading signature bytes rather than extensions, and why that matters in forensics.
check: What magic bytes begin a PNG, a JPEG, and a ZIP/Office file?
Why can a file named photo.jpg actually be a ZIP, and how would you tell?
How does the 'file' command decide a type without trusting the extension?
a: PNG: 89 50 4E 47 (.PNG); JPEG: FF D8 FF; ZIP/OOXML: 50 4B 03 04 (PK..).
The extension is just a label; inspecting the header bytes (e.g. PK.. for ZIP) reveals the true format.
It matches the content against libmagic's database of signature patterns at known offsets.

t: Carve embedded files out of a blob with binwalk
desc: Run binwalk on an image or firmware blob to find embedded file signatures, then extract the contained files (binwalk -e / dd at reported offsets) and inspect them.
check: You extract at least one embedded file and identify it with 'file'
You can read the offset table binwalk produced and explain each hit
You verify an extracted file opens/parses correctly

t: Find data hidden after a JPEG EOI or PNG IEND marker
desc: Inspect an image's raw bytes for content appended after the end-of-image marker (FFD9 for JPEG, IEND for PNG) and extract the trailing hidden data.
check: You locate the end marker and recover the appended bytes
You can state the end-of-image marker for the format you examined
You explain why viewers ignore data after the marker but it still rides along

t: Recover LSB-hidden data from a PNG with zsteg
desc: Run zsteg across bit planes and channel orderings of a suspicious PNG/BMP to find least-significant-bit encoded text or files, then extract the payload.
check: You recover the hidden message or file from a bit plane
You identify which channel/bit/order held the data
You can explain what 'b1,rgb,lsb,xy' style zsteg parameters mean

t: Understand LSB image steganography and its detectability
desc: Learn how data is hidden in the least significant bits of pixel values and why it is visually invisible yet statistically detectable.
check: Why does flipping the least significant bit of a pixel channel not visibly change the image?
Roughly how much data can 1-bit-per-channel LSB hide in a WxH RGB image?
What statistical signs or tools reveal LSB stego?
a: The LSB changes a channel value by at most 1 of 256 levels, below human perception.
About W*H*3 bits, i.e. W*H*3/8 bytes (minus any header/length overhead).
Unnatural LSB randomness shows up in chi-square or sample-pair analysis; tools like zsteg, stegsolve, and StegExpose flag it.

t: Extract a passphrase-protected payload with steghide
desc: Use steghide to detect and extract an embedded payload from a JPEG or WAV carrier, recovering the passphrase by wordlist (stegcracker/stegseek) if it is not given.
check: You extract the hidden file/message from the carrier
If needed, you recover the passphrase from a wordlist and document which one
You can explain which carrier formats steghide supports

t: Follow a TCP stream in Wireshark and extract a transferred file
desc: Open a PCAP, use Follow TCP Stream / Export Objects to locate a file transfer (HTTP/FTP), and reconstruct the transferred file from the captured bytes.
check: You export or reassemble the transferred file and open it
You can identify the protocol and the stream carrying the file
You verify the file's integrity (magic bytes / expected content)

t: Reconstruct data exfiltrated over DNS from a PCAP
desc: Analyze a capture where data was tunneled through DNS queries (e.g. encoded subdomain labels), extract the query names, strip the base domain, and decode the concatenated payload.
check: You reassemble and decode the exfiltrated payload
You isolate only the relevant DNS queries and preserve their order
You identify the encoding (hex/base32/base64) used in the labels

t: Understand PNG chunk structure and CRC validation
desc: Learn how a PNG is built from typed chunks with CRCs and why corrupting or fixing specific chunks breaks or restores rendering.
check: What fields make up a PNG chunk, and which chunks are mandatory?
What does the IHDR chunk store, and why can editing it change the visible image size?
What is each chunk's CRC computed over, and why might a viewer still render despite a bad CRC?
a: Each chunk has a 4-byte length, 4-byte type, data, and 4-byte CRC; IHDR, IDAT, and IEND are required.
IHDR holds width, height, bit depth, and color type; wrong dimensions crop/misrender the decoded pixels.
The CRC covers the chunk type plus data; many decoders ignore CRC mismatches, which is why tampered PNGs often still display.

t: Repair a corrupted PNG header to reveal the image
desc: Fix a broken PNG by restoring the 8-byte signature and/or correcting IHDR width/height (and CRC) using a hex editor or script until the image renders and shows the flag.
check: The repaired PNG opens and reveals the hidden content
You correctly restored the signature or IHDR dimensions
You recomputed or bypassed the IHDR CRC so decoders accept it

t: Recover deleted files from a disk image with photorec/testdisk
desc: Mount or scan a raw FAT/ext disk image, use photorec to carve deleted files by signature and testdisk to inspect the partition/filesystem, and recover the target artifact.
check: You recover the deleted file containing the flag/evidence
You can explain the difference between file-carving (photorec) and filesystem recovery (testdisk)
You note why deleted file contents often remain until overwritten

t: Understand EXIF metadata and what it can leak
desc: Learn what metadata cameras and apps embed in images and why it is a privacy and forensic goldmine.
check: Name three kinds of information EXIF can store in a photo.
How can EXIF deanonymize where or when a photo was taken?
Why does stripping EXIF matter before publishing an image?
a: GPS coordinates, timestamps, and camera/device make/model (plus software, orientation, thumbnails).
Embedded GPS tags give exact location and the DateTimeOriginal gives the capture time.
Because the file otherwise carries location, time, and device identifiers that reveal the author or subject.

t: Pull metadata and hidden info with exiftool
desc: Run exiftool on an image/document to dump all metadata, looking for GPS coordinates, comments, embedded thumbnails, or custom fields that hide the flag.
check: You surface the hidden info (coords/comment/custom tag) from the metadata
You can map GPS EXIF fields to an actual location if present
You check for an embedded thumbnail that may differ from the main image

t: Reveal a spectrogram-hidden message in audio
desc: Open an audio file in Audacity or Sonic Visualiser, switch to spectrogram view, and adjust the frequency/scale to read text or an image drawn into the frequency domain.
check: You read the hidden message from the spectrogram
You adjusted window size/frequency range so the content is legible
You can explain why the message is invisible in the waveform but visible in the spectrogram

t: Understand how data hides in audio (spectrogram, DTMF, LSB)
desc: Learn the common audio stego techniques so you know what to check and with which view/tool.
check: How does spectrogram stego differ from LSB-in-samples stego?
What is DTMF and how would you decode digits hidden as tones?
Why is the waveform view usually useless for spotting spectrogram stego?
a: Spectrogram stego paints content in the frequency/time image; LSB stego alters the low bits of each PCM sample value.
DTMF encodes each key as a pair of simultaneous tones; a DTMF decoder (or matching the two frequencies) recovers the digit.
The hidden shape only emerges when amplitude is mapped across frequency bins, which the time-domain waveform does not show.

t: Analyze a memory dump with Volatility to find a rogue process
desc: Use Volatility on a RAM image: identify the OS/profile, list processes (pslist/psscan), spot a suspicious one, and dump its memory or extract strings/artifacts tying it to the incident.
check: You identify the malicious/suspicious process and justify why
You extract an artifact (command line, dumped exe, strings) from it
You can explain why pslist and psscan might disagree

t: Understand the Volatility workflow: profiles, pslist vs psscan
desc: Learn how memory forensics with Volatility starts from the right symbol profile and why multiple process-listing plugins exist.
check: Why must you select the correct profile/symbol table before most plugins work?
How does pslist enumerate processes, and what can hide from it?
How does psscan find processes differently, and what does a pslist/psscan mismatch suggest?
a: Plugins need the OS's kernel structure layouts to parse the dump; the wrong profile misreads memory.
pslist walks the active EPROCESS doubly linked list, so a process unlinked by a rootkit can be hidden from it.
psscan scans physical memory for EPROCESS pool signatures, finding hidden or exited processes; a mismatch hints at unlinking/rootkit activity.

t: Recover a flag from a .git directory and its history
desc: Given a repository or recovered .git folder, inspect the log, reflog, dangling objects (git fsck), and old commits/stashes to recover a secret that was committed and later removed.
check: You recover the removed secret from history, reflog, or a dangling object
You can show the commit or object where it lived
You explain why 'deleting' a file in a later commit does not remove it from history

t: Extract the payload from a malicious Office macro
desc: Use oletools (olevba/oledump) on a macro-enabled Office document to extract the VBA, deobfuscate it, and recover the dropped URL/command or embedded payload (indicators of compromise).
check: You extract and deobfuscate the VBA to readable logic
You recover the IOC (URL, command, or decoded payload)
You can explain how autoexec triggers (AutoOpen/Document_Open) fire the macro

t: Understand a stego/forensics triage order
desc: Learn a sensible, cheap-first order for examining a suspicious file so you do not miss easy wins or waste time.
check: Why run strings, file, and exiftool before heavier tools?
When do you reach for binwalk versus zsteg versus steghide?
Why should early steps be non-destructive and keep the original intact?
a: They are instant and often reveal flags, embedded text, or metadata without any guessing.
binwalk for appended/embedded files, zsteg for PNG/BMP LSB bit planes, steghide for passworded JPEG/WAV payloads.
So you preserve evidence and can re-run different approaches; always work on a copy and hash the original first.

t: Trace a full TCP handshake and teardown in Wireshark
desc: Capture loopback or a curl to a plain HTTP site, isolate one TCP stream, and label every segment: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, data, and the FIN/ACK or RST close. Note the sequence and ack number progression.
check: You can point to the exact three segments of the handshake and the relative seq/ack on each
You identify how the connection closed (graceful FIN exchange vs RST) and why
You show where the initial sequence numbers came from and how ack = next expected byte

t: Understand why TCP needs a three-way handshake, not two
desc: Reason through what SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK each accomplishes, what breaks with only two messages, and the role of initial sequence numbers in rejecting stale or spoofed connection attempts.
check: Why can't a two-message handshake reliably establish a connection?
What problem do randomized initial sequence numbers solve beyond ordering?
What happens if the final ACK is lost, and how does TCP recover?
a: Both sides must confirm the other received their ISN; two messages leave one side's ISN unacknowledged, so it can't safely send data.
They defuse old duplicate SYNs from prior connections and make off-path spoofing hard since the attacker must guess the ISN.
The server retransmits SYN-ACK on a timer; the client's first data segment also carries the ACK, so the connection still opens.

t: Map a destination IP to the right subnet with CIDR math
desc: Given addresses like 10.12.33.17/20, compute network address, broadcast, usable host range, and host count by hand in binary, then verify that two given hosts share a subnet.
check: For 10.12.33.17/20, what is the network address and the broadcast address?
How many usable host addresses does a /20 provide, and why minus two?
Are 10.12.15.1 and 10.12.17.1 in the same /20? Show the boundary that decides it.
a: /20 masks the first 20 bits; network is 10.12.32.0, broadcast is 10.12.47.255 (third octet 32-47).
2^(32-20)=4096 addresses, minus network and broadcast = 4094 usable.
Yes; both fall in 10.12.32.0-10.12.47.255. The /20 block boundaries step every 16 in the third octet (0,16,32,...).

t: Resolve a name manually with dig +trace from the root
desc: Run dig +trace for a domain and follow the referrals: root servers to TLD servers to authoritative servers. Then query an authoritative server directly with dig @ns and inspect A, NS, and SOA records.
check: Your trace output shows the referral chain root -> TLD -> authoritative with NS records at each step
You query the authoritative nameserver directly and get an authoritative (aa flag) answer
You can read the SOA record and explain the serial and the negative-cache TTL fields

t: Distinguish TCP from UDP and when each is the right choice
desc: Compare delivery guarantees, ordering, flow and congestion control, and header overhead, then justify the transport choice for DNS, video calls, bulk file transfer, and DHCP.
check: Why do DNS queries and DHCP use UDP despite UDP having no reliability?
What does TCP provide that a real-time voice call would rather do without?
How does a UDP-based protocol like QUIC still deliver reliable, ordered streams?
a: Transactions are short request/response with their own retry; UDP avoids handshake and connection-state cost, and DHCP must work before IP config exists.
In-order reliable delivery means head-of-line blocking and retransmit delay; voice prefers fresh data over a late-but-perfect packet.
QUIC rebuilds acknowledgements, retransmission, and ordering in user space on top of UDP, with independent streams to avoid head-of-line blocking.

t: Watch an ARP request/reply and a stale entry expire
desc: Flush the ARP cache, ping a host on your LAN, and capture the broadcast ARP who-has and the unicast reply. Inspect your neighbor table and observe an entry move through reachable to stale state.
check: Your capture shows a broadcast who-has and a unicast is-at carrying the MAC
ip neigh shows the resolved entry and later a STALE or FAILED state for an idle/absent host
You can explain why ARP only resolves addresses within the same broadcast domain

t: Explain how NAT rewrites packets and why it breaks some protocols
desc: Work through source NAT / PAT: what fields a home router rewrites outbound and inbound, how the translation table is keyed, and why inbound-initiated connections and embedded-address protocols like FTP or SIP struggle.
check: What exact header fields does PAT rewrite outbound, and what keys the return-path lookup?
Why can't an external host initiate a connection to a device behind NAT without extra setup?
Why does classic active-mode FTP break through NAT, and what works around it?
a: It rewrites source IP (and usually source port) outbound; the table is keyed by the chosen public ip:port mapped back to the internal ip:port and protocol.
There is no translation entry until the inside host sends first, so the router has no rule mapping the inbound packet to an internal host.
Active FTP puts the client's private IP/port in the control payload; NAT doesn't rewrite it, so the data connection fails. Passive mode or an ALG fixes it.

t: Build a TCP client/server and observe Nagle vs delayed ACK
desc: Write a small socket client and echo server. Send many tiny writes, then capture packets to see coalescing from Nagle's algorithm; disable it with TCP_NODELAY and compare segment counts and latency.
check: With Nagle on, your capture shows small writes coalesced into fewer segments
Setting TCP_NODELAY produces one segment per write and you measure the latency difference
You can describe the Nagle + delayed-ACK interaction that can add ~40ms stalls

t: Complete a TLS 1.3 handshake and read it in Wireshark
desc: Capture an HTTPS connection, find ClientHello and ServerHello, and identify the negotiated cipher suite, key-share group, and SNI. Export the session keys via SSLKEYLOGFILE and decrypt the application data.
check: You locate ClientHello/ServerHello and read the chosen cipher suite and key-share group
Using a key log file, Wireshark decrypts and shows the HTTP/2 or HTTP request inside
You can explain why TLS 1.3 completes in one round trip versus TLS 1.2's two

t: Reason about MTU, fragmentation, and path MTU discovery
desc: Understand what MTU limits, how IPv4 fragmentation works versus IPv6 (which forbids router fragmentation), and how Path MTU Discovery uses ICMP and the Don't Fragment bit, plus why black-hole PMTUD fails.
check: How does IPv6 handle a too-big packet differently from IPv4?
What is a PMTUD black hole and what commonly causes it?
Why does a 1500-byte MTU with a PPPoE or tunnel overlay often need lowering?
a: Routers never fragment IPv6; they drop the packet and send ICMPv6 Packet Too Big, so only the source fragments (or reduces size).
A firewall drops the ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages, so the sender never learns to shrink packets and large transfers stall.
Tunnel/PPPoE headers consume bytes, so the usable payload MTU drops (e.g. ~1492 or ~1460); otherwise oversized packets get dropped or fragmented.

t: Capture and decode a DHCP DORA exchange
desc: Release your lease and capture a fresh acquisition: Discover, Offer, Request, Ack. Identify the broadcast/unicast behavior, the transaction ID tying them together, and the offered lease, gateway, and DNS options.
check: Your capture shows all four DORA messages sharing one transaction ID (xid)
You identify which messages are broadcast and why the client has no IP yet
You read the DHCP options for subnet mask, router, DNS, and lease time from the Ack

t: Trace how a browser request becomes bytes across the stack
desc: Follow one HTTPS GET end to end: DNS resolution, TCP connect, TLS, HTTP request, and the encapsulation down through TCP, IP, and Ethernet, including what each router and switch along the path reads and changes.
check: At each hop, which addresses change and which stay constant: MAC vs IP?
Where does the TTL field get decremented, and what happens when it hits zero?
Which layers does a switch read versus a router, and why does that matter for broadcast domains?
a: L2 MAC addresses are rewritten hop to hop; L3 source/destination IPs stay end to end (absent NAT).
Every router decrements TTL; at zero the router drops the packet and returns ICMP Time Exceeded, which traceroute exploits.
A switch reads L2 (MAC) and forwards within a broadcast domain; a router reads L3 (IP) and separates broadcast domains/subnets.

t: Explain TCP congestion control: slow start to CUBIC
desc: Work through the congestion window lifecycle: slow start, congestion avoidance, the role of ssthresh, fast retransmit/fast recovery, and how loss-based CUBIC differs from delay/rate-based BBR.
check: What triggers the switch from slow start to congestion avoidance?
How does a triple-duplicate ACK lead to a different response than a timeout?
What signal does BBR use to find bandwidth that loss-based algorithms ignore?
a: Reaching ssthresh: below it cwnd grows exponentially, above it grows ~linearly (one MSS per RTT).
Triple-dup ACK means later packets arrived, so fast retransmit halves cwnd and does fast recovery; a timeout signals worse loss and resets cwnd to ~1 MSS.
BBR estimates the bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation time to set the rate, rather than treating packet loss as the sole congestion signal.

t: Diagnose reachability with ping, traceroute, and mtr
desc: Pick a remote host and characterize the path: use ping for loss/RTT, traceroute to see hops, and mtr for sustained per-hop loss. Distinguish a hop that merely rate-limits ICMP from a real loss point.
check: You produce an mtr run and identify where persistent loss actually begins versus a hop that only deprioritizes ICMP
You explain why a middle hop can show loss while the final destination shows none
You can state why traceroute hops may differ between runs or show asymmetric latency

t: Set up two namespaces with a veth link and route between them
desc: Use ip netns to create two network namespaces, connect them with a veth pair (or via a bridge), assign addresses, enable forwarding, and ping across. Then add a NAT rule so one namespace reaches the outside.
check: Each namespace has its own interface and you ping from one to the other
ip route / ip addr inside each namespace reflects the topology you built
With forwarding and a masquerade rule, the inner namespace reaches an external address

t: Compare IPv6 addressing and SLAAC to IPv4 + DHCP
desc: Learn IPv6 address scopes (link-local, global, unique-local), how SLAAC uses Router Advertisements and prefixes, the role of NDP replacing ARP, and why a host can hold several IPv6 addresses at once.
check: How does a host form a global IPv6 address with SLAAC, and what does the router provide?
What replaces ARP in IPv6, and what message types does it use?
Why does fe80::/10 (link-local) exist and when is it actually used?
a: The Router Advertisement supplies the /64 prefix; the host appends an interface identifier (EUI-64 or random/privacy) to form the full address.
Neighbor Discovery Protocol over ICMPv6: Neighbor Solicitation/Advertisement for L2 resolution and Router Solicitation/Advertisement for config.
Link-local is auto-configured on every interface for on-link communication and control traffic (NDP, routing protocols); it's non-routable beyond the link.

t: Capture and interpret a DNS over UDP vs TCP fallback
desc: Query a name with a large response (e.g. many records or DNSSEC) and capture how the resolver handles truncation: the TC bit set over UDP and the retry over TCP. Compare with EDNS0 advertising a larger UDP buffer.
check: Your capture shows a UDP response with the TC (truncated) bit and a subsequent TCP query
You find the EDNS0 OPT record advertising a UDP payload size larger than 512
You can explain when DNS uses TCP by default (e.g. zone transfers) versus as a fallback

t: Write a raw-socket tool that crafts and sends an ICMP echo
desc: Build a small program that constructs an ICMP echo request by hand: fill the type/code/id/seq, compute the checksum correctly, send via a raw socket, and read the echo reply, matching id and sequence.
check: Your tool elicits a real echo reply from a live host and matches the id/seq you sent
Your checksum implementation validates (zeroing the field, 16-bit one's-complement sum)
You handle the reply including the IP header and extract the ICMP payload correctly

t: Understand HTTP/2 multiplexing versus HTTP/1.1 limits
desc: Learn why HTTP/1.1 suffers head-of-line blocking and connection sprawl, how HTTP/2 streams/frames multiplex over one TCP connection, and why TCP-level head-of-line blocking still motivated HTTP/3 over QUIC.
check: What problem in HTTP/1.1 did pipelining try and fail to solve, and why?
How do HTTP/2 streams avoid application-layer head-of-line blocking?
Why does a single lost TCP segment still stall all HTTP/2 streams, and how does HTTP/3 fix it?
a: Pipelining allowed queued requests but responses had to return in order, so one slow response blocked the rest; proxies also handled it poorly.
Requests/responses are split into frames tagged with stream IDs and interleaved on one connection, so they don't block each other at the HTTP layer.
All HTTP/2 streams share one TCP byte-stream, so a lost segment stalls delivery of everything behind it; QUIC gives each stream independent delivery over UDP.

t: Explain how BGP picks routes and why misconfig causes outages
desc: Learn BGP as path-vector routing between autonomous systems: how prefixes and AS-paths propagate, the main path-selection attributes, and how route leaks or hijacks (announcing someone else's prefix) cause global incidents.
check: What does the AS-path attribute prevent, and how does it influence selection?
How can one AS accidentally black-hole traffic for a prefix it doesn't own?
Why is a more-specific prefix announcement so powerful (and dangerous) in BGP?
a: It records every AS a route traversed; a router rejects a path containing its own AS, preventing loops, and shorter AS-paths are generally preferred.
By announcing a prefix (a leak/hijack), it attracts that traffic; if it can't deliver, the packets are dropped, black-holing the victim's traffic.
Longest-prefix-match routing always prefers the more-specific route, so a bogus /24 overrides a legitimate /16 globally until it's filtered.

t: Rescue a detached HEAD and recover lost commits with reflog
desc: Create commits on a detached HEAD, switch away so they look lost, then use git reflog to find the dangling commit hashes and git branch to re-anchor them. Confirm nothing was actually deleted yet.
check: You recover the 'lost' commits onto a named branch using a hash from the reflog
You can explain why the commits survived (reflog + unreachable objects not yet GC'd)
You identify how long dangling commits typically persist before git gc prunes them

t: Rewrite history cleanly with interactive rebase
desc: On a scratch branch with 5+ messy commits, use git rebase -i to squash, reword, reorder, and drop commits into a clean sequence. Then force-push-with-lease to a remote branch and verify the new graph.
check: The final branch has the squashed/reordered commits with rewritten messages you chose
You used --force-with-lease and can explain why it is safer than --force
You can explain why the commit hashes changed and what that means for collaborators

t: Understand what git merge vs rebase actually do to the graph
desc: Compare how a merge creates a merge commit with two parents versus how rebase replays commits onto a new base, producing new commits. Reason about when each is appropriate and the risks of rebasing shared history.
check: What exactly does rebase do to the original commits, and why do their hashes change?
When does a merge create a merge commit versus a fast-forward, and why?
Why is rebasing a branch others have already pulled considered harmful?
a: It creates new commits that reapply each change onto the new base; content may match but parent/metadata differ, so SHA-1s change.
Fast-forward happens when the target's tip is a direct ancestor (no divergence); otherwise git must record a merge commit with two parents.
Everyone else's history still references the old commits; after a rebase their branches diverge and merges create duplicate/conflicting commits.

t: Bisect a regression to the exact commit with git bisect
desc: Take a repo where a test started failing, mark a known-good and known-bad commit, and run git bisect (ideally with git bisect run and a script) to binary-search to the first bad commit. Confirm with the test.
check: git bisect identifies a single first-bad commit and you verify the test fails there but passes on its parent
You used git bisect run with a script returning proper exit codes
You can state how many steps bisect needs for N commits and why (log2)

t: Reason about file permissions, setuid, and sticky bits
desc: Work through rwx for user/group/other, the meaning of setuid/setgid on files and directories, and the sticky bit on /tmp. Predict the octal for a few scenarios and what setgid on a directory does.
check: What does the sticky bit on /tmp prevent, concretely?
What is the difference between setgid on an executable versus on a directory?
Why can a non-root user change their password via a setuid binary without write access to the shadow file?
a: It stops users from deleting or renaming files they don't own in a world-writable directory; only the owner (or root) may remove a file.
On an executable it runs with the file's group; on a directory new files inherit the directory's group, aiding shared workspaces.
passwd is setuid root, so during execution the effective UID is root, granting the temporary privilege to edit /etc/shadow.

t: Build a text pipeline with grep, sort, uniq, awk, and cut
desc: Take a real log file (e.g. an access log) and answer a concrete question like top 10 client IPs by request count, using a single pipeline. Then rewrite the counting step as a one-line awk program.
check: Your pipeline outputs the top 10 IPs with counts, correctly sorted numerically
You produce an awk one-liner that aggregates counts in an associative array
You can explain why sort | uniq -c requires the input to be sorted first

t: Master quoting, word splitting, and globbing in bash
desc: Work through how the shell expands variables, performs word splitting on IFS, and does filename globbing, and why unquoted variables break on spaces. Predict the output of several tricky expansions before running them.
check: Why does rm $file break when $file contains spaces, but rm "$file" does not?
In what order does bash perform expansion, word splitting, and globbing?
What is the difference between $@ and $* inside double quotes?
a: Unquoted, the value undergoes word splitting on IFS and globbing, so spaces create multiple arguments; quoting passes it as one argument.
Brace -> tilde -> parameter/arithmetic/command substitution -> word splitting -> filename globbing (quote removal last).
"$@" expands to each argument as a separate quoted word; "$*" joins all arguments into one word separated by the first IFS char.

t: Write a systemd service with a timer and inspect its journal
desc: Create a .service unit running a small script and a .timer unit to trigger it periodically. Enable both, confirm activation, and use journalctl to read its logs filtered by unit and time window.
check: systemctl list-timers shows your timer and the service runs on schedule
journalctl -u yourunit shows the script output with correct timestamps
You can explain the difference between a .timer and a cron job for this task

t: Debug a running process with strace and ltrace
desc: Pick a program that fails or hangs (e.g. can't find a config file) and strace it to find the failing syscall (e.g. an ENOENT on open). Use ltrace to see library calls, and -f to follow forked children.
check: You pinpoint the exact syscall and errno explaining the failure (e.g. openat returning ENOENT)
You follow child processes with -f and filter to relevant syscalls with -e
You can explain how strace works (ptrace) and why it slows the target

t: Find and fix which process holds a deleted-but-open file
desc: Fill a filesystem, delete a large log that a daemon still has open, and observe that df still shows it full. Use lsof to find the process holding the deleted inode and reclaim space by truncating or restarting it.
check: lsof shows the process with the file marked (deleted) and you reclaim the space
You can explain why df and du disagreed until the fd was closed
You reclaim space without deleting more files (e.g. : > /proc/PID/fd/N or restart)

t: Understand hard links, symlinks, and inodes
desc: Reason about what a hard link and a symlink actually point to, how inodes and link counts work, why you can't hard-link across filesystems or to directories, and what happens when the target of a symlink moves.
check: What breaks if you move the target of a symlink versus a hard link?
Why can't a hard link cross filesystem boundaries?
When you rm a file with link count 2, what happens to the data?
a: A symlink stores a path, so it dangles if the target moves; a hard link points to the same inode, so it keeps working regardless of the original name.
Hard links share an inode number, which is only unique within one filesystem; a cross-fs link would have no valid inode to reference.
rm unlinks one name and decrements the link count to 1; the inode and data persist until the last link is removed (and no process holds it open).

t: Edit efficiently in vim: motions, text objects, macros
desc: Do a realistic refactor in vim using operator+motion (ci", dap, >i{), recording and replaying a macro with q and @, and a global substitution with :%s and :g. Avoid arrow keys and the mouse entirely.
check: You change text inside quotes/brackets with ci" / ci{ without manual selection
You record a macro once and apply it across many lines with @@ or a count
You run a :g/pattern/ command (e.g. delete or normal) on matching lines only

t: Resolve a real merge conflict including a rename + edit
desc: Construct two branches that both edit a file one side also renamed, then merge. Read the conflict markers, resolve the content, use git rerere or a mergetool, and verify with git diff that the result is intentional.
check: The merge completes with a correct, hand-verified resolution (not just accepting one side)
You can explain what <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> delimit and which side is which
You handle the rename-vs-edit case so no changes are silently dropped

t: Understand exit codes, signals, and pipelines in bash
desc: Reason about $?, how pipelines report status, set -e / set -o pipefail, and what SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGKILL do. Predict the exit status of a few pipelines and why set -e sometimes fails to catch an error.
check: What exit status does a | b report by default, and how does pipefail change it?
Why can't a process catch or ignore SIGKILL (signal 9)?
Give a case where set -e does NOT abort despite a failing command.
a: By default the status of the last command (b); with pipefail it's the rightmost non-zero status, catching failures earlier in the pipe.
SIGKILL is handled by the kernel, which terminates the process without delivering it to user code, so it can't be trapped or ignored.
A command in an if/while condition, part of &&/||, or followed by || is exempt; e.g. 'cmd || true' or 'if cmd; then' won't trigger set -e.

t: Profile where disk space and I/O are going
desc: On a machine or container, find the largest directories with du, identify big or deleted-but-open files, and watch live I/O with iostat or iotop to attribute throughput to a process. Produce a short findings note.
check: You rank the top space consumers and confirm numbers against df
You attribute live read/write throughput to a specific process
You distinguish space used by data vs by inodes (df -i) when relevant

t: Explain how $PATH, shell builtins, and command lookup work
desc: Reason through how the shell resolves a typed command: aliases, functions, builtins, then $PATH search with hashing. Understand type, which, command -v, and why 'cd' can't be an external program.
check: In what order does bash resolve a command name (alias, function, builtin, PATH)?
Why must cd be a shell builtin rather than an external binary?
What does the shell's command hash table cache, and when does it go stale?
a: Alias -> shell function -> builtin -> executable found by scanning $PATH left to right (use 'type -a' to see all).
cd must change the current shell's working directory; an external process could only change its own and exit, leaving the shell unaffected.
It caches resolved full paths of commands to skip PATH scans; it goes stale if a binary is moved/installed, fixed with 'hash -r'.

t: Capture and analyze a performance flamegraph with perf
desc: Run perf record on a CPU-bound program, generate a flamegraph (or perf report), and identify the hottest call paths. Then make one targeted change and confirm the hotspot shifted or shrank.
check: You produce a flamegraph/report and name the function consuming the most CPU
After one change, you show the hotspot measurably shrank or moved
You can explain sampling vs tracing and why perf needs symbols/frame pointers

t: Understand environment variables and process inheritance
desc: Reason about the difference between shell variables and exported environment variables, how child processes inherit the environment, why a subshell can't change its parent's environment, and where login vs non-login shells read config.
check: Why can a script you run not change your interactive shell's variables, but 'source' can?
What is the difference between a shell variable and an exported one for a child process?
Which files does a login shell read versus an interactive non-login shell?
a: A script runs in a child process with a copied environment; source executes commands in the current shell, so its assignments persist.
Only exported variables are copied into a child's environment; unexported shell variables are invisible to child processes.
Login: /etc/profile and ~/.bash_profile (or ~/.profile); non-login interactive: ~/.bashrc (and /etc/bash.bashrc).

t: Use tmux to run, detach, and reattach a long job
desc: Start a long-running command inside a tmux session, detach, reconnect over a fresh terminal (simulating a dropped SSH session), split panes, and scroll the output buffer. Confirm the job kept running while detached.
check: You reattach to the session and the long job is still running with its output intact
You split the window and run a monitor (e.g. top) in a second pane
You can explain why tmux survives SSH disconnects while a plain background job may not

t: Set up SSH key auth, agent forwarding, and a jump host
desc: Generate an ed25519 key, install the public key on a server, disable password auth in your client config, and configure a ProxyJump to reach an inner host through a bastion. Use the agent so the key isn't copied around.
check: You log in with the key and no password prompt, reaching the inner host via ProxyJump
ssh-add -l shows your key loaded and the inner host authenticates via the agent
You can explain the risk of agent forwarding and why ProxyJump is safer than it

t: Write a program that forks, execs, and reaps a child
desc: Write C that forks, has the child exec a command, and the parent wait()s and reads the exit status. Then deliberately not wait and observe a zombie in ps, and orphan a child to see it reparented to init/systemd.
check: Your parent prints the child's exit code decoded via WIFEXITED/WEXITSTATUS
You reproduce a zombie (Z state) and explain exactly what keeps it around
You orphan a child and show its parent PID becomes 1 (or a subreaper)

t: Understand virtual memory, pages, and the MMU
desc: Reason about virtual vs physical addresses, page tables, the TLB, and how the MMU translates on each access. Understand why two processes can both use address 0x400000 without conflict.
check: How can two processes both map address 0x400000 to different physical memory?
What is the TLB and why does a context switch often hurt performance?
What happens on a TLB miss followed by a valid page-table entry?
a: Each process has its own page tables; the MMU maps the same virtual address to different physical frames per address space.
The TLB caches recent virtual-to-physical translations; a switch can flush it (absent tagging), so early accesses pay page-walk costs again.
The hardware (or kernel) walks the page table, loads the translation into the TLB, and retries the access transparently.

t: Trigger and read every page-fault type with mmap
desc: Use mmap to create anonymous and file-backed regions, touch pages to cause minor faults, and read /proc/self/stat or getrusage to count minor vs major faults. Then provoke a segfault by writing to a PROT_READ region.
check: You observe minor fault counts rise as you touch fresh anonymous pages
You cause a major fault by reading an un-cached file-backed page and see the count rise
You trigger SIGSEGV writing to a read-only mapping and explain why it's a fault, not a return error

t: Explain how a syscall actually enters the kernel
desc: Trace the mechanics of a system call on x86-64: the syscall instruction, register convention for the number and arguments, the switch to kernel mode and stack, and how the return value and errno are delivered.
check: Which register holds the syscall number and which hold arguments on x86-64 Linux?
What privilege transition happens on 'syscall' and why can't userspace just call kernel code directly?
How is an error returned from a syscall, and how does libc turn it into errno?
a: rax holds the number; arguments go in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9 (note r10, not rcx, which syscall clobbers).
The CPU switches from ring 3 to ring 0 with a kernel stack; direct calls are blocked because kernel memory isn't accessible/executable from user mode.
The kernel returns a negative errno value in rax; libc's wrapper detects the negative range, negates it into errno, and returns -1.

t: Understand the CFS scheduler and nice levels
desc: Learn how Linux's CFS picks the next task using virtual runtime and a red-black tree, how nice values weight CPU share, and what preemption and time slices mean. Reason about fairness between CPU-bound and interactive tasks.
check: How does CFS decide which runnable task to run next?
What does a nice value actually change about a task's CPU allocation?
Why do interactive tasks tend to get scheduled promptly under CFS?
a: It picks the runnable task with the smallest virtual runtime (leftmost node in the rbtree), keeping accumulated CPU time balanced.
Nice changes the task's weight; lower nice = higher weight = vruntime advances slower, so it gets a larger share of CPU.
They sleep often, accumulating little vruntime, so when they wake they have a small vruntime and are chosen quickly.

t: Measure copy-on-write fork behavior in practice
desc: Write a program that allocates a large array, forks, and has the child read it (no COW break) then write to it (COW break). Watch RSS and /proc/PID/smaps to see shared pages become private on write.
check: RSS stays low until the child writes, then rises as pages become private
smaps shows Shared_Clean dropping and Private_Dirty rising after the write
You can explain why fork() is fast despite a large address space

t: Build and load a hello-world loadable kernel module
desc: Write a minimal LKM with init/exit functions logging via printk, build it against your running kernel headers, insmod it, read dmesg, then rmmod. Add a module parameter and read it back from /sys.
check: insmod loads the module and dmesg shows your init message; rmmod shows the exit message
lsmod lists your module and a module parameter is visible/settable
You can explain why a module bug can panic the whole system unlike a userspace crash

t: Understand file descriptors, the open file table, and dup
desc: Reason about the three-level structure: per-process fd table, system-wide open file description (with the offset), and the inode. Understand what dup2 shares, and why two fds from separate open() calls have independent offsets.
check: Why do fds created by dup share a file offset, but two separate open()s of the same file do not?
What exactly does the open file description hold that the fd and the inode do not?
What happens to the offset when one process reads via an fd that was inherited across fork?
a: dup/dup2 copy a reference to the same open file description, which stores the offset; separate open()s create distinct descriptions.
It holds the current offset, the status flags (e.g. O_APPEND), and a pointer to the inode; it's the shared middle layer.
The inherited fd shares the same open file description, so a read by either parent or child advances the shared offset for both.

t: Demonstrate a race condition and fix it with a mutex
desc: Write a multithreaded C program where several threads increment a shared counter without synchronization and show the result is wrong/non-deterministic. Fix it with a mutex (or an atomic) and confirm correctness.
check: The unsynchronized version produces a final count less than expected, reproducibly
Adding a mutex or atomic yields the exact correct count every run
You can explain why counter++ is not atomic at the machine level

t: Explore a process's memory map via /proc/PID/maps
desc: Pick a running process and read /proc/PID/maps: identify the text, data, bss, heap, stack, shared libraries, and anonymous mappings with their permissions. Correlate an address from a pointer with its region.
check: You label each major region (text/data/heap/stack/libs) and its r/w/x permissions
You explain why text is r-x and the stack is rw- (no x on modern systems)
You locate which mapping a given runtime address falls into

t: Understand how pipes, blocking, and SIGPIPE work
desc: Reason about pipe buffers, when a write blocks (full buffer) or read blocks (empty buffer), what happens when the read end closes (SIGPIPE/EPIPE), and why 'yes | head' terminates cleanly.
check: What happens to a process writing to a pipe whose read end has closed?
Why does 'yes | head -n5' stop rather than run forever?
When does a read() on a pipe return 0 versus block?
a: The write gets SIGPIPE (terminating by default) or, if ignored/blocked, write() returns -1 with errno EPIPE.
head reads 5 lines then exits, closing the pipe's read end; yes then gets SIGPIPE on its next write and dies.
read() returns 0 only when all write ends are closed (EOF); otherwise it blocks until data arrives or a writer closes.

t: Trace kernel behavior with ftrace or a bpftrace one-liner
desc: Use ftrace (function_graph) or bpftrace to observe a specific kernel path, e.g. count openat syscalls per process, or trace which functions run during a block I/O. Capture output and interpret one interesting call chain.
check: You capture real kernel-side events tied to a userspace action you trigger
You aggregate by process or latency and read a meaningful result
