You can explain the overhead/safety difference between ftrace and a kprobe-based tool

t: Explain the page cache, dirty pages, and writeback
desc: Learn how the page cache buffers file I/O, how writes become dirty pages flushed asynchronously by writeback, the role of fsync, and why free memory 'used' by cache isn't really used. Understand read-ahead.
check: Why does 'free' show little free memory, and why is that not a problem?
What guarantee does fsync give that a plain write() does not?
What happens to dirty pages if the machine loses power before writeback?
a: Most RAM is page cache, which is reclaimable on demand; it speeds up I/O and is freed instantly when applications need memory.
fsync forces the file's dirty pages (and metadata) to stable storage before returning; write() may only reach the page cache.
Un-flushed dirty pages are lost, which is why databases fsync and journaling/ordered modes exist to bound the damage.

t: Compare I/O multiplexing: select vs poll vs epoll
desc: Write a tiny echo server first with select(), then with epoll. Open many idle connections and reason about the cost difference. Measure or argue why epoll scales to thousands of fds where select does not.
check: Both servers handle multiple concurrent clients correctly
You can state select's FD_SETSIZE and per-call O(n) scan limitation
You explain how epoll's readiness list makes it O(1) in the number of ready fds

t: Understand the stack, heap, and calling conventions
desc: Reason about how a function call sets up a stack frame on x86-64 (return address, saved rbp, locals), where arguments go per the SysV ABI, how the heap is grown via brk/mmap, and why stack memory is reclaimed automatically.
check: Where do the first six integer arguments go under the SysV x86-64 ABI?
Why is stack allocation essentially free while heap allocation is not?
What does the saved return address on the stack enable an attacker to do if overwritten?
a: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9; further arguments and large/aggregate types go on the stack.
The stack just moves a pointer (rsp) and frees on return; the heap needs an allocator tracking free/used blocks and may call the kernel.
Overwriting it redirects control flow on ret (e.g. to injected code or a ROP chain), the basis of stack buffer-overflow exploits.

t: Build a minimal container with namespaces and cgroups by hand
desc: Use unshare/clone to put a shell in new PID, mount, UTS, and network namespaces, chroot/pivot_root into a minimal rootfs, and set a memory limit via a cgroup. Confirm the isolated process sees itself as PID 1.
check: Inside the new namespace, ps shows your shell as PID 1 and a private mount/hostname
A memory cgroup limit is enforced (an over-limit allocation is OOM-killed inside)
You can explain which isolation comes from namespaces versus which limiting comes from cgroups

t: Observe signal delivery, masking, and handlers
desc: Write a program that installs a SIGINT handler with sigaction, blocks a signal with sigprocmask during a critical section, and shows the pending signal is delivered after unblocking. Note what is safe inside a handler.
check: Ctrl-C is caught by your handler instead of terminating the program
A signal raised while blocked stays pending and fires once unblocked
You can name why only async-signal-safe functions are legal inside a handler

t: Explain what happens from power-on to PID 1
desc: Trace the Linux boot path at a conceptual level: firmware/UEFI, bootloader loading the kernel and initramfs, kernel decompression and init, mounting the real root, and exec of the init process (systemd) as PID 1.
check: What is the initramfs for, and why can't the kernel always mount the real root directly?
How does the kernel transition from its own init to running userspace PID 1?
What distinguishes PID 1's responsibilities from an ordinary process?
a: It's a temporary RAM root with drivers/modules needed to find and mount the real root (e.g. LVM, encryption, exotic storage) before pivoting to it.
After setup the kernel exec()s the init program (from initramfs, then the real root's /sbin/init), which never returns and becomes PID 1.
PID 1 reaps orphaned children, can't be killed by default signals, and its exit panics the kernel; it manages system startup/shutdown.

t: Understand deadlock conditions and how to avoid them
desc: Learn the four Coffman conditions for deadlock, construct a classic two-lock ordering deadlock mentally, and reason about prevention strategies: lock ordering, try-lock with backoff, and avoiding hold-and-wait.
check: What are the four necessary conditions for deadlock, and which one is easiest to break?
How does a consistent global lock-ordering discipline prevent deadlock?
Why does adding a timeout/try-lock avoid deadlock but risk livelock?
a: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait; breaking circular wait (via lock ordering) is usually most practical.
If every thread acquires locks in the same total order, no cycle of waits can form, so circular wait is impossible.
Try-lock lets a thread back off instead of waiting forever, but repeated collide-and-retry cycles can make no one progress (livelock).

t: Implement a simple memory allocator over mmap/sbrk
desc: Write a minimal malloc/free using a single arena from mmap, a free list, and first-fit allocation with block headers and coalescing on free. Test with a mix of allocation sizes and verify no corruption.
check: Your allocator satisfies a varied sequence of mallocs/frees without overlap or corruption
Freed adjacent blocks coalesce so repeated alloc/free doesn't fragment forever
You can explain the role of block headers and alignment in your design

t: Inspect a process's handles and tokens with Process Explorer
desc: Open Process Explorer, pick a running process, and examine its open handles (files, keys, mutants), its security token (groups, privileges, integrity level), and its loaded DLLs. Find a handle leak candidate by sorting handle counts.
check: You enumerate a process's handles and identify at least one file and one registry key it holds
You read the token's integrity level and enabled privileges for the process
You can explain what a 'mutant' handle is and how it differs from a Linux file descriptor

t: Understand the Windows process vs thread model
desc: Learn that in Windows a process is just a container (address space, handle table, token) and threads are the scheduled units, how CreateProcess differs from fork, and what a thread's quantum and priority class mean.
check: Why is there no fork() equivalent in the Win32 API, and what does CreateProcess do instead?
What resources belong to the process versus the thread?
How do priority class and thread priority combine into the scheduler's base priority?
a: CreateProcess builds a fresh process from an image with a new address space and one thread; there is no copy-on-write clone of the caller.
Process owns the address space, handle table, and token; each thread owns its stack, registers, and scheduling state.
The process's priority class and the thread's relative priority map to a base priority level (0-31); the scheduler also applies dynamic boosts.

t: Explain Windows access tokens, SIDs, and integrity levels
desc: Learn how a token carries the user SID, group SIDs, privileges, and a mandatory integrity level, how DACLs grant access, and how UAC splits an admin into a filtered and an elevated token.
check: How does the Mandatory Integrity Control level restrict a Low-IL process writing to a Medium-IL object?
What are the two tokens UAC creates for an administrator, and when is each used?
How is an access decision made from a token and an object's DACL?
a: MIC enforces no-write-up by default: a lower-IL subject can't modify a higher-IL object regardless of the DACL (e.g. sandboxed browser tabs run Low).
A filtered (standard-user) token used by default and a full elevated token used only after a UAC consent prompt.
The system walks the DACL's ACEs, matching the token's user/group SIDs, accumulating granted/denied rights until the requested access is resolved.

t: Trace a Win32 API call down to a syscall with an API monitor
desc: Use API Monitor or a debugger to watch a call like CreateFileW flow through kernel32 -> KernelBase -> ntdll's NtCreateFile, and observe the syscall stub. Note the Nt vs Zw naming and the user/kernel transition point.
check: You trace a documented Win32 call to its underlying Nt* function in ntdll
You identify the syscall stub (e.g. the syscall instruction with a service number)
You can explain the Nt vs Zw prefix and why ntdll is the user-mode boundary

t: Understand the Windows registry's structure and hives
desc: Learn how the registry is organized into hives backed by files, the role of HKLM vs HKCU, where HKCU and HKCR are really projected from, and how volatile keys and the SAM/SYSTEM hives fit in.
check: Where does HKEY_CURRENT_USER actually come from on disk and per logon?
What is HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT a merged view of, and why?
Which hive holds local account password hashes, and why is it locked at runtime?
a: HKCU is a per-user link to that user's NTUSER.DAT hive loaded under HKEY_USERS\<SID> at logon.
HKCR merges HKLM\Software\Classes (machine-wide) with HKCU\Software\Classes (per-user), so per-user associations override machine ones.
The SAM hive; it's held open/exclusively by the system (and protected) so it can't be read offline while Windows runs.

t: Watch file and registry activity live with Process Monitor
desc: Run Process Monitor while launching an app, then filter by process name and operation to find exactly which files and registry keys it reads/writes at startup, including failures like NAME NOT FOUND that reveal config lookups.
check: You filter the firehose down to one process and read its startup file/registry accesses
You spot a NAME NOT FOUND or PATH NOT FOUND and explain what the app was probing for
You can read the call stack of one operation to see which module issued it

t: Analyze a user-mode crash dump in WinDbg
desc: Capture a crash dump of a program that throws an access violation, open it in WinDbg, run !analyze -v, inspect the faulting thread's stack with k, and identify the faulting instruction and the bad address.
check: !analyze -v and the stack trace point to the function that faulted
You read the exception record and identify the access-violation address and operation
You can map the crashing address back to a line/module using symbols

t: Explain Windows virtual memory and the working set
desc: Learn user vs kernel address space split, how committed vs reserved memory differs, what the working set and standby list are, and how the page file backs committed memory. Understand why Task Manager's numbers can confuse.
check: What is the difference between reserved and committed virtual memory?
What is a process's working set, and what happens to pages trimmed from it?
Why can total commit exceed physical RAM, and what limits it?
a: Reserved just claims address ranges; committed memory is backed by RAM or page file and counts against the commit limit.
The working set is the process's pages resident in RAM; trimmed pages move to the standby (clean) or modified (dirty) list, not immediately discarded.
Committed memory is backed by RAM plus the page file, so the commit limit is roughly RAM + page-file size, not RAM alone.

t: Understand DLLs, loading, and search order hijacking
desc: Learn how the loader resolves and maps DLLs, the default DLL search order, what delayed loading and known DLLs are, and how DLL search-order and phantom-DLL hijacking become a security risk.
check: What is the default DLL search order, and how do 'KnownDLLs' change it?
How does DLL search-order hijacking let an attacker run code in a trusted process?
Why does loading a DLL run code (DllMain) and what are the loader-lock pitfalls?
a: Roughly: the app directory, then system directories, then the current directory and PATH; KnownDLLs are pre-mapped from System32 to prevent redirection.
If an app loads a DLL by name from a writable directory searched first, an attacker plants a malicious DLL there that gets loaded with the app's trust.
The loader calls DllMain under the loader lock; doing complex work there (loading more DLLs, synchronization) can deadlock or crash the process.

t: Enumerate services, drivers, and their configs
desc: Use sc query, the Services console, and Autoruns to list running services and kernel drivers, examine one service's binary path, start type, and account (LocalSystem/LocalService), and find auto-start entries across the system.
check: You list services with their start type and the account each runs under
You identify at least one kernel-mode driver versus a user-mode service
Autoruns shows you auto-start locations beyond services (run keys, scheduled tasks)

t: Explain the Windows object manager and the namespace
desc: Learn how the kernel's Object Manager represents processes, files, events, and sections as objects in a hierarchical namespace, how handles reference them with reference counts, and what symbolic links like \??\C: mean.
check: What does a handle count versus a pointer count track on a kernel object?
How does the DOS drive letter C: map to a device via the object namespace?
Why can an object persist after the creator closes its handle?
a: Handle count tracks user-mode references via handles; pointer (reference) count includes kernel references, and the object lives while either is nonzero.
C: is a symbolic link under \??\ (the per-session DosDevices) pointing to a device object like \Device\HarddiskVolumeN.
Another handle or a kernel pointer reference may remain; the object is only freed when both handle and pointer counts reach zero.

t: Capture and read an ETW trace with WPR/WPA
desc: Use Windows Performance Recorder to capture a CPU/disk trace during a slow operation, open it in Windows Performance Analyzer, and attribute time to a stack/module. Identify one hotspot or a blocking I/O.
check: You produce an ETW trace covering the operation of interest
WPA shows CPU usage by stack and you name the heaviest module/function
You can explain what ETW providers are and why ETW is low-overhead

t: Compare processes, jobs, and AppContainer isolation
desc: Create a Job object limiting a child process (e.g. memory or active-process count) and observe enforcement. Then inspect an AppContainer/UWP process in Process Explorer to see its capability SIDs and restricted token.
check: A Job object limit you set is enforced on the child process
You identify an AppContainer process and read its capability SIDs
You can explain how a Job differs from a cgroup and from an AppContainer sandbox

t: Understand structured exception handling and SEH/VEH
desc: Learn how Windows dispatches exceptions through the kernel to user mode, the difference between SEH frames, vectored exception handlers, and how __try/__except filters decide to handle, continue, or search. Contrast with C++ exceptions.
check: What are the three possible return values of an SEH filter expression and what does each do?
How does a Vectored Exception Handler differ in ordering from frame-based SEH?
How does an access violation become a catchable exception rather than an immediate crash?
a: EXECUTE_HANDLER runs the __except block, CONTINUE_SEARCH passes it up the chain, CONTINUE_EXECUTION retries the faulting instruction.
VEHs are called first, in registration order, before any frame-based SEH unwinding; SEH walks the stack frame by frame.
The CPU faults into the kernel, which builds an exception record and dispatches it to the thread's user-mode handler chain (KiUserExceptionDispatcher).

t: Explain how Windows authentication and LSASS work
desc: Learn LSASS's role, how interactive logon produces an access token, the difference between NTLM and Kerberos, and why credential material in LSASS memory is a classic attack target (pass-the-hash, ticket theft).
check: What does LSASS produce on a successful interactive logon?
What is the key practical difference between NTLM and Kerberos authentication?
Why is pass-the-hash possible, and what does it exploit about NTLM?
a: It validates credentials and creates the logon session and access token the kernel attaches to the user's processes.
NTLM is a challenge-response using the password hash directly; Kerberos uses a trusted KDC issuing time-limited tickets, enabling SSO and mutual auth.
NTLM authenticates with the hash itself, not the plaintext, so a stolen hash can be replayed without ever cracking the password.

t: Examine PE file structure with a PE viewer
desc: Open an .exe in a PE viewer (CFF Explorer/PE-bear), locate the DOS header, NT headers, section table (.text/.data/.rdata), the import address table, and the entry point. Map a section's RVA to a file offset.
check: You identify the entry point and the imported DLLs/functions from the IAT
You explain the difference between an RVA and a file offset and convert one
You find which section is executable and which holds the imports

t: Set up kernel debugging and break on a driver
desc: Configure WinDbg kernel debugging against a VM over a named pipe/network, break in, set a breakpoint on a kernel routine (e.g. NtCreateFile), trigger it from user mode, and inspect the stack and arguments in kernel space.
check: You attach the kernel debugger to the target and break into it
A breakpoint on a kernel function hits when you trigger the matching user-mode action
You read the kernel stack and the function's arguments at the breakpoint

t: Understand IRQL and why some code can't page-fault
desc: Learn the Interrupt Request Level hierarchy, why code at or above DISPATCH_LEVEL can't touch pageable memory or block, how spin locks raise IRQL, and why a page fault at high IRQL bugchecks the system.
check: Why can't code running at DISPATCH_LEVEL access pageable memory?
What does acquiring a spin lock do to the current IRQL and why?
What bugcheck results from touching paged-out memory at high IRQL?
a: The page-fault handler needs to run the memory manager, which may block/wait; that isn't allowed at DISPATCH_LEVEL or above, so it faults the system instead.
It raises IRQL to DISPATCH_LEVEL (masking the scheduler and lower interrupts) so the lock holder can't be preempted on that CPU.
IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL (bugcheck 0xA), the classic consequence of a high-IRQL access to invalid/pageable memory.

t: Explain thread scheduling, quanta, and priority boosts
desc: Learn how the Windows scheduler is priority-driven and preemptive across 32 levels, how quanta differ on client vs server, and the dynamic boosts for I/O completion, foreground windows, and starvation (balance set manager).
check: How does the scheduler choose which ready thread to run next?
Why does a thread waking from I/O get a priority boost, and in which priority range does it apply?
How does Windows prevent a lower-priority thread from starving forever?
a: It runs the highest-priority ready thread; among equal priority it round-robins by quantum, and higher priority always preempts lower.
To improve responsiveness it boosts the thread after I/O so it processes results promptly; boosts apply only in the dynamic range (1-15), not real-time (16-31).
The balance set manager periodically boosts long-starved ready threads to priority 15 for one quantum, breaking priority inversion/starvation.

t: Map a file into memory and compare with ReadFile I/O
desc: Write a small Win32 program that reads a file both via CreateFileMapping/MapViewOfFile and via ReadFile, and reason about what the memory manager does under the hood. Observe page faults backing the mapped view.
check: Both methods yield identical file contents in your program
You observe that touching the mapped view causes demand-paged faults rather than an explicit read
You can explain when a memory-mapped file is preferable to buffered ReadFile

t: Write a working pf.conf ruleset and test it on OpenBSD/FreeBSD
desc: Write a pf ruleset that blocks by default, passes outbound with keep state, allows SSH in, and NATs an internal network. Load it with pfctl, verify with pfctl -sr and -ss, and confirm a blocked connection is logged.
check: pfctl -nf validates your config and pfctl -sr shows the loaded rules
An allowed connection succeeds and a disallowed one is blocked and visible in pfctl -ss / pflog
You can explain pf's 'last matching rule wins' semantics and the role of 'quick'

t: Understand the BSD vs GPL licensing philosophy and its effects
desc: Compare the permissive BSD license with the copyleft GPL, why BSD code can be absorbed into proprietary products, and how this shaped the spread of BSD networking code and the culture of the BSD projects.
check: What practical freedom does the BSD license grant that the GPL restricts?
How did permissive licensing let BSD TCP/IP code end up in commercial OSes?
What obligation does distributing GPL binaries create that BSD does not?
a: BSD lets you use, modify, and redistribute in closed-source products without releasing your changes; GPL requires derivative works to stay open.
Vendors (e.g. early Windows, commercial Unixes, game consoles) could incorporate the BSD network stack without opening their own source.
GPL requires providing corresponding source (or a written offer) to recipients of the binary; BSD only requires preserving the copyright notice.

t: Explain the Unix philosophy through classic tool design
desc: Study the Unix design principles (do one thing well, text streams as a universal interface, composition via pipes) using concrete examples from coreutils, and reason about where the philosophy helps and where it strains.
check: Why are plain-text streams chosen as the universal interface between tools?
Give an example where composing small tools beats a monolithic program, and one where it doesn't.
How does 'do one thing well' influence a tool like cat, and what is 'cat abuse'?
a: Text is human-readable, debuggable, and lets any tool consume any other's output without shared binary formats or APIs.
Composition shines for ad-hoc log analysis (grep|sort|uniq); it strains for tasks needing rich structure or performance (parsing deeply nested data).
cat just concatenates/streams files; piping one file through cat into another tool (cat f | grep) is needless since the tool can open the file itself.

t: Build and install a program from the FreeBSD ports tree
desc: On FreeBSD, pick a small port, run make config to set options, build and install it from source via the ports framework, and inspect the resulting package metadata. Compare with installing the same via pkg.
check: The port builds and installs, and pkg info shows it as a registered package
You can explain the difference between the ports tree (source) and pkg (binary)
You successfully set a build option via make config that changes the result

t: Understand how OpenBSD mitigations harden userland
desc: Learn OpenBSD's proactive security features: W^X, pledge() and unveil() for privilege reduction, the malloc hardening, and position-independent executables by default. Reason about what class of bug each neutralizes.
check: What does pledge() do, and how does it limit a program after it drops into a restricted set?
How does unveil() differ from a chroot for restricting filesystem access?
What attack does W^X (no page both writable and executable) block?
a: pledge() declares the syscall/capability classes a process still needs; using anything outside them kills the process, shrinking the attack surface.
unveil() restricts which filesystem paths a process sees and with what permissions, without a prepared chroot or root, and can be tightened step by step.
It blocks classic code injection: an attacker can't write shellcode to a page and then execute it, pushing them toward harder ROP-style attacks.

t: Create and manage a ZFS pool with snapshots and clones
desc: On FreeBSD, create a ZFS pool (a file-backed vdev is fine), make a dataset, write data, take a snapshot, modify the data, then roll back. Create a clone from the snapshot and observe copy-on-write space usage.
check: zfs list shows your dataset and snapshot; a rollback restores the pre-change state
A clone shares blocks with its snapshot until written (space usage reflects COW)
You can explain how ZFS checksums detect and (with redundancy) self-heal corruption

t: Set up a FreeBSD jail and confine a service in it
desc: Create a FreeBSD jail with its own root filesystem and IP, start a network service inside it, and verify the jailed process can't see host processes or escape its filesystem. Manage it with jail/jexec.
check: jls shows your jail and a service runs reachable on the jail's address
A process inside the jail cannot see host PIDs or paths outside its root
You can explain how jails differ from a plain chroot in isolation guarantees

t: Learn the history: from Unix to BSD to the modern forks
desc: Trace the lineage: AT&T Unix, the Berkeley Software Distribution, the AT&T lawsuit and 4.4BSD-Lite, and the split into FreeBSD, NetBSD, and OpenBSD. Understand what each fork optimizes for today.
check: Why did the USL v. BSDi lawsuit matter for the open BSD lineage?
What distinct goal does each of FreeBSD, NetBSD, and OpenBSD emphasize?
What is the relationship between 4.4BSD-Lite and today's BSDs?
a: It cast legal doubt over BSD's AT&T-derived code; its resolution let 4.4BSD-Lite ship free of that code, clearing the way for the open forks.
FreeBSD: performance/server and desktop breadth; NetBSD: portability across many architectures; OpenBSD: security and code correctness.
4.4BSD-Lite was the clean, legally unencumbered base; the modern BSDs re-based on it to remove disputed AT&T code.

t: Understand kqueue and why BSD rejected the epoll model
desc: Learn kqueue/kevent as BSD's unified event notification mechanism, how it handles not just sockets but files, signals, timers, and process events, and how its edge/level and one-shot filters compare to Linux epoll.
check: What kinds of events can kqueue monitor beyond file-descriptor readiness?
How does registering and retrieving events in one kevent() call differ from epoll's split API?
What does an EV_ONESHOT or EV_CLEAR filter flag change about delivery?
a: File descriptors, vnode changes, signals, timers, async I/O, and process/exit events, all through one interface.
kevent() both registers changes and returns pending events in a single syscall, whereas epoll uses epoll_ctl to register and epoll_wait to retrieve.
EV_ONESHOT delivers an event once then disables the filter; EV_CLEAR resets state after reporting, giving edge-triggered-like behavior.

t: Compare init systems: rc.d scripts vs systemd mentally and in practice
desc: On a BSD (or BSD-style) system, read the rc subsystem: rc.conf, the ordered rc.d scripts with their REQUIRE/PROVIDE dependency keywords, and how rcorder sequences them. Start/stop a service via its rc.d script.
check: You enable and start a service through rc.conf and its /etc/rc.d script
You can read a script's REQUIRE/PROVIDE lines and explain how ordering is computed
You can contrast BSD rc.d's shell-script approach with systemd's declarative units

t: Understand everything-is-a-file and device nodes in Unix
desc: Reason about how Unix exposes devices, pipes, and sockets through the filesystem, the difference between character and block devices, what major/minor numbers identify, and why /dev/null and /dev/zero behave as they do.
check: What distinguishes a character device from a block device?
What do the major and minor numbers of a device node identify?
Why does writing to /dev/null succeed and reading from it return EOF immediately?
a: Character devices do byte-stream I/O (e.g. terminals); block devices do fixed-size, randomly addressable block I/O (e.g. disks) via the buffer cache.
The major number selects the driver; the minor number selects the specific device/instance that driver handles.
The null driver discards all writes (reporting success) and returns 0 bytes (EOF) on read, by design.

t: Read a piece of BSD kernel source and trace a syscall
desc: Clone an OpenBSD or FreeBSD source tree, find the implementation of a simple syscall (e.g. getpid or kill), and trace from the syscall table entry to the function. Note the coding style and documentation discipline.
check: You locate the syscall table entry and the C function implementing your chosen syscall
You follow at least one call into a helper and explain what it does
You can point to a specific design/style convention the BSD source enforces

t: Explain how the BSD socket API became the universal standard
desc: Learn the origin of the socket() / bind() / listen() / accept() / connect() interface in 4.2BSD, why it generalized across address families, and how its design choices (fd-based, protocol-agnostic) endured into every modern OS.
check: Why does the socket API use file descriptors rather than a separate handle type?
How does the sockaddr family design allow one API to serve IPv4, IPv6, and Unix sockets?
What role do listen()'s backlog and accept() play in connection handling?
a: So sockets integrate with read/write/select/close and inherit Unix's uniform I/O model, needing no parallel set of I/O calls.
A generic struct sockaddr with a family tag lets calls take any concrete address struct (sockaddr_in, sockaddr_in6, sockaddr_un) through one interface.
listen() marks a socket passive with a queue of pending connections (backlog); accept() dequeues one and returns a new fd for that connection.

t: Understand FreeBSD's base system vs the Linux distro model
desc: Learn why FreeBSD ships kernel plus userland as one coherent 'base system' from a single source tree, how that differs from a Linux distribution assembling independent projects, and the upgrade/consistency implications.
check: What is the practical benefit of kernel and userland living in one source tree?
How does this change how you upgrade a FreeBSD system versus a Linux distro?
Why can a Linux distro have version-skew problems that FreeBSD base largely avoids?
a: Kernel and core userland are developed and versioned together, so they're guaranteed mutually consistent and documented as one system.
You update the whole base as a unit (e.g. freebsd-update/source build) rather than upgrading many independently packaged components.
A distro integrates separately released projects (kernel, libc, coreutils...), so their versions and ABIs can drift and must be reconciled by the distro.

t: Configure OpenBSD's httpd and relayd for a simple site
desc: On OpenBSD, serve a static site with the base httpd, then put relayd in front as a TLS-terminating reverse proxy. Validate configs, start the daemons, and confirm the site loads over HTTPS.
check: httpd serves the static site and the config passes httpd -n
relayd terminates TLS and proxies to httpd, reachable over HTTPS
You can explain why OpenBSD ships minimal, privilege-separated daemons in base

t: Use dtrace (or DTrace on FreeBSD) to probe a live program
desc: On FreeBSD, use DTrace to count syscalls by a process, trace function entry/return with timing, or aggregate by stack. Write one D script that answers a concrete question about a running program's behavior.
check: Your D script produces a meaningful aggregation (e.g. syscall counts or latency by function)
You use a predicate to filter to one process or condition
You can explain what makes DTrace safe to run in production (no crashes, bounded overhead)

t: Set up carp failover between two BSD gateways
desc: Configure CARP (Common Address Redundancy Protocol) on two BSD hosts sharing a virtual IP, set advskew so one is master, and test failover by taking the master down and confirming the backup takes over the VIP.
check: Both hosts share a CARP virtual IP with a clear master/backup role
Killing the master causes the backup to assume the VIP within the advertised interval
You can explain how CARP differs from VRRP and why OpenBSD created it

t: Understand soft updates and journaling in UFS/FFS
desc: Learn how the BSD Fast File System orders metadata writes, what soft updates guarantee about consistency after a crash, how this differs from a journal, and why fsck behavior changed with soft updates + journaling.
check: What consistency problem do soft updates solve, and how (write ordering)?
How does a journal achieve crash consistency differently from soft updates?
Why can a soft-updates filesystem sometimes skip a full fsck after a crash?
a: They enforce a safe ordering of metadata writes so the on-disk state is always consistent enough that only space leaks (not corruption) can occur.
A journal first writes intended changes to a log, then applies them; on crash it replays or discards the log to reach a consistent state.
Because soft updates guarantee metadata is never inconsistent (only possibly leaked blocks/inodes), a background fsck can reclaim leaks without blocking mount.

t: Explain privilege separation and chroot in OpenBSD daemons
desc: Learn how OpenBSD daemons split into a small privileged process and unprivileged workers communicating over sockets, run workers chrooted and as a low-privilege user, and why this limits the blast radius of a worker compromise.
check: What does the privileged parent retain that the chrooted worker gives up?
Why does chrooting a worker reduce the impact of a remote code execution bug in it?
How do the separated processes typically communicate, and why not shared memory?
a: The parent keeps the few privileged operations (binding low ports, opening keys/logs) and hands results to workers over a pipe/socket.
A compromised worker is confined to a minimal chroot as a low-priv user, so it can't read the real filesystem or escalate easily.
Via a Unix-domain socket/pipe passing messages and file descriptors, keeping a narrow, auditable interface rather than sharing writable memory.

t: Rebuild an OpenBSD or FreeBSD kernel with a custom config
desc: Copy the generic kernel config, remove drivers you don't need or add an option, build the kernel from source, install it, and boot it. Confirm your change took effect (e.g. via dmesg or sysctl).
check: The custom kernel builds and boots successfully
dmesg or a sysctl confirms your configuration change is in effect
You can explain the role of the kernel config file versus runtime sysctl tuning

t: Solve Two Sum in one pass with a hash map
desc: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target (exactly one solution, can't reuse an element). Do it in a single pass using a value-to-index hash map.
check: Your solution runs in O(n) time and O(n) space with a single scan
For each element you look up target minus it before inserting the current element
You correctly return indices (not values) and handle duplicates like [3,3], target 6

t: Detect a cycle in a linked list with Floyd's two pointers
desc: Given the head of a singly linked list, determine whether it contains a cycle. Use a slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two; they meet iff there is a cycle. Then extend it to find the cycle's start node.
check: Your detection uses O(1) extra space (no hash set of visited nodes)
You correctly return false for a null or single-node list with no cycle
Your extension finds the entry node of the cycle and you can justify why resetting one pointer to head works

t: Find the longest substring without repeating characters
desc: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring containing no repeated characters. Use a sliding window with a map of each character's last seen index, moving the left edge past any repeat as you scan right.
check: Your solution is O(n) with the window never moving left backward
For 'abcabcbb' you return 3 and for 'bbbbb' you return 1
You can explain how you jump the left pointer when a repeat's prior index is inside the window

t: Implement binary search and its lower-bound variant correctly
desc: Write binary search on a sorted array returning an exact match index, then write lower_bound: the first index whose value is >= a target. Pay careful attention to loop invariants and off-by-one in the boundary version.
check: Exact search returns the correct index or -1 and never infinite-loops
lower_bound returns the correct insertion point, including when the target exceeds all elements (returns n)
You can state your loop invariant and why your mid computation avoids overflow

t: Solve Merge Intervals by sorting on start
desc: Given a list of intervals [start,end], merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping set. Sort by start, then sweep, extending the current interval's end when the next start is within it, else emitting it.
check: Overlapping and touching intervals (e.g. [1,3],[2,6] -> [1,6]) merge correctly
Your solution is O(n log n) dominated by the sort
You handle fully contained intervals (e.g. [1,10],[2,3]) without splitting them

t: Validate a BST with recursive min/max bounds
desc: Given a binary tree, decide whether it is a valid binary search tree: every node's value is greater than all in its left subtree and less than all in its right. Recurse carrying an allowed (low, high) range for each node.
check: You reject a tree where a deep node violates an ancestor's bound (not just the parent)
Your solution handles duplicate values per your chosen strict/non-strict rule and edge integer limits
You can explain why checking only node-vs-children is insufficient

t: Compute level-order traversal of a binary tree with BFS
desc: Given the root of a binary tree, return its values grouped level by level, top to bottom, left to right. Use a queue and process one full level per outer iteration by capturing the queue size before draining it.
check: Output groups nodes by depth in the correct left-to-right order
You handle an empty tree (return empty) and a skewed tree correctly
You can explain how capturing the level size separates levels without a sentinel

t: Solve the 0/1 Knapsack with dynamic programming
desc: Given item weights and values and a capacity W, choose a subset maximizing value without exceeding W (each item used at most once). Build a DP over items x capacity, then optimize to a 1D array iterated right to left.
check: Your 2D DP returns the optimal value and you can reconstruct which items were chosen
Your 1D optimization iterates capacity in descending order and you explain why
You can state the time and space complexity in terms of n and W

t: Find number of islands with flood fill (DFS/BFS)
desc: Given a 2D grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), count connected groups of land (4-directionally adjacent). Scan the grid; on each unvisited land cell, flood-fill its whole island (marking visited) and increment the count.
check: You count diagonally separate land as distinct islands (only 4-directional connectivity)
You avoid revisiting cells so the total work is O(rows*cols)
You handle all-water and all-land grids, and avoid stack overflow on a large grid (or note the risk)

t: Implement Dijkstra's shortest path with a min-heap
desc: Given a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights and a source, compute shortest distances to all nodes. Use a priority queue, popping the closest unfinalized node and relaxing its edges, skipping stale heap entries.
check: Distances are correct on a graph with multiple paths of differing weight
You skip outdated queue entries (lazy deletion) instead of using a decrease-key
You can explain why Dijkstra fails with negative edges and what to use instead

t: Compute the maximum subarray sum with Kadane's algorithm
desc: Given an integer array (possibly with negatives), find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum. Track a running best-ending-here, resetting it when it would go negative, and a global maximum.
check: You return the correct sum for an all-negative array (the least-negative single element)
Your solution is a single O(n) pass with O(1) extra space
You can extend it to also report the start and end indices of the best subarray

t: Generate all subsets and all permutations via backtracking
desc: Given a set of distinct integers, produce (a) all subsets (the power set) and (b) all permutations, using recursive backtracking that chooses/unchooses each element. Ensure no duplicates when the input has none.
check: You generate exactly 2^n subsets and n! permutations for n distinct elements
Your recursion correctly undoes each choice (restores state) before trying the next
You can explain how to adapt the subset code to skip duplicate subsets when inputs repeat

t: Solve Trapping Rain Water with two pointers
desc: Given an array of non-negative bar heights (unit width), compute how much water is trapped after rain. Use two pointers moving inward, tracking left-max and right-max; the shorter side determines the water at each step.
check: You return the correct total for [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] (which is 6)
Your solution is O(n) time and O(1) space (no prefix-max arrays)
You can explain why the smaller of the two running maxima bounds the water at a position

t: Implement an LRU cache with a hash map plus doubly linked list
desc: Build a cache with get(key) and put(key,value) both in O(1), evicting the least recently used entry when capacity is exceeded. Use a hash map to nodes of a doubly linked list ordered by recency; move touched nodes to the front.
check: Both get and put run in O(1) and a get counts as a use (updates recency)
Exceeding capacity evicts exactly the least-recently-used key
You correctly update both the map and the list on eviction and on overwrite of an existing key

t: Solve Course Schedule with topological sort (cycle detection)
desc: Given numCourses and prerequisite pairs [a,b] meaning b must precede a, decide whether all courses can be finished (i.e. the directed graph is acyclic). Use Kahn's algorithm on in-degrees, or DFS with a visiting/visited coloring.
check: You return false exactly when the prerequisite graph contains a cycle
With Kahn's algorithm you can also output a valid ordering of courses
You can explain how the three-color DFS distinguishes a back edge from a cross/forward edge

t: Check balanced parentheses with a stack
desc: Given a string of brackets '()[]{}', determine if it is valid: every opener has a matching closer of the same type in the correct order. Push openers; on a closer, pop and check it matches, failing fast on mismatch or empty.
check: You reject '([)]' and accept '([]{})'
An unmatched leftover opener at the end returns false
A closer with an empty stack returns false immediately

t: Reason about Big-O: amortized, average, and worst case
desc: Work through why a dynamic array's push is amortized O(1), why hash map operations are average O(1) but worst O(n), and the difference between worst-case and average-case analysis, using concrete resizing/collision examples.
check: Why is appending to a dynamic array amortized O(1) despite occasional O(n) resizes?
When does a hash map degrade to O(n) per operation, and what mitigates it?
What is the difference between amortized and average-case complexity?
a: Doubling capacity makes the total cost of n appends O(n), so the per-append average is O(1); the rare copy's cost is spread over many cheap appends.
When many keys collide into one bucket (bad hash or adversarial input); good hashing, load-factor-triggered resizing, or treeifying buckets mitigate it.
Amortized averages cost over a sequence with a per-sequence guarantee; average-case averages over an input distribution and can still have bad inputs.

t: Understand when to reach for a hash map, heap, or BST
desc: Compare the operations and complexities of hash maps, binary heaps, and balanced BSTs, and reason about which data structure fits problems needing fast lookup, top-k/priority, or ordered range queries.
check: Why can't a hash map answer 'give me the smallest key' or a range query efficiently?
When is a heap the right choice over a sorted array or a BST?
What does a balanced BST offer that a hash map does not?
a: Hash maps scatter keys with no order, so min/max and range queries would require scanning all entries (O(n)).
When you repeatedly need the min/max (or top-k) with cheap inserts and don't need full ordering; heap gives O(log n) push/pop and O(1) peek.
Ordered operations: in-order traversal, predecessor/successor, and range queries, all in O(log n), which hashing can't do.

t: Recognize the core patterns behind most array/string problems
desc: Study the recurring templates: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, binary search on the answer, and monotonic stack, and learn to map a problem's constraints to the pattern that fits before coding.
check: What signals in a problem suggest a sliding window rather than brute force?
When does 'binary search on the answer' apply, and what must be true of the predicate?
What class of problems does a monotonic stack solve in O(n)?
a: A contiguous subarray/substring with a constraint that grows/shrinks monotonically (e.g. sum <= k, at most k distinct), letting you slide instead of re-scan.
When the answer lies in a range and feasibility is monotonic (if x works, all larger/smaller do), you binary-search x and test feasibility each step.
Next-greater/next-smaller element problems: maintaining a stack that stays sorted lets you resolve each element's answer in amortized O(1).

t: Understand dynamic programming: states, transitions, and memoization
desc: Learn to formulate a DP: define the state precisely, write the recurrence (transition), identify base cases, and choose top-down memoization vs bottom-up tabulation. Reason about why overlapping subproblems make DP pay off.
check: What two properties must a problem have for DP to apply?
How do you decide the dimensions and meaning of your DP state?
When is top-down memoization preferable to bottom-up tabulation, and vice versa?
a: Optimal substructure (optimal solution built from optimal subproblem solutions) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems recur).
The state must capture just enough that the subproblem is independent of how you reached it; each varying quantity in the recurrence becomes a dimension.
Top-down is easier to write and only computes reachable states; bottom-up avoids recursion overhead/stack limits and enables space optimization over the table.

t: Clear OverTheWire Bandit levels 0 through 15
desc: Work through Bandit from level 0, practicing SSH login, reading awkward filenames, find with filters, file-type detection, and simple decoding to retrieve each level's password.
check: You reach level 16 with its password saved
You can SSH into the next level using the recovered credentials
You can explain the find and file commands you used to locate hidden passwords

desc: Continue Bandit through the harder stretch: SSL/openssl client connections, cron-based password rotation, setuid helper binaries, and a git-repository level, retrieving each password.

You exploited the cron/setuid level correctly rather than by guessing
You recovered a password from the git repo level using git history

t: Finish OverTheWire Narnia levels 0 through 4
desc: Exploit the Narnia setuid binaries: classic stack buffer overflows and environment/variable manipulation to redirect execution and obtain the next level's shell/password.

For at least one level you computed the overflow offset deliberately
You can explain how a setuid binary lets the exploit escalate privileges

t: Break the ciphers in OverTheWire Krypton
desc: Solve the Krypton wargame: ROT/Caesar, substitution via frequency analysis, Vigenere, and an ECB-mode exercise, recovering each stage's key or plaintext.
check: You complete all Krypton levels and recover the final password
You broke the Vigenere stage using key-length analysis, not brute force
You can explain why the ECB stage leaked structure

You handled 16-byte stack alignment where required

In write4 you located a writable address and a mov [reg],reg gadget
In badchars you encoded the string to avoid the forbidden bytes and fixed it up in memory

In pivot you performed a stack pivot into the provided writable region

t: Complete exploit.education Protostar stack0 through stack5

check: Each level behaves as intended (variable flipped, function called, or shellcode run)

write4 teaches writing a chosen string into memory via gadgets; badchars adds working around filtered/forbidden bytes.
Using the __libc_csu_init gadgets to set rdi/rsi/rdx and call a pointer, needed when clean argument gadgets are missing.

Curated VMs with levels that each isolate one memory-corruption bug class with minimal distractions and known mitigations.
When you want a guided, autograded syllabus that builds skills in order rather than a loose set of standalone challenges.

t: Why do almost 90% of people live in the Northern Hemisphere?
desc: Compare land area and population by hemisphere, then look at what makes the most crowded regions so habitable. Focus on land distribution, climate and farming.
check: What share of land and of people is in the Northern Hemisphere?
Why are the large southern landmasses relatively lightly populated?
What do the most populous regions (East Asia, South Asia, Europe) have in common?
a: About two-thirds of land (roughly 68%) and around 87-90% of people.
Antarctica is ice, Australia is mostly arid, and much of southern Africa and South America is desert, rainforest or mountains; the hemisphere is mostly ocean.
Fertile river plains and monsoon or temperate climates that support intensive farming of rice or wheat, plus long histories of dense settlement.

t: How plate tectonics built the Himalayas, the Andes and Iceland
desc: Learn the three kinds of plate boundary (convergent, divergent, transform) with real examples. Focus on why each produces different mountains, earthquakes and volcanoes.
check: Why do the Andes have many volcanoes while the Himalayas have almost none?
Why is Iceland above sea level when most of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is underwater?
Why does the San Andreas Fault produce big earthquakes but few volcanoes?
a: In the Andes the oceanic Nazca plate subducts and releases water that melts mantle into magma. In the Himalayas two continents collide; crust thickens instead.
A mantle hotspot sits under the ridge there, supplying extra magma that has built a thick volcanic plateau.
It is a transform boundary where plates slide past each other; with no subduction or spreading, little magma forms, but stress builds and releases.

t: Draw Africa's countries from memory, then check

check: At least 40 countries placed roughly correctly on the first attempt
Every coastal country is on the correct coast (Atlantic, Mediterranean, Red Sea or Indian Ocean)
Your second attempt at your weakest region has no errors

t: Why are deserts where they are? Hadley cells, rain shadows, cold currents
desc: Learn the four main causes of deserts: subtropical high pressure, rain shadows, cold ocean currents and distance from the sea. Match each cause to real deserts such as the Sahara, Atacama and Gobi.
check: Why do so many big deserts sit near 30 degrees north and south?
Why is the Atacama one of the driest places on Earth?
Why is the Gobi a desert despite lying far from 30 degrees?
a: Air rising at the equator descends around 30 degrees, warming and drying as it sinks; the resulting high pressure suppresses rain (Sahara, Kalahari, Australia).
The cold Humboldt Current chills and stabilises coastal air, the Andes block moisture from the east, and the subtropical high adds further dryness.
It is very far from any ocean (continentality) and sits in the rain shadow of the Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau.

t: Why every flat map lies: Mercator vs equal-area projections
desc: Learn why a sphere cannot be flattened without distortion, and compare Mercator, Gall-Peters and a compromise projection like Robinson or Winkel Tripel. Focus on what each preserves and what it sacrifices.
check: Why does Greenland look as big as Africa on Mercator, and how big is it really?
Why is Mercator still used for navigation and web maps?
Why can no flat map preserve both area and shape everywhere?
a: Mercator stretches areas more and more toward the poles. Africa is about 14 times the size of Greenland.
It preserves angles locally, so a constant compass bearing is a straight line, and zoomed-in street maps keep correct shapes.
A sphere has curvature and a plane does not (Gauss's Theorema Egregium), so flattening must distort area, shape, distance or direction somewhere.

t: How the South Asian monsoon works and why billions depend on it
desc: Study the seasonal wind reversal, the role of land-sea heating, the Himalayas and the shifting tropical rain belt. Focus on what the monsoon means for farming, floods, water and the economy.
check: What causes the winds to reverse between summer and winter?
Why do the Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau matter for the monsoon?
Why does a weak monsoon hurt more than just farmers?
a: In summer land heats faster than the ocean, creating low pressure that pulls in moist sea air; in winter the land cools and winds blow from land to sea.
They force moist air upward (heavy orographic rain), block cold northern air, and the heated plateau strengthens the summer low.
Much farmland is rain-fed, so poor harvests raise food prices and cut rural spending; reservoirs, hydropower and drinking water also suffer.

t: What does being landlocked cost a country?
desc: Study the world's roughly 44 landlocked countries, from Bolivia and Ethiopia to Switzerland and Kazakhstan. Focus on trade costs, dependence on neighbours, and why some landlocked countries thrive anyway.
check: Why do landlocked developing countries tend to be poorer than their coastal neighbours?
How did Bolivia and Ethiopia lose their coastlines?
Which two countries are doubly landlocked?
a: Higher transport costs, reliance on neighbours' ports and goodwill, border delays and conflict. Rich neighbours and high-value exports can offset this.
Bolivia lost its coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879-84); Ethiopia when Eritrea became independent in 1993.
Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan.

t: Why cities grow where they do: site and situation
desc: Take five great cities, such as Istanbul, London, Singapore, Chicago and Cairo, and work out why each grew where it did. Focus on site (the local terrain) versus situation (its place in wider networks).
check: What is the difference between a city's site and its situation?
Why has Istanbul mattered for more than 2,000 years?
Why did Chicago boom in the 19th century?
a: Site is the physical spot: a hill, river crossing, harbour or water supply. Situation is its position relative to routes, regions and resources.
It controls the Bosphorus between the Black Sea and Mediterranean and the Europe-Asia crossing, with a defensible peninsula and the Golden Horn harbour.
It linked the Great Lakes to the Mississippi system (canal opened 1848) and became the rail hub joining eastern cities to western grain and livestock.

t: Learn to read contour lines, then plan a hilly walk

t: Why is so much of the Netherlands below sea level, and how does it stay dry?
desc: Study the Rhine-Meuse delta, peat subsidence, polders and windmill drainage, and the Delta Works built after the 1953 flood. Focus on how human action both caused and solved the problem.
check: Why did the land sink below sea level in the first place?
What is a polder and how is it kept dry?
What disaster prompted the Delta Works, and what did they build?
a: Draining peat bogs for farming made the peat dry out, oxidise and compact, so the ground sank; peat cutting for fuel made it worse.
Low land enclosed by dykes, with water pumped out into canals and rivers, once by windmills and now by electric pumps.
The 1953 North Sea flood, which killed about 1,800 people; it led to dams, sluices and storm surge barriers sealing off the southwestern estuaries.

t: Why did farming start so early in the Fertile Crescent?
desc: Study why agriculture appeared in the Fertile Crescent around 10,000 BC. Focus on the wild ancestors of crops and animals there, Jared Diamond's east-west axis argument, and the criticisms of it.
check: Which crops and animals were first domesticated there?
What is the 'axis' argument about Eurasia versus the Americas and Africa?
What do critics say purely geographic explanations miss?
a: Emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentils, peas, chickpeas and flax; sheep, goats, cattle and pigs.
Eurasia's east-west spread meant similar latitudes and climates, so crops spread easily; north-south continents crossed climate zones, slowing diffusion.
That it underplays human choices, institutions and chance, overstates the axis effect, and that farming also arose independently in several other regions.

t: Why is London so much milder than Calgary at the same latitude?
desc: Study why western Europe has mild winters for its latitude. Focus on prevailing westerly winds off the ocean, the Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Current, and the debate over how much each contributes.
check: Why do mid-latitude west coasts have milder winters than continental interiors?
What does the Gulf Stream contribute, and what is the scientific debate?
Why does Vancouver have mild winters too, despite no Gulf Stream?
a: Prevailing westerlies carry air from the ocean, which stores summer heat and releases it in winter; inland areas lose heat quickly.
It carries heat north. Some researchers (e.g. Seager) argue westerly winds and atmospheric heat transport matter more; most agree the current adds real warmth.
The same westerlies blow in from the Pacific, and coastal mountains shield it from cold continental air.

t: Russia's geography: how size became both strength and burden
desc: Study Russia's terrain, climate, rivers and coastline. Focus on the open North European Plain, the search for warm-water ports, permafrost, and how these have shaped its history and economy.
check: Why has Russia historically sought warm-water ports?
Why does the North European Plain loom so large in Russian security thinking?
Why are Russia's biggest Siberian rivers of limited economic use?
a: Most northern ports freeze in winter, and exits from the Black Sea and Baltic pass through straits controlled by others.
It is flat and open, with few natural barriers; it was the invasion route for Napoleon and Hitler, so Russia has sought strategic depth and buffers.
The Ob, Yenisei and Lena flow north into the Arctic, freeze for months, and do not connect major population centres to world markets.

t: The demographic transition: why birth rates fall as countries develop
desc: Learn the stages of the demographic transition model with examples such as Niger, India and Japan. Focus on why death rates fall before birth rates and what an ageing, shrinking population means.
check: Why does population surge in the second stage?
Why do birth rates fall with urbanisation and girls' education?
What challenges does a late-stage country like Japan face?
a: Death rates fall thanks to cleaner water, vaccines and better food, while birth rates stay high for a generation, so natural increase spikes.
Children cost more and are less needed for farm work, child mortality falls, and educated women marry later, use contraception and have careers.
A shrinking workforce, rising pension and healthcare costs, labour shortages and emptying rural towns.

t: Who owns a river? The Nile, the Indus and upstream power
desc: Study transboundary river disputes through Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and Egypt, and the Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan. Focus on why being upstream gives leverage.
check: Why is Egypt so worried about the GERD?
How did the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty divide the rivers?
Why does being upstream give a country leverage, and what limits it?
a: The Nile supplies nearly all of Egypt's water and most Nile water comes from the Ethiopian highlands; dam operation in droughts could cut supply.
Eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) to India, western (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) mostly to Pakistan. India said in 2025 it was holding the treaty in abeyance.
Dams and withdrawals control the timing and volume of flow. Limits: treaties, international pressure, and the downstream state's own power.

t: Why did the Bronze Age collapse around 1177 BC?
desc: Study the fall of the interconnected Late Bronze Age world: Hittites, Mycenaean palaces, Ugarit, a weakened Egypt. Focus on the competing explanations and why a networked system of states failed together.
check: What are the main proposed causes of the collapse?
Why might dependence on long-distance trade make a collapse spread rather than stay local?
Which great power survived in weakened form, and which ones vanished?
a: Drought, earthquakes, Sea Peoples raids and migration, disrupted trade, internal revolt. Most historians favour a combination: a 'systems collapse'.
Palace economies needed imported tin and copper for bronze plus grain shipments; when one node failed, shortages and instability cascaded to the others.
Egypt survived, repelling the Sea Peoples under Ramesses III but declining afterwards. The Hittite Empire and the Mycenaean palace states disappeared.

t: How did the Mongols build the largest contiguous land empire?
desc: Study Genghis Khan's rise and the conquests from 1206 to 1279. Focus on military organisation, the use of conquered specialists, the yam relay system, and why the empire split within two generations.
check: What did Genghis Khan change about steppe society that made his army more loyal than tribal armies?
How could a nomadic cavalry force capture walled cities in China and Persia?
Why did the empire break into four khanates?
a: He broke up tribal loyalties by organising men into decimal units (10, 100, 1,000, 10,000) that mixed tribes, with promotion by merit and loyalty to him.
They recruited or conscripted Chinese and Muslim engineers for siege weapons, and used massacres of resisting cities to frighten others into surrendering.
Succession disputes, especially the civil war between Kublai and Ariq Boke after 1259, left the Yuan, Ilkhanate, Golden Horde and Chagatai acting independently.

t: The Meiji Restoration: how Japan industrialised in one generation
desc: Trace Japan from Perry's arrival in 1853 to victory over Russia in 1905. Focus on why samurai-born leaders dismantled their own class and which institutions Japan borrowed from which Western countries.
check: Why did Perry's 'black ships' undermine the Tokugawa shogunate?
Why would leaders from the samurai class abolish samurai privileges?
What did Japan's 1905 victory over Russia signal to the rest of the world?
a: Signing unequal treaties showed the shogunate could not protect Japan, so domains like Satsuma and Choshu rallied around the emperor to overthrow it.
They feared being colonised like China. A conscript army, national taxes and a central state required abolishing domains and hereditary stipends.
It was the first modern defeat of a European great power by an Asian one, inspiring anti-colonial movements and encouraging Japan's own imperial expansion.

t: Mansa Musa and the wealth of the Mali Empire
desc: Read about Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca via Cairo. Focus on where Mali's gold came from, how the trans-Saharan trade worked, and how Timbuktu became a centre of Islamic scholarship.
check: Where did Mali's wealth come from?
What reportedly happened to the value of gold in Cairo after his visit, and why?
How did the pilgrimage change how Europeans pictured West Africa?
a: Control and taxation of gold from fields like Bambuk and Bure, traded north across the Sahara for salt, copper, cloth and horses.
Accounts such as al-Umari's say his lavish spending and gifts flooded the market and depressed gold's value in Cairo for years.
He appears on the 1375 Catalan Atlas holding a gold nugget; West Africa became known as a land of gold, feeding later Portuguese ambitions.

t: How a Balkan assassination became World War I in five weeks
desc: Go beyond 'Franz Ferdinand was shot': study the alliance system, the July Crisis of 1914, mobilisation timetables and the Schlieffen Plan. Focus on how each step escalated a local crisis into a continental war.
check: Why did Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia draw in Russia and then Germany?
Why did Germany invade Belgium, and why did that bring Britain in?
What are the main positions historians take on responsibility for the war?
a: Russia backed Serbia and began mobilising; Germany had given Austria a 'blank cheque' and treated Russian mobilisation as a threat requiring war.
The Schlieffen Plan aimed to beat France fast by going through Belgium; Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality (1839) and feared German control of the coast.
Fischer: German aims drove the war. Others stress shared responsibility, Austrian and Russian choices, rigid alliances, or 'sleepwalking' (Clark).

t: Why was the 1947 Partition of India so violent?
desc: Study the end of British rule and the creation of India and Pakistan. Focus on the rushed timetable, the Radcliffe Line, and how communal politics hardened during the 1940s.
check: Why was the border drawn so fast, and what did that cause on the ground?
How did the Muslim League's demand for Pakistan gain force in the 1940s?
Roughly how many people were displaced and killed?
a: Independence was brought forward to August 1947; Radcliffe had about five weeks, and the line was published only after independence, leaving millions unsure.
Fear of Hindu-majority rule, the 1940 Lahore Resolution, the failed 1946 Cabinet Mission plan, and the Direct Action Day killings in Calcutta.
Roughly 10-20 million displaced; estimates of deaths range from about 200,000 to 2 million.

t: The Atlantic slave trade: scale, routes and long-term consequences
desc: Study the trade from about 1500 to the 1860s: where captives came from, the Middle Passage, and where they were taken. Focus on its role in the Americas' economies and its long-term effects on West and Central Africa.
check: Where did most enslaved Africans end up?
Why did sugar plantations create such relentless demand for enslaved labour?
What are the main arguments about the trade's effects on African societies?
a: Brazil and the Caribbean took the large majority of roughly 12.5 million people embarked; mainland North America received under 5%.
Sugar was labour-intensive and brutal; very high death rates and low birth rates meant planters kept buying new captives rather than populations growing.
Depopulation, more warfare and raiding, the rise of slaving states like Dahomey, and studies (e.g. Nunn) linking it to lower trust and development today.

t: How the Black Death reshaped medieval Europe
desc: Study the plague of 1347-1351 and the decades after. Focus on the economic and social consequences: labour shortages, rising wages, elite backlash, peasant revolts, and the decline of serfdom in the west.
check: Why did wages rise for survivors?
How did elites try to respond, and what did that lead to?
How did the plague travel from Central Asia into Europe?
a: Perhaps 30-50% of Europeans died. Labour became scarce while land was plentiful, so workers could demand more pay and better terms.
Laws like England's Statute of Labourers tried to cap wages; resentment fed revolts like the 1381 Peasants' Revolt, and serfdom eroded in western Europe.
Along trade routes to Crimea, including Genoese Caffa; ships carried it to Sicily and Mediterranean ports in 1347, then it spread inland.

t: Sketch the Silk Roads and mark 8 key cities from memory

t: Why did the Western Roman Empire fall but the Eastern survive?
desc: Compare the two halves of the Roman Empire from the Gothic crossing of the Danube in 376 to 476 and beyond. Focus on geography, wealth, the defences of Constantinople, and the main explanations historians give.
check: What made Constantinople so hard to capture?
Why was the West's tax base more fragile than the East's?
What are the main explanations historians give for the West's collapse?
a: Water on three sides, the Theodosian Land Walls, and naval control of the straits so it could be supplied by sea during sieges.
The East was richer and more urban. The West lost key revenue provinces, above all Africa to the Vandals in 439, so it could not pay armies: a spiral.
Barbarian pressure (Goths, Huns), civil wars and usurpers, fiscal collapse; some stress gradual 'transformation'. Most argue for a combination.

t: The Haitian Revolution: the slave revolt that founded a nation
desc: Study Saint-Domingue from 1791 to 1804. Focus on Toussaint Louverture, why France, Spain and Britain all failed to control the colony, and the price Haiti later paid for recognition.
check: Why was Saint-Domingue so valuable to France?
Why did Napoleon's 1802 expedition fail?
What was the 1825 indemnity and what did it do to Haiti?
a: It was the world's richest colony, producing a huge share of the world's sugar and coffee on the labour of about half a million enslaved people.
Yellow fever devastated French troops, and news that France was restoring slavery elsewhere, plus Toussaint's capture, reignited resistance under Dessalines.
France demanded 150 million francs (later cut to 90 million) under threat of warships; the debt and loans to pay it drained Haiti for generations.

t: Why did Qing China decline in the 19th century?
desc: Study the Opium Wars, the Taiping Rebellion and the Self-Strengthening Movement. Focus on how internal crisis and foreign pressure reinforced each other on the road to 1911.
check: Why did Britain go to war over opium?
Why was the Taiping Rebellion so deadly, and what did it reveal about the Qing state?
Why did Self-Strengthening achieve less than Japan's Meiji reforms?
a: Britain bought vast amounts of tea and balanced the deficit with Indian opium; when Lin Zexu destroyed opium stocks in 1839, Britain fought to force trade open.
A 1850-64 civil war that killed perhaps 20-30 million through fighting, famine and disease; the regular army failed and regional armies had to win it.
It bought Western arms and ships without reforming institutions, faced conservative court opposition, and depended on regional officials.

t: Chart what crossed the Atlantic in the Columbian Exchange

Every cell contains a specific fact (a name, date or number), not a generic phrase
A 3-4 sentence conclusion identifies one pattern and one revolution that breaks it

t: How the Cold War was fought in the Global South
desc: Study the Bandung Conference, the Congo Crisis of 1960-65, the Angolan civil war and the Soviet war in Afghanistan. Focus on why local conflicts became superpower battlegrounds and how non-aligned states played both sides.
check: What was the Non-Aligned Movement and why did leaders like Nehru and Nasser want it?
Why did the Congo crisis pull in the USA, the USSR and the UN?
Why did the 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan matter beyond Afghanistan?
a: A grouping (Bandung 1955, Belgrade 1961) of new states refusing to join either bloc, keeping independence and getting aid from both sides.
Congo's minerals, Katanga's secession and Lumumba's appeal to Moscow; the US and Belgium backed his opponents, and he was killed in 1961.
It ended detente; the US, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia armed the mujahideen, the war drained the USSR, and it fed later civil war and jihadist networks.
