t: The Inca Empire: running a state without writing or money
desc: Study Tawantinsuyu from about 1438 to 1533. Focus on the road network, quipu record-keeping, the mit'a labour tax, and how Pizarro's tiny force toppled it.
check: How did the Inca state collect taxes without money?
What were quipus used for?
How could about 170 Spaniards capture the Inca emperor?
a: Through mit'a: households owed labour on state lands, roads and armies. Produce went into storehouses (qollqa) and was redistributed by the state.
Knotted cords recording numbers such as census counts, tribute and storehouse contents; some scholars think they also encoded narrative.
Smallpox had killed Huayna Capac, sparking civil war between Atahualpa and Huascar; add surprise at Cajamarca, steel, horses and indigenous allies.

t: Why is the sky blue but sunsets red?
desc: Learn Rayleigh scattering: why scattering strength goes as 1/λ⁴, how the path of sunlight through air lengthens from noon to sunset, and why clouds don't follow the same rule.
check: Why isn't the sky violet, if violet light scatters even more than blue?
Why are clouds white or grey rather than blue?
Roughly how many times more strongly is 450 nm blue light scattered than 700 nm red light?
a: Sunlight has less violet than blue, some violet is absorbed high up, and our eyes are far less sensitive to violet, so the mix we see reads as blue.
Cloud droplets are much larger than light's wavelength, so they scatter all colours about equally (Mie scattering), which looks white.
(700/450)⁴ ≈ 5.9, so about 6 times.

t: How does a microwave oven actually heat food?
desc: Learn dielectric heating: how a 2.45 GHz field twists polar water molecules, why it is not a 'water resonance', and why the oven cavity has fixed hot and cold spots.
check: Why does frozen food thaw so unevenly in a microwave?
Why can you see through the metal mesh in the door while the microwaves can't get out?
Why does a microwave oven need a turntable?
a: Ice absorbs microwaves far less than liquid water, so patches that melt first absorb more and heat faster: a runaway effect.
The mesh holes are a few mm, far smaller than the ~12 cm microwave wavelength, so they block microwaves but pass visible light (~0.5 µm).
Standing waves make fixed hot and cold spots about 6 cm apart; rotating the food moves it through them to even out heating.

t: Why does ice float, and why does that keep lakes alive in winter?
desc: Learn how hydrogen bonds give ice an open crystal lattice, why liquid water is densest near 4°C, and what that means for a lake as it freezes.
check: Why does a lake freeze from the top down instead of the bottom up?
What fraction of an iceberg sits below the waterline, and why?
What would happen to lakes if ice were denser than liquid water?
a: Water near 4°C is densest and sinks; colder water stays on top and freezes there, and the ice layer then insulates the water below.
About 90%: the submerged fraction equals ice's density (~917 kg/m³) divided by seawater's (~1025 kg/m³).
Ice would sink and pile up on the bottom, shielded from the sun, so many lakes would freeze solid and stay mostly frozen.

t: Why does salt melt ice, and why does it fail in deep cold?
desc: Learn freezing-point depression: why dissolved particles make it harder for water to freeze, why the effect depends on particle count rather than type, and the limits of road salt.
check: Why does salt make ice melt even when the air is below 0°C?
Why is road salt nearly useless at -25°C?
Why does calcium chloride work better than the same number of moles of table salt?
a: Dissolved ions lower the freezing point of the water they're in, so ice at, say, -5°C is now above the brine's freezing point and melts.
Salt water can't stay liquid below its eutectic point, about -21°C for NaCl, and melting is already very slow well before that.
CaCl₂ splits into 3 ions vs 2 for NaCl, and the effect scales with particle count; it also releases heat as it dissolves.

t: Why can't you drink through a straw more than 10 metres tall?
desc: Learn what really pushes liquid up a straw, compute the 10.3 m limit from atmospheric pressure with p = ρgh, and see why a mercury barometer is only 76 cm tall.
check: Why is 'suction pulls the water up' the wrong picture?
Calculate the maximum height of a water column the atmosphere can support.
Why is a mercury barometer column about 76 cm rather than 10 m?
a: You only lower the pressure in your mouth; the atmosphere pressing on the open surface pushes the liquid up.
h = 101,325 Pa / (1000 kg/m³ × 9.81 m/s²) ≈ 10.3 m, even with a perfect vacuum at the top.
Mercury is 13.6 times denser than water, so 10.3 m / 13.6 ≈ 0.76 m.

t: How much energy is locked in mass? E=mc² with real numbers
desc: Work through E=mc² for everyday masses, learn the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve, and see why both splitting heavy nuclei and fusing light ones release energy.
check: Estimate the energy released by converting 1 gram of mass, in kilotons of TNT.
Why do splitting uranium and fusing hydrogen both release energy?
Roughly what fraction of a uranium-235 nucleus's mass turns into energy when it fissions?
a: E = 0.001 kg × (3×10⁸ m/s)² = 9×10¹³ J ≈ 21 kilotons of TNT (1 kt ≈ 4.2×10¹² J).
Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron and nickel; moving toward that peak from either side releases energy as a small loss of mass.
About 0.1%: roughly 200 MeV released out of about 220,000 MeV of rest energy.

t: How does a heat pump pull heat from cold outdoor air into a warm house?
desc: Learn the refrigeration cycle (evaporate, compress, condense, expand), why a heat pump can deliver 3 to 4 times more heat than the electricity it uses, and what limits that.
check: Why doesn't a coefficient of performance of 3 violate conservation of energy?
Why does an evaporating refrigerant absorb heat?
Why does a heat pump get less efficient as the outdoor temperature drops?
a: It moves existing heat rather than creating it: 1 kJ of work carries about 2 kJ from outside, delivering 3 kJ indoors.
Evaporation needs latent heat to pull molecules apart; at low pressure the refrigerant boils below outdoor temperature and takes that heat from the air.
The temperature lift grows; the ideal limit COP = T_hot/(T_hot - T_cold) in kelvin falls as the gap widens, and real units follow the trend.

t: Why can't ants be the size of elephants? The square-cube law
desc: Learn how area and volume scale differently with size, then apply it to bone strength, heat loss, falling, and why giant movie monsters could not stand up.
check: If an animal is scaled up 10 times in length, what happens to the stress on its leg bones?
Why do shrews and small birds need to eat a large fraction of their body weight every day?
Why can a mouse survive a fall that would kill a horse?
a: Mass grows 1000x but bone cross-section only 100x, so stress rises 10x; that's why big animals have proportionally thicker bones.
Heat loss scales with surface area but body mass with volume; small bodies have far more surface per gram, so they lose heat fast.
Drag scales with area and weight with volume, so small animals fall at a much lower terminal speed and hit with far less force per area.

t: Why do hot things glow red, then yellow, then white?
desc: Learn blackbody radiation and Wien's law (peak wavelength ≈ 2.9 mm·K / T), and use them to explain stove elements, the colours of stars, and why you glow in infrared.
check: At what wavelength does a human body at 310 K emit most strongly?
Why are there no green stars?
Why does a stove element at 400 K not glow visibly, but at 1000 K glows red?
a: λ ≈ 2.9×10⁻³ m·K / 310 K ≈ 9.4 µm, in the infrared, which is what thermal cameras detect.
When the peak is green (around 5800 K, like the Sun) the spectrum is broad enough to contain all colours, so the star looks white.
At 400 K almost nothing is emitted at visible wavelengths; by ~1000 K the short-wavelength tail reaches visible red, though the peak is still infrared.

t: Entropy: why heat flows from hot to cold and never back on its own
desc: Learn entropy as a count of microstates, the second law of thermodynamics and Carnot's limit on engines, and work through why mixing, melting and heat flow only go one way.
check: Show that moving heat Q from a hot body to a cold body increases total entropy.
How can a fridge make its inside colder without breaking the second law?
What is the maximum possible efficiency of a heat engine running between 600 K and 300 K?
a: The hot body loses Q/T_hot and the cold body gains Q/T_cold; since T_cold < T_hot the gain is bigger, so total entropy rises.
It uses work and dumps more heat into the kitchen than it removes from inside, so the room's entropy rises more than the inside's falls.
The Carnot limit: 1 - 300/600 = 50%. Real engines achieve less.

t: What actually happens inside a lithium-ion battery?
desc: Learn how lithium ions shuttle between graphite and a metal-oxide electrode through the electrolyte while electrons flow through your device, and what sets voltage, capacity and wear.
check: Why must the electrolyte conduct ions but not electrons?
Why is a cell's voltage set by its chemistry rather than its size?
Estimate the energy stored in a 4000 mAh, 3.85 V phone battery, in joules.
a: If electrons could cross inside, the cell would short and discharge internally; forcing them round the external circuit is what does useful work.
Voltage comes from the difference in lithium's chemical energy in the two electrode materials; size only changes how much charge is stored.

t: Why does each element glow its own colours? Atoms and quantized energy
desc: Learn why electrons in atoms occupy discrete energy levels, how jumps between levels emit exact wavelengths, and how that lets us read the make-up of neon signs and distant stars.
check: Hydrogen's red line is at 656 nm. What energy difference is that, in electronvolts?
Why does every element have its own unique line spectrum?
Why doesn't an electron just spiral down into the nucleus?
a: E = hc/λ ≈ 1240 eV·nm / 656 nm ≈ 1.89 eV.
Level energies depend on the nuclear charge and the electron arrangement, which differ for every element, so the allowed jumps differ too.
Electrons behave as waves; squeezing one into a smaller space raises its kinetic energy (uncertainty principle), so there is a lowest state with nothing below.

t: Measure the speed of light with a microwave and a chocolate bar

check: You found at least two distinct melted spots and measured the distance between them
Your value of c is within 10% of 3.0×10⁸ m/s

t: Fermi-estimate how many molecules of Caesar's last breath you just inhaled

You can name the assumption most likely to be wrong (complete mixing, molecules recycled by chemistry or dissolved in the oceans)

t: Measure gravity with a pendulum and a stopwatch

t: Make a red-cabbage pH indicator and rank your kitchen by acidity
desc: Simmer chopped red cabbage in water, strain it, and add the purple juice to lemon juice, vinegar, milk, water, baking soda solution and soapy water. Use only food items and soap; never mix cleaning products.

You ranked 6 liquids from most acidic to most basic
You can explain that the anthocyanin pigment changes shape, and so colour, as it gains or loses hydrogen ions

t: Measure your own power output by running up the stairs
desc: Time yourself running up a flight of stairs, measure its vertical height, and compute power = mass × 9.81 × height / time. Compare the result with a light bulb and with one horsepower.
check: You calculated your power in watts (a short stair sprint is typically 300-900 W)
You compared it with 1 horsepower (746 W)
You can explain why your body burned roughly 4 times more energy than the work you did (muscles are ~25% efficient)

t: Supercool water in your freezer, then freeze it on command
desc: Put unopened bottles of purified or still bottled water in the freezer for about 2-3 hours, checking regularly, catch one still liquid below 0°C, then trigger freezing by tapping it or pouring it onto an ice cube.
check: You had liquid water below 0°C and turned it into slush on demand
You can explain why freezing needs a nucleation site to start
You can explain why only part of it freezes at first (released latent heat warms it back to 0°C)

t: Derive how long a fall through a tunnel through the Earth would take
desc: Assuming uniform density and no air, use the shell theorem to show gravity inside Earth grows linearly with distance from the centre, solve the resulting motion, and compute the trip time.
check: You showed that inside a uniform Earth gravity equals g × r/R
You got simple harmonic motion with a one-way trip of about 42 minutes
You showed the trip takes the same time for any straight tunnel between two surface points, not just through the centre

t: Measure the width of a hair with a laser pointer
desc: Tape a hair across a card frame, shine a low-power laser pointer through it onto a wall 2-3 m away, measure the dark-fringe spacing, and use width = wavelength × distance / spacing. Never look into the beam.
check: You got a clear pattern of bright and dark fringes on the wall
You calculated a width in the 20-150 µm range
You can explain why a thinner hair gives more widely spaced fringes

t: Why do we have seasons? (It's not the distance to the Sun)
desc: Learn how Earth's 23.4° axial tilt changes the Sun's height and the length of the day through the year, and why our changing distance from the Sun barely matters.
check: What two facts prove distance from the Sun can't be the cause of seasons?
Give the two reasons summer days deliver more solar energy.
What would seasons be like if Earth's axis had no tilt?
a: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter, and the two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time.
The Sun is higher, so each square metre gets more concentrated sunlight, and days are longer, so there are more hours of heating.
Almost none: just a ~7% swing in sunlight from the slightly elliptical orbit, the same in both hemispheres.

t: Why does the Moon have phases, and why isn't there an eclipse every month?
desc: Learn how Sun-Earth-Moon geometry produces the phases, why the Moon's tilted orbit makes eclipses rare, and why we always see the same face.
check: Why is 'Earth's shadow causes the phases' wrong?
If there's a new moon every month, why isn't there a solar eclipse every month?
Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
a: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us; Earth's shadow only reaches the Moon during a lunar eclipse, at full moon.
The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's, so it usually passes above or below the Sun; eclipses need new or full moon near the crossing points (nodes).
Tidal friction locked it: it now spins exactly once per orbit (27.3 days), so the same face always points at Earth.

t: Why is the ISS constantly falling but never hitting the ground?
desc: Learn what an orbit really is, why astronauts float even though gravity at 400 km is about 90% as strong as at the surface, and the counterintuitive rules of orbital manoeuvres.
check: Why are astronauts weightless if gravity up there is still strong?
Estimate the ISS's orbital speed and period at about 400 km altitude.
To catch up with a spacecraft ahead of you in the same orbit, why do you first slow down?
a: They and the station are in free fall together, moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away as quickly as they fall.
v = √(GM/r) with r ≈ 6,770 km gives about 7.7 km/s and a period of about 92 minutes.
Slowing drops you into a lower orbit with a shorter period, so you gain on the target; then you raise your orbit to meet it.

t: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury?
desc: Compare the two inner planets' distance from the Sun, reflectivity, atmosphere and rotation, and learn how a runaway greenhouse effect made Venus about 465°C day and night.
check: Why is Venus hotter even though it's nearly twice as far from the Sun and reflects about 75% of sunlight?
Why does Mercury's night side drop to about -180°C?
Why is Venus's surface nearly the same temperature day and night, pole to equator?
a: Its crushing CO₂ atmosphere (~92 times Earth's surface pressure) traps outgoing infrared so well that the surface reaches ~465°C: a runaway greenhouse.
With almost no atmosphere to hold or move heat, the surface radiates freely to space through a long night (a Mercury solar day lasts ~176 Earth days).
The massive atmosphere stores and circulates enormous amounts of heat, evening out temperature differences.

t: How do we find planets around other stars?
desc: Learn the transit and radial-velocity methods, calculate how much a planet dims its star, and see why the planets we've found are biased toward big, close-in ones.
check: Seen from far away, how much does Jupiter dim the Sun during a transit? And Earth?
Why does the transit method miss most planetary systems?
What does the radial-velocity method measure, and why does it favour massive, close-in planets?
a: Dimming ≈ (R_planet/R_star)²: about 1% for Jupiter and about 0.008% (84 parts per million) for Earth.
The orbit must be almost exactly edge-on to us; for an Earth-like orbit around a Sun-like star the chance is only about 0.5%.
The star's Doppler wobble around the shared centre of mass; heavy, close planets swing the star faster, giving a bigger signal.

t: How GPS would fail within a day without Einstein's relativity
desc: Learn how GPS turns signal travel times into a position, and why the satellites' clocks drift relative to ground clocks because of both special and general relativity.
check: Why does a receiver need signals from at least 4 satellites, not 3?
Which effect makes satellite clocks run fast, which makes them run slow, and what's the net drift per day?
Estimate the position error after one day if that drift weren't corrected.
a: Three unknowns for position (x, y, z) plus a fourth for the receiver's own inaccurate clock.
Weaker gravity at altitude makes them gain ~45 µs/day; their orbital speed makes them lose ~7 µs/day; net ~38 µs/day fast.
38 µs × 300,000 km/s ≈ 11 km of ranging error per day.

t: What is a black hole's event horizon, really?
desc: Learn the Schwarzschild radius r = 2GM/c², what happens to light and time near a horizon, and why tidal forces depend so strongly on a black hole's mass.
check: What would the Schwarzschild radius be for the Sun, and for the Earth?
If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, what would happen to Earth's orbit?
Why would you be torn apart before reaching a small black hole's horizon but could cross a supermassive one's unharmed?
a: About 3 km for the Sun and about 9 mm for the Earth.
Nothing: gravity at Earth's distance depends only on the mass, so the orbit is unchanged (though it would get dark and very cold).
Tidal stretching at the horizon scales as 1/M²; a huge black hole has a huge horizon where the gravity gradient across your body is gentle.

t: Where were the atoms in your body made?
desc: Trace your elements to their origins: hydrogen from the Big Bang, carbon and oxygen from fusion in stars, and the heaviest elements from neutron capture in stellar explosions and collisions.
check: Which of your atoms are older than any star?
Why does fusion inside stars stop producing energy at iron?
Where does gold come from, if stars can't make it by ordinary fusion?
a: Your hydrogen atoms (about 60% of all your atoms) were made in the Big Bang; nearly everything heavier was forged in stars.
Iron and nickel have the highest binding energy per nucleon; fusing them into heavier nuclei absorbs energy instead of releasing it.
Rapid neutron capture (the r-process) in neutron star mergers and possibly rare supernovae.

t: The cosmic distance ladder: how we measured the size and age of the universe
desc: Learn parallax, Cepheid variable stars, Type Ia supernovae and Hubble's law, how each rung calibrates the next, and how 1/H₀ gives a rough age of the universe.
check: Why do we need a ladder of methods rather than a single one?
A galaxy is receding at 7,000 km/s. With H₀ ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc, how far away is it?
Show that 1/H₀ with H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc is about 14 billion years.
a: Each method only works over a limited range of distances; nearby methods like parallax calibrate the brightness of standard candles used farther out.
d = v/H₀ = 100 Mpc, about 330 million light-years.
1 Mpc ≈ 3.09×10¹⁹ km, so 3.09×10¹⁹/70 ≈ 4.4×10¹⁷ s ≈ 14 billion years (the measured age is 13.8 billion).

t: The cosmic microwave background: the afterglow of the Big Bang
desc: Learn when and why the universe became transparent, how expansion cooled that first light to 2.7 K, and what its tiny ripples reveal about galaxies and the universe's contents.
check: Why was the universe opaque for its first ~380,000 years, and why did it clear?
The CMB was released at about 3000 K. Why do we measure 2.7 K today?
Why do temperature ripples of only 1 part in 100,000 matter so much?
a: Free electrons in the hot plasma scattered light constantly; once it cooled to ~3000 K they joined nuclei into neutral atoms and light travelled freely.
Space has stretched about 1100-fold since then, stretching the light's wavelengths and lowering its temperature by the same factor: 3000/1100 ≈ 2.7 K.
They mark slight density differences that gravity grew into galaxies and clusters, and their pattern pins down the universe's age and composition.

t: What is the actual evidence for dark matter?
desc: Go through the main lines of evidence: galaxy rotation curves, cluster dynamics, gravitational lensing, the Bullet Cluster and the CMB, and why 'just ordinary dark gas' doesn't fit.
check: If visible matter were all there is, what should a galaxy's orbital speed do far from its centre, and what is observed?
Why is the Bullet Cluster hard to explain by modifying gravity alone?
Why can't dark matter just be cold gas, dust or dim stars?
a: Speed should fall off roughly as 1/√r beyond the visible disk; instead it stays roughly flat, implying lots of unseen mass.
Lensing shows most of the mass sits apart from the hot gas, which holds most of the ordinary matter, so the mass isn't where the normal matter is.
Big Bang element ratios and the CMB cap ordinary matter at ~5% of the universe vs ~27% for dark matter, and gas or dust would absorb or glow detectably.

t: The rocket equation: why rockets are mostly fuel
desc: Derive the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation Δv = vₑ ln(m₀/m_f), then use it to see why reaching orbit demands huge mass ratios and why rockets are built in stages.
check: Reaching low Earth orbit takes about 9.4 km/s including losses. With an exhaust speed of 3.5 km/s, what fraction of a single-stage rocket must be propellant?
Why doesn't doubling the fuel double the Δv?
Why does staging help so much?
a: m₀/m_f = e^(9.4/3.5) ≈ 15, so about 93% of the liftoff mass must be propellant.
Δv grows with the logarithm of the mass ratio; the extra fuel must also accelerate itself, so the returns diminish.
Dropping empty tanks and engines means later burns don't waste propellant accelerating dead mass, which raises the effective mass ratio.

t: Why do leaves turn yellow, orange and red in autumn?
desc: Learn which pigments are in a leaf all summer, which are made fresh in autumn, and why trees shed their leaves at all.
check: Where do the yellow and orange colours come from?
Why do sunny days and cool (but not freezing) nights make the reds brighter?
Why do many trees drop their leaves instead of keeping them all winter?
a: Carotenoids are present all summer but masked by chlorophyll; when the tree breaks down and recycles chlorophyll, they show through.
Red anthocyanins are made in autumn from sugars; sunny days produce sugar and cool nights keep it trapped in the leaf.
In winter leaves would lose water while the ground is frozen and risk frost damage, while making little sugar; shedding them is cheaper.

t: Where does a tree's mass come from?
desc: Learn what photosynthesis takes in and gives out, revisit van Helmont's five-year willow experiment, and track where each atom in a tree trunk came from.
check: Van Helmont's willow gained about 74 kg but the soil lost only about 57 g. Where did the mass come from?
Does the oxygen plants release come from the CO₂ or from the water?
Why do leaves look green?
a: Mostly from carbon dioxide in the air (carbon and oxygen), plus hydrogen from water; minerals from soil are only a few percent.
From water: isotope-labelling experiments show the O₂ comes from splitting H₂O, while CO₂'s oxygen ends up in sugar and water.
Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light strongly and reflects relatively more green.

t: Why are big fierce predators so rare? Energy flow in food chains
desc: Learn how energy passes between trophic levels, why typically only about 10% makes it to the next level, and what that means for food chains, populations and diets.
check: Where does the other ~90% of the energy go at each step?
If plants capture 100,000 kcal, roughly how much reaches a predator three levels up?
Why are food chains rarely longer than 4 or 5 levels?
a: Mostly released as heat by respiration for movement and body upkeep, plus parts that are never eaten or not digested.
100,000 → 10,000 → 1,000 → about 100 kcal, at roughly 10% per step.
After a few steps too little energy is left to support a viable population of the next level.

t: Mitochondria: the bacteria that moved into your cells
desc: Learn what mitochondria do with oxygen and food, the evidence that they descend from free-living bacteria, and how they are inherited.
check: What evidence shows mitochondria were once free-living bacteria?
Why do you inherit your mitochondria almost entirely from your mother?
From a mitochondrion's point of view, why do you need oxygen at all?
a: They have their own circular DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes and a double membrane, and they divide by splitting in two like bacteria.
The egg supplies nearly all of the embryo's mitochondria, and the few from the sperm are normally destroyed.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain; without it ATP yield falls from about 30 per glucose to 2.

t: How does a vaccine teach your immune system?
desc: Learn how antigens activate B and T cells, how memory cells make a second response faster and stronger, and how herd immunity thresholds are calculated.
check: Why is the second encounter with a pathogen usually so much milder?
Why do some vaccines need booster doses?
Measles has an R₀ of about 12-18. What share of people must be immune to stop it spreading?
a: Memory B and T cells persist after the first exposure and launch a faster, larger, better-targeted response before the infection takes hold.
Repeat exposure expands the memory cell pool and improves antibody binding (affinity maturation); some protection also wanes over time.
About 1 - 1/R₀, which is roughly 92-94%.

t: How much information is stored in your DNA?
desc: Learn how four bases encode proteins in three-letter codons, how big the human genome is, and how about 20,000 protein-coding genes build a whole human.
check: Estimate the information content of one copy of the human genome in megabytes.
Why does the genetic code use 3-letter codons rather than 2?
How can only about 20,000 protein-coding genes produce something as complex as a human?
a: About 3.1 billion bases × 2 bits ≈ 6.2 billion bits ≈ 775 MB (and much less after compression, since it's repetitive).
Two letters give only 4² = 16 combinations, fewer than the 20 amino acids; three give 64, enough with spares for redundancy and stop signals.
Elaborate regulation controls when and where each gene is switched on, and alternative splicing lets one gene make several proteins.

t: How does a nerve send a signal?
desc: Learn the resting membrane potential, the action potential with its sodium and potassium channels, and how myelin insulation makes signals much faster.
check: Why is an action potential all-or-nothing?
Why does myelin speed up conduction so much?
When you stub your toe, why do you feel the touch before the throbbing pain?
a: At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open, letting in sodium that opens more channels: a self-reinforcing spike of fixed size.
The signal jumps between gaps in the insulation (nodes of Ranvier), reaching up to ~100 m/s versus ~1 m/s in thin unmyelinated fibres.
Touch travels on fast myelinated fibres (~50 m/s), while dull pain uses slow unmyelinated C fibres (~1 m/s), so it arrives later.

t: Why are there roughly equal numbers of males and females?
desc: Learn Fisher's principle, the evolutionary argument for a 1:1 sex ratio, and the cases in nature where ratios are strongly skewed and why.
check: If males were rare, why would parents who produce sons be favoured by selection?
Why is 'a 1:1 ratio is best for the species' not the explanation?
Why do some wasps lay mostly female eggs?
a: Every offspring has one mother and one father, so the rarer sex averages more matings; producing it yields more grandchildren until the ratio evens out.
A mostly female population would grow faster, so 'good for the species' predicts female bias; 1:1 comes from selection on individual parents.
When brothers compete with each other for mates among their own sisters (local mate competition, e.g. fig wasps), a few sons suffice.

t: How natural selection actually works, and the myths about it
desc: Learn the three ingredients of natural selection (variation, inheritance, differential reproduction) and work through antibiotic resistance and the maths of small advantages.
check: Why is 'giraffes stretched their necks and passed it on' wrong?
Why does heavy antibiotic use lead to resistant bacteria?
How many generations does a 1% reproductive advantage take to make a variant 100 times more common relative to the rest?
a: Changes acquired during life aren't inherited; variation in neck length already existed, and longer-necked individuals left more offspring.
Antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria; rare resistant ones, already present or arising by mutation or gene transfer, survive and multiply.
1.01ⁿ = 100 gives n ≈ 460 generations, which is very fast in evolutionary terms.

t: How CRISPR-Cas9 edits DNA
desc: Learn where CRISPR came from (a bacterial immune system), how a guide RNA steers the Cas9 enzyme to a matching DNA site, and how the cell's repair of the cut produces an edit.
check: What was CRISPR originally for in bacteria?
Why is a 20-letter guide sequence enough to target one spot in a 3-billion-letter genome?
After Cas9 cuts, how does the cell's repair lead to either a gene knockout or a precise edit?
a: Storing snippets of viral DNA so Cas proteins can recognise and cut the same virus if it attacks again.
There are 4²⁰ ≈ 10¹² possible 20-letter sequences, far more than the ~6×10⁹ positions in the genome, so a well-chosen guide is usually unique.
Error-prone end joining often inserts or deletes letters, breaking the gene; if a template is supplied, homology-directed repair can copy in a precise change.

t: How could an eye evolve step by step?
desc: Follow the sequence from light-sensitive patch to cup, pinhole and lens eye, see why each stage is useful on its own, and compare the wiring of our eye with an octopus's.
check: What use is 'half an eye'?
Why do you have a blind spot when an octopus doesn't?
According to modelling studies, roughly how fast could a camera eye evolve from a flat light-sensitive patch?
a: Even a light-sensitive patch detects a predator's shadow; a cup adds direction, a pinhole forms an image, and a lens makes it bright and sharp.
Our retina's nerve fibres run in front of the photoreceptors and leave through one hole with no receptors; the octopus retina is wired from behind.
Nilsson and Pelger's 1994 model estimated under 400,000 generations, a geological eyeblink.

t: Follow a red blood cell on one lap around your body
desc: Trace blood through the heart's four chambers, the lungs, arteries, capillaries and veins; learn why the two sides of the heart differ and how long one full circuit takes.
check: Why is the left ventricle's wall much thicker than the right's?
At rest your heart pumps about 5 L per minute and you have about 5 L of blood. How long does a typical lap take?
Why is blood flow slowest in the capillaries, the narrowest vessels?
a: The left side pumps to the whole body at ~120 mmHg; the right only pushes through the nearby lungs at ~25 mmHg, and higher pressure would flood them.
About 1 minute on average, with short routes faster and long ones slower.
There are billions of them, so their total cross-section dwarfs the aorta's; the same flow through more area moves slower, leaving time for exchange.

t: Find your blind spot and measure its size
desc: Draw a cross and a dot 8 cm apart, cover one eye, stare at the cross and move the page until the dot vanishes, then map the blind spot's edges with a pencil tip and convert to degrees.
check: You can make the dot disappear reliably with either eye
You measured its width and position (about 5-6° wide, centred about 15° to the side of where you look)
You can explain why you don't notice it in daily life (the other eye covers it and the brain fills in the gap)

t: Measure your reaction time with a falling ruler
desc: Have a friend drop a ruler between your fingers without warning, record the catch distance for 10 trials with each hand, and convert distance to time with t = √(2d/g).
check: You converted catch distances to times (e.g. 20 cm ≈ 0.20 s)
You recorded the average and spread for each hand over 10 trials
You can explain why a visual reaction can't be much faster than about 0.1 s (nerve travel plus processing in the brain)

t: Dissect a flower and find every reproductive part
desc: Take apart a simple flower such as a lily, tulip or alstroemeria, lay out the sepals, petals, stamens and pistil on paper, and slice the ovary open to find the ovules.
check: You laid out and labelled sepals, petals, anthers, filaments, stigma, style and ovary
You found the ovules inside the ovary
You can explain how pollen landing on the stigma leads to seeds and fruit

t: Extract DNA from strawberries in your kitchen
desc: Mash strawberries with water, dish soap and salt, filter through a coffee filter, then gently pour ice-cold rubbing alcohol on top and spool up the white strands that appear. Keep the alcohol away from flames.
check: You collected visible white strands at the boundary between the alcohol and the strawberry liquid
You can explain what the soap and the salt each do
You can explain why DNA clumps in alcohol and why each strand you see is millions of DNA molecules, not one

t: Dissect a chicken wing to see how muscles move bones
desc: Carefully skin a raw chicken wing, pull individual muscles to see which way each bends the joint, and find tendons, ligaments and cartilage. Wash hands, tools and surfaces well afterwards.
check: You found an antagonistic muscle pair and showed one bends the elbow while the other straightens it
You identified a tendon, a ligament and joint cartilage
You can explain why muscles can only pull, never push

t: Test how temperature affects yeast with three balloons
desc: Put equal amounts of yeast and sugar in three bottles with cold, warm (about 35°C) and hot (about 60°C) water, stretch a balloon over each neck, and measure balloon circumference every 10 minutes.
check: You recorded balloon circumference over time for all three bottles
You identified which temperature produced the most gas and estimated its rate
You can explain the results in terms of enzyme activity and heat killing the yeast cells

t: Grow seedlings that bend toward light and turn to find gravity
desc: Sprout beans on damp paper towel in two jars. Light one only from the side; lay the other on its side once roots appear. Check and photograph both daily for about a week.
check: Your side-lit shoots clearly bent toward the light
Roots in the tipped jar curved to grow downward again within a day or two
You can explain how the hormone auxin redistributes to cause both kinds of bending

t: Bioblitz: find and identify 30 species within 100 m of home
desc: Search a small area thoroughly for plants, insects, spiders, birds, fungi, lichens and anything else alive, photograph each one, and identify it with a field guide or an ID app.
check: You recorded at least 30 species across at least 4 major groups (e.g. plants, insects, birds, fungi)
You noted the exact microhabitat where each was found
You can describe one feeding or other interaction between species that you actually observed

t: Steelman both sides of the trolley problem's footbridge case
desc: Lay out Foot's switch case and Thomson's footbridge case. Write the strongest case for pushing the man (consequentialist) and the strongest case against (rights, using a person as a means), then name the one premise you reject.
check: Each side is written in at least 150 words, in terms its own defenders would accept
You can state one principle that permits switching but forbids pushing, plus one case where it breaks down
You have written down your verdict and the single premise of the other side you reject

t: Why Gettier's three-page paper broke 'justified true belief'
desc: Read Edmund Gettier's 1963 'Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?' (it is about three pages) and work through his Smith and Jones cases, then look at the fake-barn case and the no-false-lemmas fix.
check: What do all Gettier cases have in common that makes the belief true by luck?
What is the no-false-lemmas response, and how does the fake-barn case defeat it?
Why do some philosophers think any JTB-plus-X analysis will face new Gettier cases?
a: The subject has good justification, but it connects to the truth only by accident: the belief comes out true for reasons unrelated to the evidence.
It says knowledge must not rest on a false belief. Among fake barns, Henry infers nothing false yet sees the one real barn by luck, so he seems not to know.
Zagzebski argued that as long as justification does not guarantee truth, you can always construct a case where bad luck is cancelled out by good luck.

t: Read Descartes' Meditations I and II: doubt, the demon and the cogito
desc: Read Meditations I and II (1641) slowly. Track the three waves of doubt (senses, dreaming, evil demon) and exactly what survives them in Meditation II, including the wax example.
check: Why is the dreaming argument not enough to doubt mathematics, and what does the demon add?
What exactly does the cogito establish, and what does it not establish?
What is the Cartesian circle objection?
a: Even in dreams 2 + 3 = 5 and squares have four sides. The deceiving demon or God could make you err even about the simplest truths.
That 'I am, I exist' is true whenever I think it, and that I am a thinking thing. Not that I have a body, nor that anything outside my mind exists.
Arnauld's point: Descartes uses clear and distinct perception to prove God exists, then uses God to guarantee clear and distinct perception.

t: Hume's problem of induction and why it is still unsolved
desc: Read Section IV of Hume's Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) and reconstruct his dilemma about inferring the future from the past. Then compare Popper's falsificationist dodge and Goodman's 'grue' riddle.
check: Why can induction be justified neither by deductive reasoning nor by experience?
How does Popper try to avoid the problem, and what is the usual objection?
What extra problem does Goodman's 'grue' add on top of Hume's?
a: No contradiction in the future differing from the past, so not deductive; arguing 'induction worked before' uses induction, so it is circular.
Science only falsifies, never confirms. Critics reply that relying on well-tested theories for future predictions quietly smuggles induction back in.
Even granting induction, the same evidence supports 'green' and 'grue' equally, so we need a reason to project some predicates and not others.

t: The Euthyphro dilemma and divine command theory
desc: Read Plato's short dialogue Euthyphro, focusing on the question at 10a: is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because it is loved? Restate it for 'good' and 'commanded by God'.
check: What are the two horns of the dilemma, and what is the problem with each?
Why is it a problem specifically for divine command theory?
How do modern theists such as Robert Adams try to escape it?
a: If God commands it because it is good, goodness is independent of God. If it is good because commanded, morality looks arbitrary (God could command cruelty).
DCT says moral rightness just is being commanded by God, which lands it on the arbitrary horn.
They ground goodness in God's unchanging nature rather than in bare will, so commands flow from a good nature and are not arbitrary.

t: Kant's categorical imperative: universal law vs treating people as ends
desc: Read Section II of Kant's Groundwork (1785) on the first two formulations. Apply both to his lying-promise example, then examine the 'murderer at the door' case from his 1797 reply to Benjamin Constant.
check: Why does a lying promise fail the universal law test?
What is the difference between a contradiction in conception and a contradiction in will?
What is the murderer-at-the-door objection, and how do sympathetic Kantians respond?
a: If everyone made false promises when convenient, no one would believe promises, so the maxim cannot even be conceived as universal law.
Conception: the universal maxim is self-defeating (lying promises). Will: it is coherent but no rational agent could want it (never helping anyone).
Kant says you may not lie even to a murderer asking where your friend is. Kantians like Korsgaard argue deceiving someone who uses deceit is permitted.

t: Mill's higher and lower pleasures: can a hedonist rank pleasures?
desc: Read Chapter 2 of Mill's Utilitarianism (1863), focusing on the 'Socrates dissatisfied' passage and his test of competent judges. Decide whether quality of pleasure fits inside hedonism.
check: What is Mill's test for which of two pleasures is higher?
Why do critics say ranking pleasures by quality abandons hedonism?
How does Mill's view differ from Bentham's?
a: Ask people who have experienced both; if almost all of them prefer one even with more discontent attached, it is the higher pleasure.
If one pleasure is better beyond its amount of pleasure, something other than pleasure must be making it better.
Bentham measured only quantity (intensity, duration and so on), 'pushpin is as good as poetry'. Mill adds quality.

t: Rawls' veil of ignorance and Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain reply
desc: Study the original position and two principles of justice from Rawls' A Theory of Justice (1971), then Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain argument from Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974).
check: What are Rawls' two principles, and which has priority?
Why would parties behind the veil choose maximin, and what does Harsanyi object?
What is the Wilt Chamberlain argument meant to show?
a: 1: equal basic liberties for all. 2: fair equality of opportunity, and inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged. 1 has priority.
Not knowing their place, they guard against the worst outcome. Harsanyi argues rational choosers would maximise average utility instead.
Start from any just pattern; free voluntary payments to Wilt upset it. So keeping a pattern requires constantly interfering with liberty.

t: Mary's room and the bat: is consciousness more than physics?
desc: Read Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' (1974) and Frank Jackson's Mary's room argument from 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' (1982). Then study the ability hypothesis reply from Lewis and Nemirow.
check: Set out the knowledge argument in three premises.
What does the ability hypothesis say Mary gains when she first sees red?
What did Jackson himself later conclude about his argument?
a: Mary knows all physical facts about colour; on seeing red she learns something new; so not all facts are physical facts.
No new fact, only new abilities: to recognise, imagine and remember red. Know-how, not know-that.
He became a physicalist by the late 1990s and argued the intuition that Mary learns a new fact is mistaken.

t: Parfit's teletransporter: does personal identity matter?
desc: Study Part Three of Parfit's Reasons and Persons (1984): the teletransporter, the branch-line case and the fission case, and his claim that identity is not what matters in survival.
check: Why does the fission case make it hard to say which person you become?
What is 'Relation R', and why does Parfit think it matters instead of identity?
What is the strongest objection to his view?
a: Both resulting people are equally continuous with you; you cannot be both (they are two), and choosing one is arbitrary.
Psychological connectedness and continuity with any cause. Fission is about as good as ordinary survival even though identity fails.
Many find it absurd that dying and being replaced by a perfect copy is not bad for you; animalists also say we are organisms, not psychologies.

t: Searle's Chinese room: can a program understand?
desc: Read John Searle's 'Minds, Brains, and Programs' (1980). Reconstruct the room, then the systems reply and the robot reply, and Searle's answer to each.
check: What conclusion is the Chinese room meant to establish?
What is the systems reply, and how does Searle answer it?
Does the argument show machines can never think?
a: Running a program (manipulating symbols by syntax) is not sufficient for understanding (semantics), so strong AI is false.
The whole system understands, not the man. Searle: let the man memorise the rules and do it in his head; he still does not understand Chinese.
No. Searle allows a machine with the right causal powers (like a brain) could think; he denies that the program alone is enough.

t: Pascal's wager: the decision matrix and the many-gods problem
desc: Read the 'Infinite-nothing' fragment from Pascal's Pensees and draw the 2x2 decision table. Then test it against the many-gods objection and the worry that belief cannot be chosen.
check: Why does infinite reward make the wager work even at tiny probabilities?
What is the many-gods objection?
What does Pascal say to someone who cannot simply decide to believe?
a: Any non-zero probability times an infinite payoff gives infinite expected value, which beats any finite cost of believing.
Many possible gods with incompatible demands each offer infinite stakes, so the wager does not tell you which to bet on.
Act as if you believe: take holy water, have masses said. Habit will bring belief and reduce the passions that block it.

t: Plato's cave, sun and divided line as one argument
desc: Read the end of Republic VI (sun analogy and divided line, 507-511) and the allegory of the cave in VII (514a-520a). Map each stage of the cave onto a segment of the line.
check: What are the four segments of the divided line?
Which part of the cave corresponds to the Form of the Good?
Why must the freed philosopher return, and what does Plato hint will happen to him?
a: Images (eikasia), physical objects (pistis), mathematical objects (dianoia), Forms (noesis). Lower two are opinion, upper two knowledge.
The sun outside the cave: it makes the Forms knowable and is the source of their being, as the sun gives sight and growth.
Justice requires rulers who know the Good to govern. The prisoners would mock him and kill him if they could, an allusion to Socrates.

t: Validity, soundness and the four basic argument forms
desc: Learn the difference between a valid and a sound argument, then the forms modus ponens, modus tollens, affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent. Write one everyday example of each.
check: Can a valid argument have a false conclusion?
Why is affirming the consequent invalid?
What is the difference between modus tollens and denying the antecedent?
a: Yes, if at least one premise is false. Validity only guarantees that true premises could not lead to a false conclusion.
'If P then Q; Q; so P' fails because Q can be true for other reasons: wet streets do not prove it rained.
Tollens: if P then Q; not Q; so not P (valid). Denying the antecedent: if P then Q; not P; so not Q (invalid).

t: Map Singer's drowning-child argument and find your weak premise
desc: Using Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972), write his argument as numbered premises and a conclusion. Pick the premise you find weakest and write your best case against it.
check: Argument is written as 3-4 numbered premises leading validly to the conclusion
You have named one premise and written at least 100 words against it
You have written Singer's likely reply to your objection in 2-3 sentences

t: Read Plato's Crito and rebut the Laws' argument for staying in prison
desc: Read the Crito in full (about 45 minutes). Reconstruct the speech of the Laws of Athens as an argument map, then write a 300-word reply on behalf of Crito.
check: Your map contains at least three separate lines of argument (harm, parent analogy, tacit agreement)
Your reply attacks a specific premise rather than the conclusion
You can explain how Socrates squares this with his defiance in the Apology

t: Decide whether you'd plug into Nozick's experience machine
desc: Read Nozick's experience machine passage (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974). Write your answer and reasons, then rerun it as De Brigard's reversed version: you learn your current life is already a simulation.
check: You have written a yes or no with three distinct reasons
You have stated what your answer implies for hedonism
You have answered the reversed case and noted whether status quo bias changed your answer

t: Find and label three informal fallacies in a real opinion piece
desc: Pick a recent opinion column or long social media thread. Identify three informal fallacies (e.g. straw man, false dilemma, ad hominem, slippery slope), quote the line and rewrite it as a fair argument.
check: Three quoted passages, each with a named fallacy
For each, one sentence explaining why the reasoning fails
Each has a rewritten version that makes the same point without the fallacy

t: Compare Hobbes' and Locke's state of nature side by side
desc: Read Hobbes' Leviathan chapter 13 and Locke's Second Treatise chapter 2. Build a comparison table (human nature, law, property, why we leave) and write a one-page verdict on which is more realistic.
check: Table has at least five rows filled in for both thinkers
You can explain why Hobbes's life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' but Locke's state of nature has a law
You have written a one-page verdict citing evidence beyond either text

t: Sort your worries with Epictetus' dichotomy of control
desc: Read Epictetus' Enchiridion sections 1-5. List ten things currently bothering you and sort each into 'up to me' and 'not up to me', then rewrite the second group as goals about your own effort and judgments.
check: Ten items are listed and sorted into the two columns
Every 'not up to me' item has a rewritten internal goal
You have noted one case where the Stoic sorting felt wrong and why

t: The bat-and-ball problem and the Cognitive Reflection Test
desc: Try Shane Frederick's three CRT items (2005) cold, then study what the test measures, how it relates to Kahneman's System 1 / System 2 framing, and the main criticisms of dual-process theory.
check: What is the correct answer to the bat-and-ball problem, and why is 10 cents so tempting?
What does a high CRT score predict besides maths ability?
What is the main criticism of the two-systems picture?
a: 5 cents (bat 1.05, total 1.10). 10 cents comes from an intuitive subtraction that feels right and goes unchecked.
A tendency to override intuitive answers: it correlates with patience in choices, fewer heuristic errors and better detection of misleading claims.
Critics say 'System 1' and 'System 2' are metaphors bundling features (fast, automatic, unconscious) that do not reliably go together.

t: Anchoring: why a random number shifts your estimates
desc: Study Tversky and Kahneman's 1974 wheel-of-fortune experiment and later anchoring work, including the Many Labs 1 replication (2014), where anchoring was one of the most robust effects.
check: What happened in the wheel-of-fortune study?
Name two proposed mechanisms for anchoring.
Does anchoring work on experts, and what is one real-world example?
a: A wheel rigged to stop at 10 or 65 changed estimates of African nations in the UN: median guesses were about 25% and 45%.
Insufficient adjustment away from the anchor, and selective accessibility (testing the anchor makes consistent information come to mind).
Yes: studies show anchors affect judges' sentencing and estate agents' price estimates, e.g. a list price shifting valuations.

t: The replication crisis: what failed, why, and what changed
desc: Study the 2015 Open Science Collaboration project, the failed replications of ego depletion and power posing, the 'False-Positive Psychology' paper (2011), and reforms like preregistration and Registered Reports.
check: What did the 2015 Open Science Collaboration find?
What happened to ego depletion and power posing?
What are p-hacking and preregistration?
a: Of 100 studies from top journals, only about 36% of replications gave significant results, and effect sizes were roughly half the originals.
A 23-lab Registered Replication (Hagger 2016) found ego depletion near zero. Power posing's hormone effects failed (Ranehill 2015); Carney disavowed it.
P-hacking: flexible analysis until p < .05. Preregistration: publicly fixing hypotheses and analysis before seeing data.

t: What really happened in the Stanford prison experiment
desc: Study Zimbardo's 1971 study as it is usually told, then the critiques: Le Texier's archive work (2018-19), coached guards, prisoner accounts, and Reicher and Haslam's BBC Prison Study (2002), which found different results.
check: What is the textbook claim of the study?
What did archival research reveal about how guards were instructed?
What did the BBC Prison Study find instead?
a: That ordinary people placed in a guard role spontaneously became abusive, showing the power of situations over personality.
Guards were briefed to create fear and powerlessness, staff encouraged toughness, and one prisoner later said his breakdown was partly acted.
Guards did not spontaneously turn tyrannical; outcomes depended on group identity and leadership, not roles alone.

t: Milgram's obedience studies: the variations matter more than 65%
desc: Study Milgram's 1963 baseline and his later variations (proximity, experimenter by phone, rebelling peers), Burger's 2009 partial replication, and Gina Perry's archive-based critique.
check: What was the baseline result, and which variations cut obedience most?
What did Burger's 2009 replication change and find?
What did Perry's critique raise?
a: 26 of 40 (65%) went to 450 V. Obedience dropped when the learner was close, the experimenter phoned orders, or two peers refused.
He stopped at 150 V for ethics; about 70% were willing to continue past it, similar to Milgram's rate at that point.
Many participants doubted the shocks were real, and the experimenter often departed from the script to pressure people.

t: The testing effect: why recall beats rereading
desc: Study Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 experiment on retrieval practice and why it is one of the best-replicated findings in learning science. Compare it with rereading and highlighting.
check: What did the 2006 study find at 5 minutes vs one week?
Why do students prefer rereading despite worse results?
Does testing help even without feedback?
a: Restudying won slightly at 5 minutes, but after a week the group that practised recall remembered substantially more.
Rereading creates fluency, which feels like learning; effortful recall feels harder, so people misjudge it as less effective.
Yes, though feedback helps more, especially when initial recall fails.

t: What the Dunning-Kruger effect actually shows (and doesn't)
desc: Read about Kruger and Dunning's 1999 'Unskilled and Unaware of It' and the later statistical critiques showing the classic graph appears even with random data. Separate the solid finding from the meme.
check: What did the original study find for the bottom quartile?
Why can random data produce the classic Dunning-Kruger graph?
What is the popular misreading of the effect?
a: Those scoring around the 12th percentile estimated themselves around the 62nd: big overestimation.
Regression to the mean plus a general better-than-average bias: everyone rates themselves above average, so the worst look most overconfident.
That incompetent people think they are better than experts. In the data, low scorers still rated themselves below high scorers.

t: The marshmallow test and its 2018 conceptual replication
desc: Study Mischel's delay-of-gratification studies and the famous follow-ups linking waiting time to later outcomes. Then study Watts, Duncan and Quan (2018) and Kidd et al. (2013) on reliability of the environment.
check: What did the original follow-ups claim?
What did Watts et al. (2018) find with a larger, more diverse sample?
What did Kidd et al. show about why children wait?
a: Preschoolers who waited longer had higher SAT scores and better social outcomes as adolescents.
The link was about half as big, and mostly disappeared after controlling for family background and early cognitive ability.
Children who first experienced an unreliable adult waited far less: waiting is partly a rational bet about trust, not just willpower.

t: Prospect theory: loss aversion, reference points and odd odds
desc: Study Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 prospect theory: the value function, probability weighting and the fourfold pattern of risk attitudes. Include the 2020 multi-country replication and the debate over loss aversion.
check: Describe the shape of the value function.
What is the fourfold pattern?
What is the current status of loss aversion?
a: Defined over gains and losses from a reference point: concave for gains, convex for losses, and steeper for losses (roughly 2x).
Risk-averse for likely gains and unlikely losses; risk-seeking for likely losses and unlikely gains (lotteries, insurance).
Ruggeri et al. (2020) replicated core patterns in 19 countries, but critics like Gal and Rucker argue loss aversion is less general than claimed.

t: Cognitive dissonance: the $1 vs $20 study and its shaky replication
desc: Study Festinger and Carlsmith's 1959 induced-compliance experiment and the theory behind it. Then look at the 2024 multi-lab replication (Vaidis et al.) that did not find the classic attitude change.
check: What happened in the $1 vs $20 study?
How does dissonance theory explain it?
What does the failed multi-lab replication imply?
a: People paid $1 to tell the next person a dull task was fun later rated it more enjoyable than those paid $20.
$20 justifies the lie; $1 does not, so people reduce dissonance by changing their attitude toward the task.
This paradigm may not reliably produce the effect. The broader theory is not refuted, but the classic demonstration is weaker than taught.

t: Asch's line experiments: how much people really conformed
desc: Study Solomon Asch's 1950s conformity experiments with the line-length task, the variations (one ally, group size, writing answers privately) and Bond and Smith's 1996 cross-cultural meta-analysis.
check: What share of critical trials and of participants showed conformity?
What single change cut conformity the most?
What did Bond and Smith's meta-analysis find?
a: About a third of answers on critical trials conformed; about 75% conformed at least once, while about a quarter never did.
Having one other person give the correct answer: conformity fell sharply, by around three quarters.
Conformity declined in the US since the 1950s and was higher in more collectivist cultures.

t: Theories of emotion from James-Lange to constructed emotion
desc: Study James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, Schachter-Singer two-factor theory (1962), Ekman's basic emotions and Barrett's constructed emotion. Include the facial-feedback saga: pen-in-mouth, its failed 2016 replication and the Many Smiles study.
check: How do James-Lange and Cannon-Bard differ on the order of events?
What did Schachter and Singer claim, and how well did it replicate?
What is the current state of the facial-feedback hypothesis?
a: James-Lange: bodily change first, the feeling is perceiving it. Cannon-Bard: body and feeling arise together and independently.
Arousal plus a cognitive label makes an emotion (epinephrine study). Later replications were inconsistent.
A 17-lab replication of pen-in-mouth found nothing (2016); Many Smiles (2022) found small effects of posed smiles but not the pen method.

t: The bystander effect beyond the Kitty Genovese myth
desc: Study Darley and Latane's 1968 seizure experiment, how the 38 silent witnesses story of Kitty Genovese was exaggerated, Fischer et al.'s 2011 meta-analysis, and Philpot et al.'s 2020 analysis of real CCTV footage.
check: What did the seizure study find?
What was wrong with the Genovese story?
What did real-world CCTV footage show?
a: 85% of people who thought they were alone helped before the seizure ended, versus 31% of those who thought four others could hear.
Few witnesses saw the attack clearly, some did call police, and one woman went to her; the '38 did nothing' was overstated.
In about 9 of 10 public conflicts someone intervened, and more bystanders made intervention more likely, not less.

t: Test your own overconfidence with ten 90% confidence intervals
desc: Write ten factual questions with numeric answers you do not know (e.g. length of the Nile, year of a treaty). Give a range you are 90% sure contains each answer, then check and score yourself.
check: Ten ranges are written down before checking any answer
You have counted how many contain the true value and compared it to the expected 9
You have retaken five new questions with wider ranges and noted the change

t: Build a spaced-retrieval deck for something you want to keep
desc: Pick a topic you recently learned and turn it into 20 question-answer cards that require recall (not recognition). Set a review schedule at roughly 1, 3, 7 and 21 days.
check: 20 cards exist, each with a single clear answer
First recall session done, with a count of what you got right
Review dates are in your calendar or a spaced-repetition app

t: Write three if-then implementation intentions for a habit
desc: Using Gollwitzer's implementation intentions (meta-analytic effect around d = 0.65), write three 'If situation X, then I will do Y' plans for a goal you keep failing, and track them for a week.
check: Three plans with a specific cue (time, place or event) and a specific action
One plan covers a predictable obstacle, not just the start
A tally sheet for seven days exists and day one is filled in

t: Practise cognitive reappraisal on three recent upsets
desc: Read a short summary of James Gross's process model of emotion regulation. Then write three recent upsetting events, your original interpretation, and two alternative appraisals for each, rating intensity before and after.
check: Three events written with original interpretation and 0-10 intensity
Each has two genuinely different reappraisals, not just 'it's fine'
After-ratings are recorded and you can say how reappraisal differs from suppression

t: Run the Stroop effect on yourself and two friends
desc: Make two lists of 20 colour words: one where ink matches the word, one where it conflicts. Time each person naming the ink colours aloud, and compare the means.
check: Both lists exist and are the same length
Times for at least three people on both lists are recorded
You can explain the slowdown in terms of automatic reading interfering with colour naming

t: Audit a viral psychology claim back to the original study
desc: Pick a popular claim (a TED talk, self-help book or headline). Find the original paper, then record sample size, effect size, whether it was preregistered and whether any direct replication exists.
check: The original paper is identified and its sample size and main result noted
You have searched for and summarised any replication attempts
You have written a one-paragraph verdict: solid, uncertain, or overstated

t: Run a pre-mortem on a real decision you are about to make
desc: Using Gary Klein's pre-mortem method, imagine it is a year later and your decision has failed badly. Write every reason it failed, then rank them and change the plan to address the top three.
check: At least ten failure reasons are written down
The top three are ranked by likelihood times impact
The plan has three concrete changes or checkpoints added

t: The birthday paradox: why 23 people are enough for a 50% match
desc: Work out why 23 people give a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday, by computing the probability that nobody does.
check: Why is the answer so much lower than most people expect?
Roughly what is the chance of a shared birthday among 70 people?
Among 23 people, what is the chance that someone shares YOUR birthday, and why is it so different?
a: What matters is pairs: 23 people form 253 pairs, and each pair is a chance for a match.
About 99.9%.
Only about 6% (1 - (364/365)²²), because that needs a match with one specific date rather than any pair matching.

t: Prove that √2 is irrational
desc: Learn the classic proof by contradiction that √2 can't be written as a fraction, then adapt it to other square roots and see exactly where it fails for perfect squares.
check: In the proof, why does a² = 2b² force both a and b to be even?
Where does the same argument break down if you try it on √4?
How do you adapt the proof to show √3 is irrational?
a: a² is even so a is even; write a = 2k, then 4k² = 2b² gives b² = 2k², so b is even too, contradicting a fraction in lowest terms.
a² = 4b² just gives a = 2b, a perfectly consistent solution, so no contradiction appears: √4 = 2/1.
If 3 divides a² then 3 divides a, because 3 is prime; the same chain of steps then shows 3 divides b.

t: The bridges of Königsberg: when can you draw a shape in one stroke?
desc: Learn Euler's solution to the Seven Bridges of Königsberg puzzle, the birth of graph theory, and the simple rule for when a figure can be traced without lifting your pen.
check: Why can't you cross each of Königsberg's 7 bridges exactly once?
Why must every graph have an even number of odd-degree vertices?
If a figure has exactly two odd-degree vertices, where must a one-stroke drawing start?
a: All four land masses touch an odd number of bridges, but a route using each edge once allows at most 2 odd-degree vertices (its start and end).
Each edge adds 2 to the total of all degrees, so that total is even, which forces the number of odd degrees to be even.
At one of the two odd vertices; the drawing will end at the other.

t: Why there are infinitely many primes, and roughly how many
desc: Learn Euclid's proof that the primes never run out, then the prime number theorem's estimate of how many primes lie below a given number and how far apart they are.
check: Is 2×3×5×7×11×13 + 1 prime? Why does Euclid's proof work either way?
Estimate how many primes there are below 1 million.
Roughly how big is the average gap between primes near 1 billion?
a: No: 30031 = 59 × 509. But none of its prime factors can be on the list, since dividing by any of them leaves remainder 1, so the list was incomplete.
About ln(10⁹) ≈ 21.

t: Bayes' theorem: why a positive test often means you're fine
desc: Learn Bayes' rule using natural frequencies (picture 1000 people), and apply it to medical screening, alarms and evidence.
check: A disease affects 1 in 1000 people. A test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific. If you test positive, what's the chance you're sick?
If a second, independent test also comes back positive, what's the chance now?
Why do false positives dominate when screening for rare conditions?
a: About 9%: per 1000 people there's ~1 true positive against ~10 false positives.
Even a small false-positive rate, applied to the huge healthy majority, produces more positives than the few real cases.

t: Why testing yourself beats rereading: spacing and retrieval practice
desc: Learn the forgetting curve, the testing effect and the spacing effect, then design a review schedule for something you actually want to remember.
check: Why does rereading feel effective but produce weaker memories than self-testing?
Why do longer gaps between reviews improve long-term retention?
Sketch a review schedule for 50 new words you must know in one month.
a: Rereading builds familiarity that feels like knowing; effortful recall strengthens the memory and exposes what you can't actually retrieve.
Some forgetting makes the next recall harder, and effortful recall consolidates memory more durably than repetition while it's still fresh.
Expanding gaps, e.g. test on days 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 28, moving easy words to longer gaps and keeping missed ones on short gaps.

t: The gambler's fallacy and why the casino always wins
desc: Learn independence, expected value and the law of large numbers, and why streaks don't 'balance out' while the house edge reliably adds up.
check: After 10 reds in a row on a fair roulette wheel, is black more likely on the next spin?
In European roulette (18 red, 18 black, 1 green zero), what's the expected loss per 100 bet on red?
Why doesn't the law of large numbers mean results 'even out'?
a: No: spins are independent, so the chance is still 18/37.
The proportion of reds approaches 18/37, but the absolute gap from the expected count typically grows like √n: it's diluted, not cancelled.

t: Cantor's diagonal argument: why some infinities are bigger than others
desc: Learn what it means for two infinite sets to be the same size, show that the fractions can be listed one by one, and prove that the real numbers cannot.
check: How can you list all positive fractions in a single infinite sequence?
Explain why any list of real numbers between 0 and 1 must miss at least one.
Are there more points on a 1 m line segment than on a 1 cm one?
a: Arrange p/q in a grid by numerator and denominator and zigzag along the diagonals, skipping duplicates; every fraction gets a finite position.
Build a number whose nth digit differs from the nth digit of the nth number listed (avoiding 0 and 9); it differs from every entry, so it's missing.
No: x → 100x pairs each point of one with exactly one point of the other, so they have the same cardinality.

t: Square any 2-digit number ending in 5 in under 3 seconds
desc: Learn the rule: for n5², multiply n by n+1 and append 25 (65²: 6×7 = 42, so 4225). Prove why it works with algebra, then drill 20 random cases.
check: You can square any number from 15 to 95 ending in 5 in under 3 seconds
You can show why (10n+5)² = 100n(n+1) + 25
You can extend it to 3-digit cases like 105² = 11025 and 115² = 13225

t: Calculate percentages instantly with the swap trick
desc: Learn that x% of y equals y% of x, plus the 10%, 5% and 1% building blocks, then drill tips, discounts and price increases on real prices.
check: You can do problems like 8% of 25 or 16% of 50 in under 5 seconds using the swap
You can compute a 15% or 18% tip on any bill under 200 in under 10 seconds
You can reverse a percentage (e.g. 64 after 20% off means the original was 80)

t: Estimate square roots in your head to 2 decimal places
desc: Learn the approximation √(n² + d) ≈ n + d/(2n) using the nearest perfect square, then drill it on random numbers and check each answer with a calculator.
check: You can estimate √50 ≈ 7.07 and √140 ≈ 11.83 in your head
Your estimates for 10 random whole numbers between 10 and 200 are all within 0.05 of the true value
You can explain why the estimate is best when d is small compared with n

t: Settle the Monty Hall problem with three cups and a coin
desc: With a friend as the host, hide a coin under one of three cups and play 30 rounds where you always stick and 30 where you always switch, then explain the result.
check: You recorded 60 rounds and switching won roughly twice as often as sticking
You can explain the answer using the 100-door version of the puzzle
You can explain why it matters that the host knows where the coin is and always reveals an empty cup

t: Multiply any two 2-digit numbers in your head
desc: Learn left-to-right cross multiplication (tens×tens, then the cross terms, then units×units) plus the near-100 shortcut, then drill 20 random problems.
check: You get at least 18 of 20 random 2-digit products right
Your average time is under 15 seconds per problem
You can do numbers just below 100 almost instantly, e.g. 97×94 = 9118

t: Build a memory palace and memorize 20 random words in order
desc: Pick 20 locations along a route through your home, generate 20 random words, place a vivid, exaggerated image of each word at one location, then test yourself.
check: You recall all 20 words in order straight afterwards
You recall at least 18 in order after 24 hours
You can recite the list backwards or name the 13th word directly

t: Compute logarithms in your head from three memorized numbers
desc: Memorize log₁₀ of 2, 3 and 7 (0.301, 0.477, 0.845), use log rules to get the logs of other numbers, and use them to estimate huge powers.
check: You can give log₁₀ of every whole number from 1 to 10 to 2 decimals without a calculator
You work out that 2⁶⁴ has 20 digits and starts with about 1.8
You can estimate log₁₀ of numbers like 3500 or 0.006 to within 0.01

t: Solve the 12-coin weighing puzzle
desc: One of 12 identical-looking coins is fake: either heavier or lighter. Using a balance scale only 3 times, find the fake and say whether it's heavy or light. Solve it before looking anything up.
check: You have a written strategy that handles all 24 possibilities
You can explain why 3 weighings give at most 27 distinguishable outcomes
You can argue why 14 coins could never be solved in 3 weighings

t: Learn the winning strategy for Nim using binary
desc: Learn to compute the nim-sum (the XOR of the pile sizes in binary) and always move to a position where it's zero. Then play against a friend or a Nim app.
check: You can compute the nim-sum of piles like 3, 5, 7 in your head
You win 5 games in a row whenever you start from a position with non-zero nim-sum
You can explain why every move from a zero nim-sum position produces a non-zero one

t: Name the weekday of any date with Conway's Doomsday rule
desc: Learn the Doomsday algorithm: the century anchors, the easy-to-remember dates (4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10, 12/12, 5/9, 9/5, 7/11, 11/7, last day of February) and the year formula.
check: You know 2026's doomsday is Saturday and can find the weekday of any 2026 date in under 10 seconds
You can do any date from 1900 to 2099 in under 30 seconds
You got 10 out of 10 random dates right, checked against a calendar

t: Memorize 50 digits of pi with the Major System
desc: Learn the Major System (each digit is a consonant sound: 0=s, 1=t/d, 2=n, 3=m, 4=r, 5=l, 6=j/sh, 7=k, 8=f/v, 9=p/b), turn digit pairs into words, and chain them into a story or memory palace.
check: You can turn any 2-digit number into a word in under 3 seconds
You recite the first 50 digits of pi without an error
You can still recite them the next day

t: Square any 2-digit number in your head in under 5 seconds
desc: Learn the method a² = (a-b)(a+b) + b², shifting to the nearest multiple of ten (47² = 44×50 + 3² = 2209), then drill until it's fast.
check: You get at least 19 of 20 random 2-digit squares right
Your average time is under 5 seconds per square
You can explain the algebra and use it for numbers like 98² = 9604 or 103² = 10609

t: Learn to read the Greek alphabet
desc: Learn the 24 Greek letters, their names and sounds, watching the false friends (P is r, H is a vowel, X is kh, v-shaped nu is n). Practise by sounding out Greek place names and the maths symbols you already know.
check: You can write all 24 letters in order, upper and lower case, with their names
You can sound out 10 Greek words or place names, such as Athina and Thessaloniki, written in Greek script
You can explain the sounds of the look-alike letters P, H, X, Y and lower-case nu

t: Learn to read Russian Cyrillic in an hour
desc: Learn the 33 letters in three groups: true friends (A, K, M, O, T), false friends (B, H, P, C, Y, X) and new shapes (zh, sh, shch, ya, yu). Practise on borrowed words like restoran, telefon and metro written in Cyrillic.
check: You can write all 33 letters with their sounds from memory
You can read aloud 10 loanwords and city names (e.g. Moskva) printed in Cyrillic
You can explain why Cyrillic P sounds like r and C like s (both come from Greek letters)

t: Why does English spelling make so little sense?
desc: Study how English spelling froze around the arrival of printing while pronunciation kept moving. Focus on the Great Vowel Shift, Norman French scribes, and Renaissance spellings that imitated Latin.
check: What was the Great Vowel Shift, and how does it explain the spellings of 'bite' and 'name'?
Why did printing lock spelling in at an awkward moment?
Why does 'debt' contain a silent b?
a: From about 1400 to 1700 long vowels shifted: 'bite' once sounded like 'beet', 'name' like 'nahm'. Spelling kept the older values.
Caxton's press (1476) and later printers standardised spellings mid-shift, often using older conventions, while speech kept changing.
Middle English had 'dette' from French; Renaissance scholars added a b to show its Latin origin 'debitum', though it was never pronounced.

t: How was writing invented, and how many times?
desc: Study the early writing systems of Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica. Focus on how accounting records became cuneiform and how pictures became sound signs through the rebus principle.
check: Why do scholars think writing began with accounting?
What is the rebus principle, and why was it the key step?
Which inventions of writing are clearly independent, and which are debated?
a: The earliest Uruk tablets (about 3300-3200 BC) are overwhelmingly records of grain, livestock, rations and labour, likely developing from clay counting tokens.
Using a sign for its sound rather than its meaning (like 'bee' + 'leaf' for 'belief'); it lets you write names, grammar and abstract words.
Mesopotamia, China (Shang oracle bones) and Mesoamerica are widely accepted as independent; Egypt is debated, possibly inspired by Mesopotamia.

t: The alphabet was invented once: trace its family tree
desc: Follow the alphabet from Proto-Sinaitic (around 1900-1700 BC) through Phoenician to Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic. Focus on what changed at each step and what the Greeks added.
check: What did the Greeks add to the Phoenician script?
How is the letter A connected to an ox?
Which modern scripts descend from Aramaic?
a: Full vowel letters, made by repurposing Phoenician consonant signs Greek did not need (aleph became alpha, he became epsilon).
Proto-Sinaitic 'alp' (ox) was drawn as an ox head; rotated and simplified it became Phoenician aleph, Greek alpha and Latin A.
Hebrew square script, Arabic (via Nabataean), Syriac and others; Brahmi, ancestor of most Indian scripts, is often linked to Aramaic but debated.

t: Learn to read Japanese hiragana
desc: Learn the 46 basic hiragana row by row (a, ka, sa, ta, na, ha, ma, ya, ra, wa, n) using a mnemonic for each. Then write them from memory and read simple words.
check: You can write all 46 basic hiragana from memory in order
You can read 10 words such as sakura, sushi and arigatou written in hiragana
