You know what the dakuten marks do (ka to ga, ha to ba) and can read 5 words using them

t: How linguists reconstructed Proto-Indo-European
desc: Learn how comparing Sanskrit, Greek, Latin and Germanic revealed a lost ancestor language. Focus on regular sound correspondences such as Grimm's Law and the main theories of where its speakers lived.
check: Why do 'father', 'pater' and 'pitar' show common descent rather than borrowing?
What is Grimm's Law?
What are the main hypotheses about the Proto-Indo-European homeland?
a: The match is systematic: the same sound correspondences recur across core vocabulary (kin, numbers, body parts) that is rarely borrowed.
A regular Germanic consonant shift: p to f, t to th, k to h, as in pater/father, tres/three, centum/hundred.
The steppe (Yamnaya) hypothesis, now favoured by ancient DNA, and the Anatolian farming hypothesis; some recent work proposes a Caucasus-area origin.

t: How tones work in Mandarin and other tonal languages
desc: Learn what makes a language tonal, the four Mandarin tones plus the neutral tone, and the classic 'ma' examples. Focus on how pitch changes word meaning and how tonal languages still mark questions and emotion.
check: What does 'ma' mean in each of the four tones?
Roughly how common are tonal languages, and where are they concentrated?
If pitch already distinguishes words, how do tonal languages signal questions?
a: Tone 1 mother, tone 2 hemp, tone 3 horse, tone 4 to scold.
Estimates range from about 40% to over half of languages, concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, East and Southeast Asia, and parts of the Americas.
Mostly with particles (Mandarin's question particle 'ma'), plus overall pitch range and register laid over the word tones rather than replacing them.

t: Learn 20 survival phrases in a language you've never studied
desc: Pick a language new to you, such as Swahili, Turkish or Vietnamese. Learn greetings, please and thank you, numbers 1-10, 'how much', 'where is' and 'I don't understand', and drill them with flashcards.
check: You can say all 20 phrases from memory when given the English cue
You can count 1-10 forwards and backwards
You can perform a 4-line dialogue ordering food and asking the price

t: Learn the Arabic letters and read your first words
desc: Learn the 28 letters, how most change shape at the start, middle and end of a word, and the short vowel marks. Read right to left and practise on words like kitab (book) and salam (peace).
check: You can write all 28 letters in isolated form with their sounds
You can name the 6 letters that never join to the following letter (alif, dal, dhal, ra, zay, waw)
You can sound out 5 short vowelled words without help

t: Why Korean Hangul looks the way it does
desc: Learn how King Sejong's scholars designed Hangul (created 1443, published 1446), with consonants shaped like the speech organs. Then learn the basic letters and how they stack into syllable blocks.
check: What do the shapes of basic consonants like giyeok (g) and nieun (n) depict?
Why was Hangul created when Korea already used Chinese characters?
How are letters arranged into syllable blocks?
a: Speech organs: giyeok the back of the tongue raised to the soft palate, nieun the tongue tip at the ridge behind the teeth, mieum the mouth, siot a tooth.
Classical Chinese was hard to learn and fitted Korean poorly; Sejong wanted commoners to read. Elites resisted; it became dominant only in the 20th century.
Each block is one syllable: initial consonant plus vowel, with an optional final consonant underneath, e.g. h + a + n = han.

t: Do all languages have the same colour words?
desc: Study Berlin and Kay's research on basic colour terms and experiments on Russian's two words for blue. Focus on whether language shapes perception, and what the evidence actually shows.
check: In what order do languages typically gain basic colour terms?
What did experiments on Russian 'goluboy' and 'siniy' find?
What is the difference between strong and weak versions of the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis?
a: Dark/light first, then red, then green and yellow, then blue, then brown, then purple, pink, orange and grey (Berlin and Kay 1969, later refined).
Russian speakers distinguished light from dark blue slightly faster across their category boundary, and the edge disappeared under verbal interference.
Strong: language determines thought (largely rejected). Weak: language nudges perception, attention and memory in modest ways (some support).

t: How pidgins become creoles
desc: Study how pidgins arise from trade and plantation contact and how new generations turn them into full languages. Focus on Tok Pisin, Haitian Creole and the emergence of Nicaraguan Sign Language.
check: What is the difference between a pidgin and a creole?
Why do many creoles take most words from a European language but have quite different grammar?
What did Nicaraguan Sign Language reveal about how children build languages?
a: A pidgin is a simplified contact language with no native speakers; a creole is a full language with native speakers, often grown from a pidgin.
The socially dominant language supplied vocabulary, while grammar was shaped by the speakers' first languages, universal tendencies and children's innovations.
Deaf children brought together in schools from the late 1970s created a new sign language; younger cohorts made its grammar more systematic.

t: From Latin to Spanish, French, Italian and Romanian
desc: Learn how spoken Latin split into the Romance languages after Rome fell. Compare the words for 'night', 'eight' and 'milk' across four languages to see regular sound changes in action.
check: What pattern do noche, nuit, notte and noapte reveal?
Why did spoken Latin split into separate languages?
Why is Romanian a Romance language despite being surrounded by Slavic and Hungarian?
a: Latin 'ct' (noctem, octo, lactem) became 'ch' in Spanish, 'it' in French, 'tt' in Italian and 'pt' in Romanian.
After the Western Empire collapsed, regions were cut off under different rulers, with different local substrates and Germanic, Arabic or Slavic influences.
It descends from Latin spoken in the Roman Danube provinces; later Slavic and Hungarian contact added vocabulary but not its Latin core.

t: Transcribe your own accent with the International Phonetic Alphabet
desc: Learn the IPA symbols for English consonants (including theta, eth, esh and eng) and the main vowels. Then transcribe 10 everyday words as you actually say them.
check: You can write the different IPA symbols for 'th' in 'thin' and 'this', and for 'sh' and 'ng'
10 words are transcribed with stress marks
You found at least one word your accent pronounces differently from a dictionary's transcription

t: Why do some languages give nouns a gender?
desc: Learn how grammatical gender works, from two genders in French to German's three to the many noun classes of Bantu languages. Focus on where gender comes from and whether it affects how people think.
check: Why is the German word 'Maedchen' (girl) neuter?
How do Bantu noun classes, as in Swahili, work?
Does grammatical gender change how speakers think about objects?
a: The diminutive suffix -chen always makes nouns neuter, so grammatical gender follows the word's form, not its meaning.
Nouns carry class prefixes (m-tu person, wa-tu people; ki-tabu book, vi-tabu books) and verbs and adjectives agree with that class.
Some studies claimed effects (e.g. how Germans vs Spaniards describe a bridge), but replications are mixed; any effect appears small.

t: How do children learn language so fast?
desc: Study the stages from babbling to full sentences and the debate between Chomsky's innate grammar and usage-based learning. Focus on evidence such as overregularisation errors and critical periods.
check: Why is a child saying 'goed' or 'mouses' important evidence?
What is the poverty-of-the-stimulus argument, and how do critics answer it?
What evidence supports a critical period for language?
a: They never heard those forms, so they must have extracted a rule (add -ed, add -s) and over-applied it, rather than simply imitating.
Children get limited, messy input yet master complex grammar, implying innate constraints; usage-based critics say statistical learning from input suffices.
Deaf children exposed to sign language late, rare cases of isolated children, and lasting accents in late learners; the exact age limits are debated.

t: Write and record a one-minute self-introduction in a new language
desc: In a language you are learning or want to start, write 6-8 sentences about your name, home, work and interests. Check grammar with a dictionary and grammar guide, memorise it and record yourself.
check: Script is written and every sentence checked against a grammar reference
You have recorded the full introduction without reading from the script
You can answer 3 likely follow-up questions (where do you live, what do you do, why this language)

t: Why are languages dying, and can they be revived?
desc: Study language endangerment: of roughly 7,000 languages, a large share have few speakers. Focus on why communities shift languages and on revival efforts for Hebrew, Maori and Welsh.
check: Why do communities shift to a dominant language?
What made the revival of Hebrew unusually successful?
What do Maori 'language nests' (Kohanga Reo) do?
a: Jobs, schooling, urbanisation, prestige and sometimes coercive policies; once parents stop passing the language to children, it declines fast.
Strong ideological commitment, families raising children in it, a new state that made it official, and immigrants needing a shared language.
Since 1982, preschool immersion centres where young children are cared for entirely in Maori, often by fluent elders.

t: How sign languages work, and why they aren't universal
desc: Learn how sign languages are structured and how they spread. Focus on the building blocks of a sign, the role of facial grammar, and why American and British Sign Language are unrelated.
check: Why is American Sign Language closer to French Sign Language than to British Sign Language?
What are the basic parameters that make up a sign?
What evidence shows sign languages are full languages?
a: ASL grew from French Sign Language brought by Laurent Clerc to the first US deaf school (1817), mixed with local signing; BSL developed separately.
Handshape, location, movement and palm orientation, plus non-manual markers such as facial expressions that carry grammar.
They have phonology, morphology and syntax, children acquire them on the same timetable, and left-hemisphere damage causes sign aphasia.

t: Compound interest: why starting ten years earlier matters so much
desc: Learn simple vs compound interest and the rule of 72. Work through the same monthly saving started at age 25 versus 35 and see where most of the final total comes from.
check: Why does compound growth look slow at first and then speed up?
Using the rule of 72, roughly how long does money take to double at 6% a year?
Why does compounding make high-interest debt so dangerous?
a: Each period earns interest on earlier interest, so the yearly gain itself keeps growing; most of the total arrives in the later years.
About 12 years (72 divided by 6).
Unpaid card balances compound too, often at 20% or more, so a debt can double in about four years if left alone.

t: Build a budget spreadsheet from one month of real spending
desc: Export or list last month's transactions, categorise them (housing, food, transport, subscriptions and so on), and compare the totals with a 50/30/20 split of needs, wants and savings.
check: Every transaction from one full month is in the sheet with a category
Totals and percentage of income are calculated for each category and for needs, wants and savings
You have written 2 specific changes with the monthly amount each would free up

t: What is inflation, and what actually causes it?
desc: Learn how inflation is measured with a consumer price basket, and its main causes: demand-pull, cost-push, money growth and expectations. Use the 1970s and 2021-23 as case studies.
check: What is the difference between demand-pull and cost-push inflation?
Why do many central banks target about 2% inflation rather than zero?
What were the main causes of the 2021-23 inflation surge?
a: Demand-pull: spending outruns what the economy can produce. Cost-push: input costs such as energy or wages rise and firms pass them on.
A small positive rate guards against deflation, leaves room to cut real interest rates in recessions, and allows for measurement overstating inflation.
Pandemic supply bottlenecks, strong demand from stimulus and savings, and energy and food shocks after Russia invaded Ukraine; their relative weight is debated.

t: How central banks steer interest rates and the economy
desc: Learn what a central bank like the Federal Reserve or ECB does, how a policy rate change ripples into mortgages, savings and jobs, and what quantitative easing is.
check: Why does raising interest rates tend to bring inflation down?
What is quantitative easing, and when is it used?
Why are central banks usually made independent of governments?
a: Borrowing gets dearer and saving more attractive, so spending and investment slow, demand cools, and price rises ease, usually with a lag of a year or more.
Buying government bonds and other assets with newly created reserves to push down long-term rates, used when short-term rates are already near zero.
To stop politicians printing money or cutting rates before elections; credible independence helps anchor inflation expectations.

t: Calculate your real hourly wage
desc: Take your monthly take-home pay, subtract work-related costs (commute, work clothes, bought lunches), and divide by all work-related hours including commuting. Then price 3 recent purchases in hours of work.
check: Your real hourly figure is calculated with every cost and hour written down
You have compared it with your nominal hourly wage and noted the gap as a percentage
3 recent purchases are converted into hours of work

t: Why diversification is called the only free lunch in investing
desc: Learn what risk, return and correlation mean, why combining assets that don't move together lowers risk, and what index funds are. Educational only, not investment advice.
check: Why can holding many different assets reduce risk without necessarily lowering expected return?
What kind of risk cannot be diversified away?
Why do most actively managed funds trail their benchmark index over long periods?
a: Company-specific shocks partly cancel out when assets are not perfectly correlated, while each still contributes its expected return.
Systematic or market risk, such as recessions or interest rate shifts, that hits nearly everything at once.
Before costs, active investors as a group earn the market average; fees and trading costs then push most below it, as S&P's SPIVA reports show.

t: What GDP measures, and what it misses
desc: Learn the expenditure formula (C + I + G + net exports), nominal vs real, and per capita and purchasing power parity figures. Focus on what GDP leaves out: unpaid work, inequality and environmental damage.
check: Why compare years using real rather than nominal GDP?
Why do country rankings change when GDP is measured at purchasing power parity?
Name two things that raise GDP without making people better off.
a: Nominal GDP rises with prices; real GDP strips out inflation so it tracks the volume of goods and services produced.
Non-traded goods and services are cheaper in poorer countries, so money goes further; PPP adjusts for this and lifts their measured output.
Rebuilding after a disaster, cleaning up pollution, longer commutes, and spending on security because of crime.

t: Supply and demand: explain concert tickets, fuel prices and rent control
desc: Learn demand and supply curves, equilibrium, shifts versus movements along a curve, and price elasticity. Then apply them to three real cases: ticket resale, fuel price swings and rent control.
check: What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
Why do fuel prices swing a lot when supply changes only a little?
What do most economists predict rent control does, and what do supporters argue?
a: A change in the good's own price moves you along the curve; changes in income, tastes or other goods' prices shift the whole curve.
Short-run demand is inelastic because people still need to drive and heat homes, so a small supply cut needs a large price rise to balance.
Lower rents for sitting tenants but less rental supply, maintenance and mobility over time; supporters stress tenant stability and modern, softer designs.

t: What caused the 2008 financial crisis?
desc: Trace the chain from US subprime mortgages through securitisation, credit ratings and leverage to the collapse of Lehman Brothers. Focus on why a housing problem became a global banking crisis.
check: How did securitisation spread US mortgage risk around the world?
Why did high leverage and short-term funding make banks so fragile?
Why did governments bail out banks despite the moral hazard?
a: Mortgages were bundled into securities and CDOs, often rated AAA, and sold to banks and investors worldwide, so losses were widespread and hard to locate.
At 30-to-1 leverage, a roughly 3% fall in asset values wipes out equity, and overnight funding like repo can vanish in a panic.
To stop a credit freeze collapsing payments, lending and the real economy, as bank failures had in the 1930s.

t: Compare the true cost of a loan at different rates and terms
desc: In a spreadsheet, use the PMT function to compute the monthly payment and total interest for one loan amount under 3 scenarios, e.g. 15 vs 30 years and two interest rates.
check: PMT formula correctly set up for all 3 scenarios with rate converted to monthly
Total interest paid is calculated and compared across scenarios
You can explain in 2 sentences why the longer term costs more in total despite a lower monthly payment

t: Comparative advantage: why trade can benefit the less productive country
desc: Work through Ricardo's two-country, two-good example and the idea of opportunity cost. Then look at who loses from trade and why it stays politically contentious.
check: What is the difference between absolute and comparative advantage?
Why can a country that is worse at making everything still gain from trade?
Who tends to lose when trade opens up?
a: Absolute: producing more with the same resources. Comparative: producing at a lower opportunity cost in terms of other goods given up.
If each specialises where its opportunity cost is lower, total output rises, so both can consume more after trading.
Workers and firms in import-competing industries, often clustered in specific towns, as with the 'China shock' to US manufacturing regions.

t: Why emergency funds usually come before investing
desc: Learn what an emergency fund is, the common guideline of 3-6 months of essential expenses, where people typically keep one, and how it fits with paying down high-interest debt. Focus on the reasoning.
check: Why keep cash earning little instead of investing it?
Why size the fund from essential expenses rather than income?
Why do many guides prioritise paying off high-interest debt early?
a: It is insurance: it avoids selling investments at a loss or borrowing at high rates when job loss or a big bill hits.
What you must cover in a crisis is your essential spending, which is usually less than your income.
Paying off a card at 20% or more is a guaranteed saving that beats typical savings or investment returns.

t: Audit every subscription and recurring payment
desc: Go through 3 months of bank and card statements and list every recurring charge. Mark each keep, downgrade or cancel, and annualise the total.
check: Every recurring charge is listed with its monthly and annual cost
Each one is marked keep, downgrade or cancel with a one-line reason
The annual saving from your cancel and downgrade decisions is calculated

t: Calculate income tax by hand: marginal vs effective rates
desc: Using your country's current income tax bands, compute the tax on a sample salary bracket by bracket. Then test the myth that a raise into a higher bracket can lower your take-home pay.
check: Tax is calculated band by band and matches an official online calculator
You have stated both the marginal rate and the effective (average) rate for that salary
You have calculated how much of a 1,000 raise you would keep, and named any benefit taper that changes the answer

t: What did Keynes and Hayek disagree about?
desc: Study the 1930s debate about recessions: Keynes on aggregate demand and government spending, Hayek on credit-driven booms and malinvestment. Then see how each view shaped responses to 2008 and 2020.
check: Why did Keynes think an economy could get stuck with high unemployment?
What did Hayek think caused booms and busts?
How did government responses to the 2020 pandemic reflect Keynesian ideas?
a: Falling spending causes layoffs, which cut incomes and spending further; wages and prices adjust slowly, so without stimulus slumps can persist.
Credit kept too cheap by central banks distorts price signals and fuels unsustainable long-term investment that must later be liquidated.
Large deficit spending, furlough schemes and direct payments to support incomes and demand, alongside central bank rate cuts and bond buying.

t: Model long-term savings growth in a spreadsheet
desc: Build a sheet projecting savings year by year from a monthly contribution, an assumed real return (try 2%, 4% and 6%) and a number of years. An exercise in testing assumptions, not a financial plan.
check: Year-by-year table showing contributions, growth and balance
Three return scenarios plotted together on one chart
You have noted how much the final value changes if contributions start 5 years later

t: How hyperinflation happens: Weimar Germany, Zimbabwe, Venezuela
desc: Study three hyperinflations side by side. Focus on the common pattern of governments printing money to cover deficits, collapsing output and lost confidence, and how each episode ended.
check: What triggered Weimar Germany's 1923 hyperinflation?
Why does printing money to pay the government's bills feed on itself?
How did these hyperinflations end?
a: War debts and reparations, then the 1923 French-Belgian occupation of the Ruhr; the government printed money to fund passive resistance.
Rising prices erode real tax revenue, so more printing is needed, and people spend cash faster, which pushes prices up even more.
Germany: the Rentenmark and fiscal discipline. Zimbabwe: dropping its currency for the US dollar (2009). Venezuela: informal dollarisation and spending cuts.

t: Read a company's annual report: find the numbers that matter
desc: Pick a large public company whose products you use. In its annual report, find revenue, net profit, total debt and operating cash flow, then compute the profit margin. A literacy exercise, not stock analysis.
check: All 4 figures found and noted with the statement they came from
Net profit margin calculated correctly
You can explain in 2 sentences why net profit and operating cash flow differ for this company

t: What is money, really? From the barter myth to fiat currency
desc: Study the functions of money and its history: credit, commodity money, coins, paper and fiat currency. Focus on why the 'barter came first' story is doubted and what gives modern money its value.
check: What are money's three classic functions?
Why do anthropologists doubt that barter economies came before money?
What gives fiat money its value?
a: Medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value.
Little evidence of barter-based societies; communities used credit, debts and gifts (Humphrey, Graeber). Barter appears mainly between strangers or in crises.
Trust in the issuer's restraint, legal tender laws, and above all the state requiring taxes to be paid in it.

t: How commercial banks create money when they lend
desc: Learn how a bank loan creates a new deposit, the role of reserves and capital requirements, and why the textbook money multiplier is misleading. The Bank of England's 2014 explanation is a good guide.
check: What happens to the money supply when a bank makes a loan?
Why does the Bank of England call the money multiplier model misleading?
What actually limits how much banks can lend?
a: The bank credits the borrower with a new deposit, creating broad money; repaying the loan destroys it.
Banks lend first and obtain any reserves needed afterwards; central banks set the price of reserves (interest rates) rather than fixing their quantity.
Profitable lending opportunities and creditworthy borrowers, capital and liquidity rules, and the interest rate set by the central bank.

t: Read and write standard cube notation: R, U', F2, wide moves, slices, rotations
desc: Learn the six face letters (U D L R F B), prime and double turns, lowercase/w wide moves, the M E S slices and x y z rotations, then execute 3 written scrambles on a solved cube.
check: What exactly does R' do, and from which viewpoint is its direction judged?
How does r (or Rw) differ from R, and which face does M follow in direction?
What do the rotations x, y and z do, and which face turn does each follow?
a: R' turns the right face 90 degrees counterclockwise, judged as if you were looking straight at the right face.
r/Rw turns the right face plus the middle slice together; R turns only the outer face. M turns in the same direction as L.
They turn the whole cube without moving pieces relative to each other: x follows R, y follows U, z follows F.

t: Solve the first layer: white cross plus all four white corners
desc: Build a white cross whose edges also match the side centres, then put each white corner above its slot and repeat R U R' U' until it drops in correctly oriented. Practise on fresh scrambles.
check: First layer completed on 5 different scrambles without a guide
Every cross edge matches its side centre (a coloured 'T' on each side)
All four first-layer corners correctly placed and oriented on each attempt

t: Finish your first complete solve with the beginner layer-by-layer method
desc: After the first layer: insert middle edges (U R U' R' U' F' U F or its mirror), make the yellow cross (F R U R' U' F'), orient corners with Sune (R U R' U R U2 R'), then permute corners and edges.
check: One full solve completed using your notes
Three full solves completed from memory with no notes
Every algorithm used written out correctly from memory

t: Drill the Sune and Anti-Sune until both are automatic
desc: Sune is R U R' U R U2 R'; Anti-Sune is R U2 R' U' R U' R' (they are inverses). Set up each case by doing the other algorithm, then recognise and solve it on sight. Repeat 20 times each.
check: Each algorithm executed 10 times in a row with no mistakes
Sune executed in under 2 seconds
Correct algorithm chosen from the top-layer pattern 5 out of 5 times

t: Learn 2-look PLL: 2 corner algorithms and 4 edge algorithms
desc: Corners first: headlights on one side -> T-perm, no headlights -> Y-perm. Then edges: Ua, Ub, H and Z perms. Drill recognition on random last layers before chasing speed.
check: All 6 algorithms performed from memory
Correct case recognised 10 out of 10 times
Permutation step finished in under 20 seconds on 5 consecutive solves

t: Learn 2-look OLL: 3 edge cases and 7 corner cases
desc: Edges: line -> F R U R' U' F'; L shape -> f R U R' U' f'; dot -> do both. Corners: Sune, Anti-Sune, H, Pi, Headlights (U), T and L (bowtie). Learn one case at a time, drilling each 10 times.
check: All 10 algorithms performed from memory
Top face completed in two looks on 10 scrambles in a row
Each of the 7 corner cases named on sight within 2 seconds

t: Understand intuitive F2L: pairing a corner and edge without algorithms
desc: Learn why F2L replaces separate corner and middle-edge steps: pair each first-layer corner with its edge in the top layer, then insert with triggers like R U R' or R U' R'. Experiment slowly on a solved cross.
check: Which two pieces make an F2L 'pair', and where do they end up?
Why does a trigger like R U R' leave the cross intact?
What do you do if the corner is stuck in the wrong slot?
a: A first-layer corner and its matching middle-layer edge; together they fill one of the four slots between the cross and the top layer.
R moves the cross edge into the middle layer, U only turns the top layer so it can't touch it, and R' puts it straight back.
Take it out with a trigger (e.g. R U R') so it lands in the top layer, then pair it with its edge and insert normally.

t: Complete cross plus intuitive F2L on 5 scrambles with no algorithm sheet
desc: Solve the cross then all four F2L pairs on 5 scrambles, working out each pair by hand. Count moves per pair and redo any pair that took more than 15 moves until you find a shorter way.
check: Cross plus 4 pairs completed on 5 scrambles
No pair needed more than 15 moves on the last 2 scrambles
Cross still intact after the final pair every time

t: Plan your whole cross during the 15-second inspection
desc: Scramble, inspect for 15 seconds and plan every cross move, then execute without pausing (try eyes closed). Any cross can be solved in 8 moves or fewer, so aim for that.
check: Cross executed without pausing on 7 of 10 scrambles
Cross correct with eyes closed on at least 3 of 10
Average cross length of 8 moves or fewer

t: Finger-trick the sexy move: 6 reps of R U R' U' in under 3 seconds
desc: From home grip: R with the right wrist, U with a right index flick, R' with the wrist, U' with a left index flick. Six repetitions return the cube to solved, so the drill checks itself.
check: 6 reps return the cube to solved
6 reps completed in under 3 seconds
No regrips during the 6 reps

t: Learn 6 more PLLs: Aa, Ab, Ja, Jb, Ra and F perm
desc: Pick one algorithm source and learn these one at a time, including recognition from two sides (headlights, blocks, bars). Added to T, Y, Ua, Ub, H and Z, you will know 12 of the 21 PLLs.
check: All 6 new algorithms performed from memory
Each case recognised correctly from at least 2 angles
Each new algorithm executed in under 3 seconds

t: Understand the Roux method: blocks, CMLL and the last six edges
desc: Learn Roux's four steps: build a 1x2x3 block on the left, another on the right, solve the top corners (CMLL), then the last six edges (LSE) with only M and U moves. Try building a first block slowly.
check: What are the four steps of Roux, in order?
Why can LSE use only M and U moves?
Why does Roux usually need fewer moves than CFOP?
a: First block (left 1x2x3), second block (right 1x2x3), CMLL (top corners), LSE (last six edges).
M and U never disturb the two 1x2x3 blocks, and U only shifts the solved corners together, fixed by a final U turn.
Blocks are built intuitively without preserving a cross, and LSE is very efficient; good Roux solves are often under 50 moves.

t: Build both Roux blocks on 10 scrambles
desc: On 10 scrambles, build the left 1x2x3 block, then the right one using mostly R, r, U and M moves so the first block is untouched. Finish with any last layer method or just rescramble.
check: Both blocks built on 10 scrambles
First block in 12 moves or fewer on at least 3 scrambles
Second block built without breaking the first every time

t: Solve a 2x2 cube using 3x3 algorithms you already know
desc: Build one full layer whose side colours match each other (there are no centres), then orient the top with your corner OLLs (Sune etc.) and swap corners with a T-perm or Y-perm.
check: 5 solves completed without help
Average of 5 under 40 seconds
First layer correct every time (side colours match), not just one face

t: Solve a Pyraminx: tips, centres, first layer, last three edges
desc: Twist the four tips to match, align the three-colour centre pieces, solve one face with its three edges, then learn a single 3-edge-cycle algorithm to finish the last layer.
check: 5 solves completed without notes
Average of 5 under 60 seconds
Tips solved during inspection on every solve

t: Why some cube states are impossible: piece counts and invariants
desc: Learn how many positions a 3x3 has, why a single flipped edge or twisted corner can never come from turning, and what God's number means. Try to explain each to a friend.
check: Roughly how many positions does a 3x3 Rubik's Cube have?
Why can't a legally turned cube have exactly one twisted corner?
What is God's number for the 3x3 and what does it mean?
a: Every legal move keeps total corner twist at 0 (mod 3), so one twisted corner means the cube was taken apart or twisted by hand.
20: every position can be solved in 20 moves or fewer (half-turn metric), proved by computer in 2010.

t: Blindfolded basics: Old Pochmann for edges and letter-pair memo
desc: Learn Old Pochmann edges: letter every sticker (Speffz scheme), trace targets from the buffer, then solve each with a setup move, a T-perm and the exact undo of the setup.
check: In Old Pochmann edges, which positions does the T-perm swap?
What rule must setup moves follow?
What do you do when the buffer piece returns to the buffer before all edges are solved?
a: The buffer at UR with the swap position UL (it also swaps two corners, which cancel out with an even number of targets).
Only bring the target to UL without disturbing UR, then undo them in exact reverse after the T-perm.
That is a cycle break: shoot to any unsolved edge to start a new cycle and keep tracing from there.

t: Solve all 12 edges of a 3x3 blindfolded with Old Pochmann
desc: Scramble, memorise only the edge targets as letter pairs, put on a blindfold (or close your eyes) and execute. Check the result, find the mistake, and repeat for 3 attempts.
check: Edge memo completed in under 5 minutes
At least 1 of 3 attempts with every edge solved
Cause identified for each failed attempt (memo, setup or execution)

t: Understand speedcubing averages and inspection rules, then compute yours
desc: Learn how WCA-style ao5 and ao12 are computed and how inspection penalties work, then do 12 timed solves and calculate both averages by hand.
check: How is an average of 5 (ao5) calculated?
Why are the best and worst times dropped?
How long is WCA inspection and what happens if you go over?
a: Drop the single best and single worst of 5 times and take the mean of the middle 3. An ao12 drops best and worst and averages 10.
So one lucky scramble or one disaster doesn't distort the number; it reflects your typical speed.
15 seconds. Starting after 15 s but before 17 s gives a +2 penalty; starting after 17 s is a DNF.

t: Train lookahead: 10 slow solves with pause-free F2L
desc: Do 10 solves turning at roughly half speed while finding the next F2L pair during the current insertion. A metronome at 1-2 turns per second helps keep the pace steady.
check: 10 solves with no F2L pause longer than 1 second
Next pair located before the current one is inserted on most pairs
Average within 10 seconds of your normal average despite slower turning

t: Checkmate with king and queen vs lone king within 15 moves
desc: Set up K+Q vs K. Keep the queen a knight's move from the enemy king to shrink its box, bring your own king up, then mate on the edge. Practise against an engine or a friend.
check: Mate delivered from 5 different starting positions
Each mate within 15 moves
No stalemate in any attempt

t: Checkmate with king and rook vs lone king within 25 moves
desc: Use the box method: the rook cuts the king off, your king walks up, and when the kings stand in opposition the rook checks along the edge. Shrink the box whenever it is safe.
check: Mate from 3 different positions against a defending engine
Each mate in 25 moves or fewer
Rook never left en prise to the enemy king

t: Win the Lucena rook endgame by 'building a bridge'
desc: Set up your king on the queening square in front of your 7th-rank pawn, the enemy king cut off by a file. Check it one file further away, put your rook on the 4th rank, walk your king out, and block checks with the rook.
check: Won the Lucena against an engine defending, 3 times
Rook placed on the 4th rank before the king stepped out every time
Pawn promoted without ever losing it to a check or skewer

t: Hold the draw: the Philidor position in rook endgames
desc: Learn the classic defence against rook and pawn: king on the queening square, rook on your own 3rd rank to keep the enemy king out, then switch to checks from behind once the pawn advances. Play it vs an engine.
check: Where does the defending rook stand at first, and why?
What must the defender do the moment the pawn steps onto the 3rd rank (from the defender's side)?
Where should the defending king be?
a: On the defender's 3rd rank (e.g. 6th rank for Black), stopping the enemy king from advancing to that rank.
Drop the rook to the far end and check from behind; the pawn now blocks the king's shelter, so checks can't be escaped.
On the pawn's queening square or directly in front of the pawn.

t: Opening principles: centre, development, king safety
desc: Learn the core opening principles, then play one game obeying them: control the centre, develop knights and bishops quickly, castle early, avoid moving a piece twice, and connect your rooks.
check: What does controlling the centre mean, and which squares matter most?
Why is bringing the queen out early often bad?
How do you know your development is complete?
a: Occupying or attacking e4, d4, e5 and d5 so your pieces have room and the opponent's are cramped.
The opponent develops with tempo by attacking it, gaining time while your queen keeps retreating.
Minor pieces are out, the king has castled, and the rooks are connected with nothing between them.

t: Set up 6 classic checkmate patterns from memory
desc: Learn back-rank, smothered, Anastasia's, Arabian, Boden's and Epaulette mates. Set each up on a board with the fewest pieces and name which piece covers each escape square.
check: All 6 patterns set up correctly from memory
Every escape square in each pattern accounted for by a named piece
10 puzzles featuring these mates solved

t: Solve 30 tactics puzzles on forks, pins and skewers
desc: Do 10 puzzles each on forks, pins and skewers. Before moving, name the motif and say the whole forcing line aloud; only then play it. Review every miss until you see why.
check: 30 puzzles completed
At least 24 solved on the first try
Motif named correctly before moving on every puzzle

t: Understand the opposition and key squares in king and pawn endings
desc: Learn direct opposition, key squares and the rook-pawn exception, then test yourself on 5 K+P vs K positions by predicting win or draw before checking with an engine.
check: What is direct opposition and who 'has' it?
What are the key squares for a white pawn on e4?
Why is a rook pawn often a draw?
a: Kings on the same file or rank with one square between them; the side NOT to move has the opposition.
d6, e6 and f6: if the white king reaches any of them, the pawn queens whoever is to move.
If the defending king reaches the corner it can't be driven out, so the attacker can only stalemate or fail to promote.

t: Win king and pawn vs king using opposition and key squares
desc: Set up K+P vs K with the defending king in front of the pawn. Take the opposition, reach a key square and promote; then swap sides and defend the drawn positions.
check: Promotion forced in 3 winning positions against an engine
Held the draw as defender in 2 drawn positions
Correctly predicted win or draw for 5 positions before playing them

t: Play 3 rapid games and annotate your critical moments
desc: Play three 15+10 games online or over the board. Afterwards, before using an engine, mark the 3 most important moments per game and write what you were thinking; then compare with the engine.
check: 3 games played to completion
3 annotated moments per game written before the engine check
One recurring mistake identified and written as a rule for next time

t: Learn the ideas of the Italian Game: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4
desc: Learn the main ideas behind 3.Bc4 and Black's two main replies, 3...Bc5 (Giuoco Piano) and 3...Nf6 (Two Knights). Play through the plans on a board, then play 2 games with it.
check: Which Black weakness does 3.Bc4 aim at?
In the Giuoco Piano, what is the point of c3 followed by d4?
After 3...Nf6, why is 4.Ng5 tempting and what is Black's main reply?
a: f7, which at the start is defended only by Black's king.
c3 supports d4, building a broad pawn centre that gains space and hits the bishop on c5.
Knight and bishop both attack f7. Black's main reply is 4...d5, blocking the bishop at the cost of a pawn.

t: Play 5 rapid games with a checks-captures-threats scan every move
desc: Before each move, list every check, capture and threat for both sides. Play 5 games of 10+5 or slower and track how often you hang a piece or miss a tactic.
check: 5 games completed
No piece hung in one move in at least 4 of the 5 games
2 moves noted where the scan changed your choice

t: Checkmate with two bishops vs lone king
desc: Set up K+B+B vs K. Place the bishops side by side as a diagonal wall to herd the king to any corner, bring your king close, then mate. Watch for stalemate in the final phase.
check: Mate achieved from 2 positions against a defending engine
Each mate within 50 moves (the 50-move rule)
No stalemate in any attempt

t: Checkmate with bishop and knight using the W manoeuvre
desc: Drive the king to the edge, then into a corner of your bishop's colour, using the knight's W-shaped route to keep it trapped. This is the hardest basic mate; aim to finish within 50 moves.
check: King driven into the corner matching the bishop's colour
W manoeuvre performed with the knight at least once
Mate within 50 moves from at least 1 starting position

t: Go basics: liberties, capture, ko and two eyes
desc: Learn the rules of Go on a 9x9 board: placing stones, liberties, capturing, the ko rule and why living groups need two eyes. Try each idea with stones on a board or app.
check: When is a stone or group captured?
What does the ko rule forbid?
Why does a group with two separate eyes live?
a: When the opponent occupies all of its liberties (the empty points directly adjacent along lines).
Immediately recapturing a single stone in a way that would repeat the previous position; you must play elsewhere first.
The opponent can only fill one eye per move and a stone in either eye alone would be suicide, so both can never be filled.

t: Play 3 games of 9x9 Go and score them correctly
desc: Play three 9x9 games against a friend or a beginner bot. At the end, agree which stones are dead, count territory (or area), add komi (commonly 6.5 or 7.5) and decide the winner.
check: 3 games played to the end
Each game scored with dead stones agreed and komi added

t: Memorise Psalm 23 word for word
desc: Choose one translation and memorise all six verses of Psalm 23, using first letters of each word as a cue sheet. Note the shift from 'he' to 'you' in verse 4.
check: You can recite all six verses without the text and with no errors
You can say which verse switches from speaking about God to speaking to God
You have recited it again after a one-hour break

t: Build a comparison table of the four resurrection accounts
desc: Read Matthew 28, Mark 16:1-8, Luke 24 and John 20. Make a table: who goes to the tomb, what they find, who speaks to them, first appearance of Jesus, and how each ends.
check: Table complete for all four Gospels across at least five rows
You have listed three differences and one detail all four share
You can explain why most modern Bibles mark Mark 16:9-20 as absent from the earliest manuscripts

t: Practise lectio divina on Matthew 11:28-30
desc: Use the four steps described by the 12th-century monk Guigo II: read (lectio), reflect (meditatio), respond (oratio), rest (contemplatio). Read the passage slowly three times, about 7 minutes per step.
check: You have read the passage aloud three times
You have written down the word or phrase that stood out and why
You have written a short response and noted what the silence was like

t: Read the Gospel of Mark in one sitting
desc: Read Mark 1:1-16:8 straight through (about 90 minutes), as early hearers would have. Keep a running list of moments when the disciples misunderstand and when Jesus tells people to keep quiet.
check: Whole Gospel read in one sitting
List of at least six misunderstandings and four commands to silence
One paragraph on how ending at 16:8 ('they were afraid') affects the story

t: Compare the two versions of the Lord's Prayer
desc: Put Matthew 6:9-13 and Luke 11:2-4 side by side. Mark the differences and the origin of the closing doxology, then write your own line-by-line paraphrase of Matthew's version.
check: Side-by-side text with every difference marked
You can explain that the doxology is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew and appears in the Didache
A paraphrase of each line in your own words is written down

t: Map Paul and Barnabas' first missionary journey (Acts 13-14)
desc: Read Acts 13-14 and sketch a map from Antioch in Syria through Cyprus to Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe and back. Label each stop with one key event.
check: Map shows at least nine stops in order, including Salamis, Paphos and Perga
Each stop has a verse reference and one event (e.g. Lystra 14:8-19)
You can say where John Mark left them and why it matters later in Acts 15:37-39

t: Write your own lament modelled on Psalm 13
desc: Read Psalm 13 and mark its three movements: complaint (1-2), petition (3-4), and trust and praise (5-6). Write your own six-line lament about a real situation following the same shape.
check: Psalm 13's movements are marked by verse
Your lament has all three movements in order
You can name two other lament psalms (e.g. 22, 88) and how 88 differs
